lessons.title: Understand STIGs, SCAP and checklists
lessons.summary: A Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) is DISA's configuration standard for one product, and every scan and checklist in this course measures against one. Learn how a rule is identified, rated and traced to NIST SP 800-53, which rules a scanner can read and which a person must answer, then record which STIGs apply to each controller.
steps: Start with the two layers the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) publishes. A Security Requirements Guide (SRG) states requirements for a class of technology, such as general-purpose operating systems; a STIG turns them into checks and fixes for one product, so every STIG rule traces back to an SRG requirement.

Read a rule's identity and weight. Each rule has a Group ID (V-…), a Rule ID (SV-…r…_rule, where the r number is its revision), a STIG ID naming the product and check, and a severity category: CAT I (high) when exploiting the weakness directly and immediately causes loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability, CAT II (medium) when it has the potential to, and CAT III (low) when it degrades the protections against that loss.

Separate what a scanner can read from what a person must answer. A Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) benchmark is the automated part of a STIG — rules written in XCCDF with OVAL checks — which the SCAP Compliance Checker (SCC) evaluates on a host. Every other rule is a manual check, and STIG Viewer is where you build a checklist for each assessed asset, import SCC's results and record the human answers.

Trace rules to controls and keep a scan's limits honest. Each rule cites Control Correlation Identifiers (CCIs), DISA's single, actionable requirement statements, each mapped to a NIST SP 800-53 control, so a result can serve as control evidence. A scan shows settings on one host, at one moment, against one release: it can err or miss, it says nothing about procedures, and a pass is not an authorization.

Record what applies. These controllers take the Windows Server STIG (its domain controller rules included) plus the Active Directory Domain and Active Directory Forest STIGs. They also run DNS and Windows Defender Firewall, which have STIGs of their own — list those with an owner and a review date instead of dropping them silently.
lessons.command:
Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object CSName, Caption, Version
(Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem).DomainRole   # 5 = primary domain controller (holds the PDC emulator role), 4 = backup domain controller
Get-WindowsFeature AD-Domain-Services, DNS | Select-Object Name, InstallState
Get-ADForest | Select-Object Name, ForestMode, Domains
lessons.check: The applicability record lists each controller's operating system and roles, the STIGs that apply with the release you will measure against, and the later-scope STIGs with an owner and a review date.
lessons.evidence: Keep the applicability record: host, operating system, roles, each applicable STIG with its release, the later-scope STIGs with owner and date, and the command output behind each line.
objectives: Explain how SRGs, STIGs, SCAP benchmarks and CCIs relate.
Read a STIG rule's identifiers and severity category.
Record which STIGs apply to each controller, and what a scan can and cannot prove.

quizzes.question: What does a CAT I severity mean?
answers: The scanner checks the rule first
Exploiting the weakness directly and immediately results in loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability
The rule applies only to domain controllers
quizzes.explanation: DISA rates rules by consequence: CAT I is direct and immediate loss, CAT II the potential for loss, and CAT III degraded protection against it.

quizzes.question: Which part of a STIG can SCC evaluate on its own?
answers: The rules in the SCAP benchmark — XCCDF rules with OVAL checks that read the host's configuration
Every rule in every STIG
Only the CAT I rules
quizzes.explanation: The benchmark is the automatable part of the STIG. Manual rules, and whole STIGs such as the Active Directory ones, need a person in STIG Viewer.

quizzes.question: What does a CCI on a STIG rule give you?
answers: The rule's revision number
The scanner's confidence in its result
A traceable link from the rule to a NIST SP 800-53 control, so the result can serve as control evidence
quizzes.explanation: Each Control Correlation Identifier is one testable statement mapped to a NIST control. It is how a technical result reaches the authorization record.

recap: SRGs set requirements for a technology class; STIGs implement them for one product.
Every rule has its identifiers, a CAT severity, and CCIs that reach a NIST control.
SCC measures the benchmark, STIG Viewer holds the human answers, and neither is an authorization.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 carries the DISA content across the air gap: the tools, the benchmarks, the STIGs and the GPO package course 1.5 will import.

lessons.title: Stage the DISA content across the air gap
lessons.summary: Everything this course and the next one use is downloaded DISA content: the SCAP Compliance Checker (SCC), STIG Viewer, the SCAP benchmarks, the STIGs and the Group Policy object (GPO) package. It crosses the boundary the way everything does here — reviewed, hashed, and carried on approved removable media.
steps: On an approved connected system, download from DISA's Cyber Exchange: SCC for Windows and STIG Viewer 3 with their published checksums; the SCAP benchmarks for Windows Server and for the Windows client; the Windows Server, Windows client, Active Directory Domain and Active Directory Forest STIGs and the CCI list from the document library; and the current GPO package. The Windows client content waits for the Tier 2 seat in course 1.8 and the fleet in course 1.13, and the GPO package travels now so course 1.5 imports policies from the same quarterly release as the STIGs you measure; note each file's version and release.

Check SCC and STIG Viewer against DISA's published checksums, then hash every file with Get-FileHash into connected-side-hashes.csv, which travels with the media, and transfer the set with the approved removable-media procedure. No live link to the lab is created for convenience.

In the lab, at SBD-DC01's console, copy the files into C:\Staging\DISA and the hash list into C:\Evidence\baseline\transfer, and compare every hash before opening anything; repeat on SBD-DC02 with the same full set, so its comparison is one-to-one as well, although it needs only SCC and the Windows Server benchmark. A mismatch stops the work, exactly as it will in the course 1.6 signing ceremony.

Install SCC on both controllers and STIG Viewer on SBD-DC01, then install the Windows Server benchmark into SCC on each controller. Until course 1.8 builds AdminJumpBox01, administration happens at the controllers' consoles; course 1.8 then moves both tools there and removes them from the controllers. Record SCC's, STIG Viewer's, each benchmark's and each STIG's version, and leave the GPO package (for course 1.5) and the Windows client content hashed in C:\Staging\DISA.
lessons.command:
Get-ChildItem C:\Staging\DISA -File | Select-Object Name, Length, LastWriteTime
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\baseline\transfer -Force | Out-Null
Get-ChildItem C:\Staging\DISA -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\baseline\transfer\lab-side-hashes.csv -NoTypeInformation
# connected-side-hashes.csv came with the media; no output means every hash matches
Compare-Object (Import-Csv C:\Evidence\baseline\transfer\connected-side-hashes.csv).Hash (Import-Csv C:\Evidence\baseline\transfer\lab-side-hashes.csv).Hash
lessons.check: Every transferred file's hash matches the value recorded on the connected side on both controllers, SCC and STIG Viewer match DISA's published checksums, SCC runs on both controllers and STIG Viewer on SBD-DC01, and every version is written down.
lessons.evidence: Keep the transfer record in C:\Evidence\baseline\transfer on SBD-DC01: file names, versions and releases, both hash lists, the comparison result on each controller, media custody, and the date.

model.label: Get updates, step 1
model.text: The same controlled import, carrying update material to SBD-WSUS01: approved media across the air gap and no network session.

objectives: Identify the DISA artifacts this course and the courses after it need.
Move them across the air gap with hashes compared on both sides.
Record versions so scans stay comparable over time.

quizzes.question: Why hash the files on both sides of the transfer?
answers: To prove the same files arrived unaltered
To compress them for the media
Because SCC refuses unhashed input
quizzes.explanation: An independently recorded hash is how a human-controlled transfer proves integrity across the boundary.

quizzes.question: Which release cadence do the DISA GPO package and STIGs follow?
answers: Weekly
Quarterly
Only at new Windows releases
quizzes.explanation: DISA refreshes STIG content on a quarterly cycle, and course 1.5 sets its standing rescan cadence to follow it.

quizzes.question: A hash mismatch appears on the lab side. What now?
answers: Open the file and inspect it manually
Stop, set the media aside, and repeat the approved transfer
Regenerate hashes until they match
quizzes.explanation: A mismatch means the file is not the one that was reviewed. Unverified content never gets opened inside the boundary.

recap: SCC, STIG Viewer, the benchmarks, the STIGs and the GPO package come from DISA's Cyber Exchange.
Hashes are recorded on both sides of the boundary and compared on both controllers.
Versions are evidence, and the GPO package and client content wait, verified, for later courses.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 measures both controllers before anything is hardened.

lessons.title: Capture the pre-hardening baseline
lessons.summary: Measure before you change. A scan of the freshly built controllers shows the honest starting point, teaches what the operating system already secures by default, and becomes the before picture every later scan is compared against.
steps: On each controller's console, run SCC locally against the Windows Server STIG benchmark staged in lesson 2. DISA content offers several mission assurance category (MAC) and confidentiality profiles: use the one your direction calls for, the same on both controllers, and record it. Each scan is a dated session; note SCC's version and the benchmark's version and release with it.

Open the results and read, don't just count. Note which checks already pass: the newest Windows Server release ships with defaults such as required signing on outbound SMB connections and LDAP sealing on new deployments, so part of the STIG is green before you touch anything.

Separate the automated results from the manual checks. SCAP answers what a scanner can read; the manual rules, and any check that returned an error rather than a pass or a fail, go to STIG Viewer for a human answer in lesson 4.

Store the raw results unmodified, with recorded hashes: copy each session into C:\Evidence\baseline\<host name> and hash it, then carry SBD-DC02's set to the evidence folder on SBD-DC01, where its hashes must match again. The baseline is evidence; a cleaned-up copy is a summary, not the record.
lessons.command:
# On each controller, after its SCC scan. Adapt the path to SCC's results directory.
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\baseline -Force | Out-Null
$session = Get-ChildItem "$env:USERPROFILE\SCC\Sessions" -Directory | Sort-Object Name | Select-Object -Last 1
Copy-Item $session.FullName -Destination "C:\Evidence\baseline\$env:COMPUTERNAME" -Recurse
Get-ChildItem "C:\Evidence\baseline\$env:COMPUTERNAME" -Recurse -Filter '*XCCDF-Results*.xml' | Select-Object Name, LastWriteTime
Get-ChildItem "C:\Evidence\baseline\$env:COMPUTERNAME" -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv "C:\Evidence\baseline\$env:COMPUTERNAME-hashes.csv" -NoTypeInformation
# On SBD-DC02: carry its set to SBD-DC01. Then, on SBD-DC01, no output means the copy is identical.
Copy-Item C:\Evidence\baseline\SBD-DC02, C:\Evidence\baseline\SBD-DC02-hashes.csv -Destination '\\SBD-DC01\C$\Evidence\baseline\' -Recurse
Compare-Object (Import-Csv C:\Evidence\baseline\SBD-DC02-hashes.csv).Hash (Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\baseline\SBD-DC02 -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256).Hash
lessons.check: Both controllers have a dated baseline session from the same SCC version, benchmark release and profile; the already-compliant operating system defaults are noted; and both raw result sets sit hashed in C:\Evidence\baseline on SBD-DC01, with SBD-DC02's hashes matching after the copy.
lessons.evidence: Keep the per-host result sets and their hash lists in C:\Evidence\baseline, the SCC version, benchmark release and profile, and a short note of what the operating system defaults already covered.

model.label: SBD-DC01
model.text: The controller you scan first, with its services and the controls the model maps to it.

objectives: Run a SCAP baseline scan against both domain controllers.
Distinguish automated results from manual-review items.
Preserve raw results as evidence with hashes and versions.

quizzes.question: Why scan before applying any GPO?
answers: The scanner requires an unhardened system
A dated before record makes every later change measurable and attributable
Scanning after GPOs is not possible
quizzes.explanation: The baseline is the comparison point. Without it, course 1.5's rescan proves only a state, not what your hardening changed.

quizzes.question: Several checks pass before any hardening. What is the likely reason on the newest Windows Server release?
answers: The scanner is misconfigured
Earlier lessons secretly applied GPOs
The OS ships secure defaults, such as required SMB signing, that satisfy those checks
quizzes.explanation: The newest Windows Server release raised several security defaults, so a fresh build already meets part of the benchmark.

quizzes.question: What happens with checks the scanner marks for manual review?
answers: They are ignored as not applicable
They count as failures forever
A person answers them in STIG Viewer with recorded rationale
quizzes.explanation: SCAP automates what a scanner can read; manual checks need a reviewer's observed evidence to be defensible.

recap: The baseline is measured, dated, and stored unmodified.
Secure-by-default items are recognized, not claimed as your work.
Manual checks are queued for human review.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 builds the STIG Viewer checklists and answers what the scanner could not.

lessons.title: Build the checklists and answer the manual checks
lessons.summary: A scan answers only what it can read. In STIG Viewer on SBD-DC01, build a checklist for each controller and one for the directory, let the SCC results fill the automated rules, and answer every remaining rule with what you observed.
steps: On SBD-DC01, open STIG Viewer, add the staged STIGs to its library, and create three checklists: SBD-DC01 and SBD-DC02, each with the Windows Server STIG, and sbd.test with the Active Directory Domain and Active Directory Forest STIGs, whose rules assess the domain and the forest rather than one host. Fill in each controller's target data — host name, fully qualified domain name, address, and the domain controller role.

Import each controller's XCCDF results from C:\Evidence\baseline into its own checklist with Import XCCDF or CMRS Results, and record the import summary: rules matched, rules matched with a different revision, and rules not matched. A revision mismatch means the rule changed between the benchmark and the STIG release in the checklist, so align the releases or review those rules by hand — don't include loosely matched results blindly.

Work every rule still Not Reviewed — the manual checks, the whole sbd.test checklist, and anything the scan could not evaluate. Read the check text, look at the system, and set Open, Not A Finding, or Not Applicable. Write what you observed in Finding Details (the command or screen and what it showed) and the context in Comments (who reviewed, when, and any related decision).

Change an automated result only with evidence in Finding Details, and never lower a severity to improve the numbers: STIG Viewer requires an override reason because an assessor will read it. Save the checklists in STIG Viewer's CKLB format in C:\Evidence\baseline\checklists as SBD-DC01.cklb, SBD-DC02.cklb and sbd.test.cklb, then hash them.
lessons.check: All three checklists hold the intended STIG releases and target data, each import matched by exact revision or had its mismatches reviewed, no rule is left Not Reviewed, and every manual answer carries its observation in Finding Details.
lessons.evidence: Keep the three .cklb files with their hashes, each import's summary counts, the status counts per checklist, and any severity override with its reason.
objectives: Create checklists for both controllers and the directory from the staged STIG releases.
Import the SCC results and resolve any rules that do not match.
Answer every remaining rule with a status, finding details and comments.

quizzes.question: STIG Viewer's import reports rules that matched with a different revision. What does that tell you?
answers: The rule changed between the benchmark and the checklist's STIG release, so align the releases or review those rules by hand
The scanner found new vulnerabilities
Those rules passed
quizzes.explanation: Rule IDs carry a revision. A mismatch means the check text may have changed, so a loosely matched result could describe a different requirement.

quizzes.question: You checked a manual rule and found the controller compliant. What makes Not A Finding defensible?
answers: The green status icon
Finding details recording what you examined and what it showed, such as the command and its output
A comment that says 'checked'
quizzes.explanation: A status without an observation is an assertion. The recorded observation is what another reviewer or an assessor can repeat.

quizzes.question: Why do the Active Directory Domain and Forest STIGs get their own checklist, sbd.test, instead of one copy per controller?
answers: STIG Viewer allows each STIG in only one checklist
SBD-DC02 is a read-only domain controller
Their rules assess the domain and the forest the two controllers share, so one set of answers covers both
quizzes.explanation: Answering domain-wide rules twice invites two different answers to one question. The directory gets one checklist, and each controller's checklist holds its own host rules.

recap: Two controller checklists and one for the directory, built from the same release as the benchmark.
Automated results are imported by exact revision; a person answers the rest.
Every status carries its observation, and no rule is left Not Reviewed.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 turns the three checklists into the findings record course 1.5 works from.

lessons.title: Write the findings record for hardening
lessons.summary: A checklist full of statuses is not yet a decision. Turn the open items from all three checklists into one findings record — counted by severity, classified, owned, and traced from rule to CCI to NIST control — that course 1.5 can harden against and prove.
steps: Export the open rules from all three checklists into one findings record, C:\Evidence\baseline\findings\findings-record.csv, and count them per checklist by severity. Read the CAT I items first: their exploitation directly and immediately causes loss.

Classify every open item with one of three values. Fix by GPO: the DISA package sets it, so course 1.5's import should close it. Deviation candidate: the setting conflicts with a design decision — for example a rule expecting the PDC emulator to synchronize with an authorized external time source, where the course 1.3 design declares and checks its own clock — and course 1.5 decides and records it. POA&M candidate: the fix lies outside Group Policy, such as the PKI server certificate the STIG expects on every domain controller, which the course 1.6 PKI issues, so it needs an owner and a planned date — the start of a Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) entry.

Trace each finding to its controls. A rule's CCIs map to NIST SP 800-53 controls in DISA's CCI list, and STIG Viewer shows them with each rule — CCI-000366, for example, is implementing the security configuration settings under CM-6 — so the record tells an assessor which control each open item weakens.

Write the handoff course 1.5 works from as C:\Evidence\baseline\findings\handoff.txt: SCC's version, the benchmark release and profile, the STIG releases, the GPO package release waiting hashed in C:\Staging\DISA, and where the checklists and this record live. Then hash the whole folder into C:\Evidence\baseline-manifest.csv. Course 1.5 checks that manifest, rescans with exactly those versions into C:\Evidence\hardened, updates copies of the checklists there, and closes or records every item.
lessons.command:
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\baseline\findings -Force | Out-Null
$rows = foreach ($t in 'SBD-DC01', 'SBD-DC02', 'sbd.test') {
  $ckl = Get-Content "C:\Evidence\baseline\checklists\$t.cklb" -Raw -Encoding UTF8 | ConvertFrom-Json
  $ckl.stigs.rules | Where-Object status -eq 'open' | Select-Object @{n='Target';e={$t}}, @{n='GroupId';e={$_.group_id}}, @{n='StigId';e={$_.rule_version}}, @{n='Severity';e={$_.severity}}, @{n='CCIs';e={$_.ccis -join ' '}}, @{n='Title';e={$_.rule_title}}, Classification, Owner, TargetDate
}
$rows | Group-Object Target, Severity | Select-Object Name, Count
$rows | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\baseline\findings\findings-record.csv -NoTypeInformation
# After you fill in Classification, Owner and TargetDate and write handoff.txt, close the baseline:
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\baseline -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\baseline-manifest.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\baseline-manifest.csv
lessons.check: The findings record lists every open rule from the three checklists with target, severity and CCIs; each carries one of the three classifications and an owner, POA&M candidates also a planned date; the counts by severity are recorded; and handoff.txt and the manifest give course 1.5 every version, path and hash it reuses.
lessons.evidence: Keep findings-record.csv, the counts by severity per checklist, the CCI-to-control notes for the open items, handoff.txt, and C:\Evidence\baseline-manifest.csv with its own hash.
objectives: Count open findings per checklist by severity category.
Classify every open item as fix by GPO, deviation candidate, or POA&M candidate.
Trace findings to NIST SP 800-53 controls through their CCIs and hand the record to course 1.5.

quizzes.question: An open rule's setting is in the DISA GPO package. How is it classified?
answers: POA&M candidate
Fix by GPO — course 1.5's import should close it, and its rescan will prove it
Not Applicable
quizzes.explanation: If the package sets it, the fix is policy. The rescan with the same versions shows whether the import actually closed it.

quizzes.question: Why carry each finding's CCIs into the record?
answers: They trace the rule to the NIST SP 800-53 control it supports, so findings read as control evidence
STIG Viewer won't save a checklist without them
They set the finding's severity
quizzes.explanation: The CCI is the bridge between a configuration rule and a control. Without it, an assessor has to rebuild the trail from scratch.

quizzes.question: What must course 1.5 keep the same when it rescans?
answers: Only the host names
Nothing — newer content is always better
SCC's version, the benchmark release and the profile, so the comparison measures the hardening rather than a change of content
quizzes.explanation: A different measuring stick changes which checks exist and how they evaluate. Matched versions make every change attributable to a policy.

recap: Open items are counted by severity, CAT I first.
Every open item is fix by GPO, deviation candidate, or POA&M candidate, with an owner.
The record, the checklists, the versions and the manifest hand straight to course 1.5.

lessons.title: Design and build the OU structure
lessons.summary: Organizational units exist for delegation and Group Policy targeting, not to mirror an org chart. Build the structure the hardening policies will hang on before importing any of them.
objectives: Design an OU structure around delegation and Group Policy targeting.
Create protected OUs and redirect the default Computers and Users containers.
Explain why the built-in Domain Controllers OU stays untouched.
steps: Design the structure by administration: a top-level SBD OU containing Servers, Workstations, Users, Groups, and an Admin OU for privileged accounts. The built-in Domain Controllers OU stays where it is and keeps its name.
Create the planned OUs with accidental-deletion protection enabled. Record each OU's purpose and who will administer its contents; an OU with no delegation or policy purpose is clutter.

Redirect the default containers with redircmp and redirusr: new computer accounts to the Workstations OU and new user accounts to the Users OU. Group Policy cannot be linked to the default containers, so anything landing there would get only domain-level policy, never the OU-linked hardening. Join servers straight into the Servers OU with Add-Computer -OUPath, so they never pass through the workstation policies.

Keep privileged accounts and systems separate: the Admin OU holds the identities that administer the domain controllers. The domain-joined PKI servers from course 1.6 and SBD-DHCP01 from course 1.7 join the Servers OU, and course 1.8 adds a Tier 0 Servers OU and the admin seats' sub-OUs. Do not nest deeper than the delegation plan requires.
lessons.command:
New-ADOrganizationalUnit -Name SBD -Path 'DC=sbd,DC=test' -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion $true
'Servers', 'Workstations', 'Users', 'Groups', 'Admin' | ForEach-Object { New-ADOrganizationalUnit -Name $_ -Path 'OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion $true }
redircmp 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test'
redirusr 'OU=Users,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test'
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\hardened -Force | Out-Null
Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter * -Properties ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion | Select-Object Name, DistinguishedName, ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\hardened\ou-design.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object ComputersContainer, UsersContainer
Get-ADDomainController -Filter * | Select-Object Name, ComputerObjectDN
lessons.check: The planned OUs exist with deletion protection, the computer and user redirects point at the Workstations and Users OUs, both controllers are still in the Domain Controllers OU, and each OU has a recorded purpose and administrator.
lessons.evidence: Keep the OU design sheet: each OU's distinguished name, purpose and delegated administrator, the ou-design.csv export in C:\Evidence\hardened, and the redirect commands with their output.

quizzes.question: What should drive the shape of the OU structure?
answers: Group Policy targeting and delegated administration
The company org chart
Alphabetical order of departments
quizzes.explanation: OUs are an administrative tool. Policy and delegation boundaries define them; reporting lines belong in HR systems.

quizzes.question: Why redirect the default Computers container?
answers: It makes domain join faster
Group Policy cannot be linked to the default containers, so new machines would miss the OU-linked hardening
It is required before DNS works
quizzes.explanation: Redirection sends newly joined machines into an OU where policy applies from their first start.

quizzes.question: Where do the two domain controllers live after this lesson?
answers: In the new Servers OU
In the built-in Domain Controllers OU, unchanged
In the Users container
quizzes.explanation: Domain controllers stay in their built-in OU — it is where the DC hardening policies link in lesson 3.

recap: OUs follow administration, not the org chart.
The default containers are redirected so nothing joins unmanaged.
The Domain Controllers OU remains the link point for DC policies.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 explains how Group Policy decides what applies, before you link anything to these OUs.

lessons.title: Learn how Group Policy applies
lessons.summary: Before the DISA settings arrive, learn how a computer decides which Group Policy objects (GPOs) apply and which setting wins. Map the order, build the central store the import will use, and record what both controllers apply today.
objectives: Predict which GPO wins from processing order, link order, inheritance, Enforced and Block Inheritance.
Explain how security filtering, WMI filters and loopback processing change a GPO's reach.
Build the central store and record each controller's starting policy with gpresult.
steps: Know where a GPO lives. Its settings sit in two halves — a container object in Active Directory and a template folder in SYSVOL — and they replicate separately, by directory replication and by DFS Replication. A change made on SBD-DC01 therefore reaches SBD-DC02 in two steps: before you judge a result there, check that the GPO's AD and SYSVOL version numbers agree.

Learn the order. Policy applies local first, then site, domain and OU, parent OU before child, so the GPO linked closest to the computer is applied last and wins a conflict; at one OU, link order 1 is processed last and wins. Different settings add up across GPOs, but a single setting's values generally don't merge: the highest-precedence GPO that configures it wins, so a user-rights list in one GPO replaces another's instead of adding to it.

Treat the two overrides as exceptions. Block Inheritance on an OU stops GPOs linked above it; Enforced on a link makes that GPO win over everything below it and pierces Block Inheritance. Enforced is not a shortcut — it hides a precedence problem instead of solving it — so this network uses neither unless the exception record says why.

Read what narrows a GPO's reach. Security filtering applies it only to accounts with both Read and Apply group policy (Authenticated Users by default), and computers still need Read on GPOs that apply only to users, because user policy is read in the computer's security context; a WMI filter applies it only where its query is true. Loopback processing gives anyone who signs in to a computer the user settings from that computer's GPOs — merge adds them after the user's own, replace uses only the computer's — so use it only where the computer should decide; lesson 3 meets the one place this course needs it.

Know when policy arrives, and build the central store. Members refresh in the background every 90 minutes with a random offset of up to 30, controllers every five minutes, and gpupdate /force reapplies everything at once, though some extensions run only at startup or sign-in. On SBD-DC01, copy C:\Windows\PolicyDefinitions with its en-US folder to \\sbd.test\SYSVOL\sbd.test\Policies\PolicyDefinitions: from then on, every Group Policy editor in the domain uses these templates instead of its local ones.

Record the starting state before anything is imported. On both controllers, save a gpresult report of the Resultant Set of Policy (RSoP), what actually applied: the Default Domain Policy and the Default Domain Controllers Policy should be the only domain GPOs listed. Read the applied and filtered-out lists — the reasons gpresult gives, such as a security denial or a false WMI filter, are how you will troubleshoot the import.
lessons.command:
# Once, on SBD-DC01: create the central store from the controller's own templates
Copy-Item C:\Windows\PolicyDefinitions -Destination \\sbd.test\SYSVOL\sbd.test\Policies\PolicyDefinitions -Recurse
# On SBD-DC01: links in precedence order, and each GPO's AD and SYSVOL versions
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'DC=sbd,DC=test'
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Domain Controllers,DC=sbd,DC=test'
foreach ($dc in 'SBD-DC01', 'SBD-DC02') { Get-GPO -All -Server $dc | Select-Object @{n='DC';e={$dc}}, DisplayName, GpoStatus, @{n='AD';e={$_.Computer.DSVersion}}, @{n='SYSVOL';e={$_.Computer.SysvolVersion}} }
# On each controller's console; carry SBD-DC02's report to the same folder on SBD-DC01
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\hardened\policy-before -Force | Out-Null
gpresult /r /scope:computer
gpresult /h "C:\Evidence\hardened\policy-before\$env:COMPUTERNAME-gpresult.html" /f
lessons.check: You can list both controllers' GPOs in precedence order and say why each applies, nothing is Enforced or blocked, every GPO's AD and SYSVOL versions agree, the central store holds SBD-DC01's templates, and each controller's starting gpresult report is saved.
lessons.evidence: Keep both starting gpresult reports in C:\Evidence\hardened\policy-before, the inheritance output for the domain and the Domain Controllers OU, the GPO version listing, and a note of the central store's source and date.

model.label: SBD-DC01
model.text: Its service list includes Group Policy and SYSVOL over SMB 445: the path every domain member uses to read the GPOs whose order this lesson explains.

quizzes.question: A GPO linked at the domain and a GPO linked to the Domain Controllers OU configure the same administrative template setting differently, and neither link is Enforced. Which value does a controller end up with?
answers: The domain GPO's, because the domain is the higher level
Whichever GPO was edited last
The Domain Controllers OU GPO's, because it is applied after the domain's
quizzes.explanation: Local, site, domain, then OU: the GPO linked closest to the computer is applied last and wins, unless a link above it is Enforced.

quizzes.question: A setting doesn't take effect on a controller. Why is setting the link to Enforced a poor fix?
answers: It hides the precedence problem instead of explaining it, and makes the next conflict harder to trace
Domain controllers ignore Enforced links
Enforced removes the GPO's security filtering
quizzes.explanation: Enforced makes a GPO win over everything below it and pierces Block Inheritance. Find out why the setting lost — link order, filtering, or a closer GPO — and fix that instead.

quizzes.question: Someone removes Authenticated Users from a user-settings GPO's security filtering and adds a group of users. Now its settings reach none of them. What is missing?
answers: A WMI filter
Read permission for the computers, because user policy is read in the computer's security context
Loopback processing in replace mode
quizzes.explanation: Since security update MS16-072, Windows reads user policy in the computer's context. Give computers Read — through Authenticated Users or Domain Computers — while only the user group keeps Apply group policy.

recap: The closest link applies last and wins; at one OU, link order 1 wins.
Enforced and Block Inheritance are exceptions to record, not tools to reach for.
gpresult shows what actually applied, and why the rest was filtered out.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 imports the DISA policies course 1.4 staged and links them where they belong.

lessons.title: Import and link the DISA GPOs
lessons.summary: Group Policy is how the STIG becomes configuration. Import the package course 1.4 staged, link each policy where its systems live so the findings marked fix by GPO can close, and keep the lab's deliberate deviations written down rather than silently skipped.
objectives: Verify the staged package and add its templates to the central store.
Import DISA's policies and link them by OU, with account policies at the domain root.
Handle lab-specific deviations with documentation instead of silent edits.
steps: Start from course 1.4's handoff. Read the package release in C:\Evidence\baseline\findings\handoff.txt, confirm the package in C:\Staging\DISA still matches its connected-side hash, and only then extract it. Copy its ADMX files and their en-US ADML files into the central store from lesson 2, without replacing a newer Microsoft template with an older copy of the same file.

Import each policy this network uses into a new GPO with the GPMC Import Settings wizard or Import-GPO: the Windows Server domain controller, member server and user policies, and the Windows client policies for your fleet's release, which stay unlinked until courses 1.8 and 1.13 link them. Keep DISA's names behind an SBD prefix so the source release stays identifiable. An import replaces every setting in the target GPO and brings no links, security filtering or WMI filter. Where the package's user-rights settings name placeholder groups such as ADD YOUR DOMAIN ADMINS, map them to sbd.test's real groups with a migration table — check the package's support files for one before building your own in GPMC's Migration Table Editor.

Link by OU. Link the domain controller policy to the Domain Controllers OU at link order 1, above the Default Domain Controllers Policy, and the member-server policy to the Servers OU, so the systems later courses build there are hardened from first boot. Domain controllers read password, lockout and Kerberos policy only from GPOs linked at the domain root: if the package carries account policies, set those values in a GPO linked there above the Default Domain Policy, because at an OU they do nothing for domain accounts. Use neither Enforced nor Block Inheritance.

Apply the user policy where people sign in. Its settings belong to every session on a hardened server, whoever signs in — an administrator from the Admin OU, or the built-in Administrator in the default Users container, where no GPO can link. So link the DISA user policy to the Domain Controllers and Servers OUs and, in a small GPO linked to both, enable Configure user Group Policy loopback processing mode set to Merge. Record that decision — it is the only loopback this course uses — and compare it with the package's own instructions for its user policy.

Walk the settings that need a decision in this network — anything that assumes infrastructure the lab does not have or conflicts with an earlier design — and record each deviation with its rationale instead of deleting the setting. Check each fix-by-GPO item in course 1.4's findings record against the imported settings, so you know which ones the rescan should show closed. Then, once SBD-DC02 shows the same GPO versions, refresh policy on both controllers and confirm with gpresult that the SBD DISA GPOs apply and that replication still succeeds both ways. Finally, confirm the course 1.3 time design is intact with no time setting from Group Policy: w32tm /query /configuration must show no (Policy) value, and any Windows Time Service setting an imported GPO carries goes back to Not Configured, with the change recorded.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-DC01. True means the package matches the hash recorded on the connected side.
$package = Get-ChildItem C:\Staging\DISA -Filter '*GPO*.zip' | Select-Object -First 1
(Get-FileHash $package.FullName -Algorithm SHA256).Hash -in (Import-Csv C:\Evidence\baseline\transfer\connected-side-hashes.csv).Hash
Expand-Archive $package.FullName -DestinationPath C:\Staging\GPO
# Per policy; take the exact names and folders from the package:
Import-GPO -BackupGpoName '<DISA GPO name>' -TargetName 'SBD <DISA GPO name>' -Path '<package GPOs folder>' -MigrationTable '<migration table>' -CreateIfNeeded
New-GPLink -Name 'SBD <DISA domain controller GPO name>' -Target 'OU=Domain Controllers,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Order 1
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Domain Controllers,DC=sbd,DC=test'
# On each controller's console; carry SBD-DC02's report to SBD-DC01:
gpupdate /force
gpresult /r /scope:computer
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\hardened\import -Force | Out-Null
gpresult /h "C:\Evidence\hardened\import\$env:COMPUTERNAME-gpresult.html" /f
w32tm /query /source   # SBD-DC01: Local CMOS Clock; SBD-DC02: a domain controller
w32tm /query /configuration | Select-String '\(Policy\)'   # expected: no output, so no time setting comes from Group Policy
repadmin /replsummary
lessons.check: The package matched its connected-side hash, the central store serves its templates, placeholder groups map to real ones, the links follow the OU design with the domain controller policy at link order 1 and nothing Enforced or blocked, gpresult on both controllers lists the SBD DISA GPOs as applied, time and replication are unchanged with no time setting from Group Policy, and every deviation has a written reason and owner.
lessons.evidence: Keep the import record — package release and hash check, each GPO's name and source, the migration table, the links with their order, the loopback decision, and both gpresult reports in C:\Evidence\hardened\import — and the deviation list with rationale and owner.

model.label: Sign in, step 4
model.text: After sign-in, members read Group Policy over LDAP and SMB from SYSVOL. That is how the GPOs you link reach every machine.

quizzes.question: Why does the OU work from lesson 1 matter here?
answers: GPOs link to OUs, so the structure decides which systems receive which hardening
OUs make the GPO files smaller
DISA requires an OU named DISA
quizzes.explanation: Policy targeting is the OU structure's whole job: domain-controller policies to the Domain Controllers OU, server policies to the Servers OU.

quizzes.question: Where do the ADMX templates go so every domain controller's editor agrees?
answers: Each administrator's desktop
The Group Policy central store in SYSVOL
The offline root CA
quizzes.explanation: The central store replicates with SYSVOL, so every Group Policy editor in the domain reads the same definitions.

quizzes.question: A STIG setting assumes infrastructure the lab doesn't have. What is the right move?
answers: Delete the setting from the GPO quietly
Mark the whole package not applicable
Record a deviation with rationale and keep it visible for the assessment
quizzes.explanation: Documented deviations keep the hardening honest. A silent edit hides a decision an assessor will later need to see.

recap: The central store keeps policy definitions consistent across controllers.
Links follow the OU design; account policies live at the domain root.
Deviations are documented decisions, not deletions.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 rescans with course 1.4's versions to prove what the policies changed.

lessons.title: Rescan, reconcile, and record
lessons.summary: The second scan is the verdict. Rescan with exactly the versions course 1.4 used, compare each controller with its own baseline, update copies of the course 1.4 checklists, and give every remaining open item an answer.
objectives: Rescan with course 1.4's SCC version, benchmark release and profile, and compare against the baseline.
Update copies of the course 1.4 checklists and re-answer what the policies changed.
Close or classify every item in the findings record.
steps: Check that the baseline is untouched: the hash of C:\Evidence\baseline-manifest.csv must match the one course 1.4 recorded, and every file in C:\Evidence\baseline must still match the manifest. Read handoff.txt, confirm SCC and the benchmark on each controller are still those versions, and rescan both controllers locally with the same profile. Changing anything between scans makes the comparison meaningless.

Copy each new session into C:\Evidence\hardened\<host name> and hash it, and carry SBD-DC02's set to SBD-DC01 as in course 1.4. Compare each controller with its own baseline: which rules moved from open to pass, which stayed open, and whether any regressed. Attribute each change to the GPO that caused it — the gpresult report names the winning GPO for every setting.

Copy the three checklists from C:\Evidence\baseline\checklists into C:\Evidence\hardened\checklists and open only the copies in STIG Viewer, so nothing it saves can touch the baseline. Import each controller's new XCCDF results into its copy — with the benchmark and the checklist's STIG release unchanged, the import summary should match course 1.4's — then revisit every manual answer the policies may have changed, sbd.test's included, updating Finding Details and Comments with what you observed and when. Save and hash the copies; the baseline checklists stay exactly as hashed.

Work through the findings record. Every fix-by-GPO item should now be closed; if one isn't, find out why — the GPO didn't apply, a closer GPO won, or the setting needs the domain root or a restart. Work in a copy, C:\Evidence\hardened\findings\findings-record.csv: give each item a Resolution — closed by GPO, deviation (for lesson 5's exception record) or POA&M candidate (Plan of Action and Milestones), with its owner and date — and the Evidence that shows it. Treat any new open item as a finding to fix or classify.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-DC01: the manifest's hash must match course 1.4's record; no Compare-Object output means no baseline file changed
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\baseline-manifest.csv
Compare-Object (Import-Csv C:\Evidence\baseline-manifest.csv).Hash (Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\baseline -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256).Hash
Get-Content C:\Evidence\baseline\findings\handoff.txt   # the SCC version, benchmark release and profile to reuse
# On each controller, after its SCC rescan (adapt the path to SCC's results directory); SBD-DC02 then copies its set to SBD-DC01
$session = Get-ChildItem "$env:USERPROFILE\SCC\Sessions" -Directory | Sort-Object Name | Select-Object -Last 1
Copy-Item $session.FullName -Destination "C:\Evidence\hardened\$env:COMPUTERNAME" -Recurse
Get-ChildItem "C:\Evidence\hardened\$env:COMPUTERNAME" -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv "C:\Evidence\hardened\$env:COMPUTERNAME-hashes.csv" -NoTypeInformation
Copy-Item C:\Evidence\hardened\SBD-DC02, C:\Evidence\hardened\SBD-DC02-hashes.csv -Destination '\\SBD-DC01\C$\Evidence\hardened\' -Recurse   # on SBD-DC02
# On SBD-DC01: verify the copy, then list each changed rule twice, <= its baseline result and => its result now
Compare-Object (Import-Csv C:\Evidence\hardened\SBD-DC02-hashes.csv).Hash (Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\hardened\SBD-DC02 -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256).Hash
function Read-Xccdf($dir) { Get-ChildItem $dir -Recurse -Filter '*XCCDF-Results*.xml' | Select-Xml -XPath "//*[local-name()='rule-result']" | ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{ Rule = $_.Node.idref; Result = $_.Node.result } } }
foreach ($h in 'SBD-DC01', 'SBD-DC02') { Compare-Object (Read-Xccdf "C:\Evidence\baseline\$h") (Read-Xccdf "C:\Evidence\hardened\$h") -Property Rule, Result | Sort-Object Rule | Export-Csv "C:\Evidence\hardened\$h-changes.csv" -NoTypeInformation }
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\hardened\checklists, C:\Evidence\hardened\findings -Force | Out-Null
Copy-Item C:\Evidence\baseline\checklists\*.cklb C:\Evidence\hardened\checklists
Import-Csv C:\Evidence\baseline\findings\findings-record.csv | Select-Object *, Resolution, Evidence | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\hardened\findings\findings-record.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\hardened\checklists -Filter *.cklb | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\hardened\checklists-hashes.csv -NoTypeInformation   # after the STIG Viewer updates
lessons.check: The manifest hash matched and no baseline file changed, both rescans used the SCC version, benchmark release and profile in handoff.txt, each controller's changes are listed and attributed, the checklist copies carry the new results and re-checked answers while the baseline copies keep their hashes, and every findings-record item has a resolution.
lessons.evidence: Keep both rescan sessions with their hash lists, the two change lists, the updated checklist copies with their hashes, and the findings record with a resolution and evidence for every item, all in C:\Evidence\hardened.

quizzes.question: Why keep the same benchmark and SCC versions for the rescan?
answers: Newer versions cost more
Results are only comparable when the measuring stick didn't change
DISA forbids upgrading mid-quarter
quizzes.explanation: A version change alters which checks exist and how they evaluate, so the before/after comparison would mix causes.

quizzes.question: A check is still open and the lab intends to leave it that way, with a reason. What is that called?
answers: A false positive
A passing result
A documented deviation — and possibly, later, a POA&M entry
quizzes.explanation: An intentional, justified open item is a deviation; one that will be fixed on a plan becomes a POA&M entry in the authorization path.

quizzes.question: What makes a checklist entry for a manual check defensible?
answers: The reviewer's observed evidence and rationale are recorded with it
The box is checked
It was green in the automated scan
quizzes.explanation: A manual answer without recorded evidence is an assertion. The observation is what an assessor can verify.

recap: Same versions, honest comparison.
Copies of the checklists carry the new results; the baseline stays sealed.
Open items end the lesson classified, never mysterious.
lessons.next: The final lesson turns this into a standing practice with an exception record, owners and triggers.

lessons.title: Set the rescan cadence and exception record
lessons.summary: Hardening is a state you maintain, not a step you finish. Close the course with an owned exception record and a recorded policy state — reports and links, while course 1.19 backs the GPOs up — and decide who rescans, when, and which event forces an early look.
objectives: Consolidate deviations into an owned, dated exception record.
Define the quarterly and event-driven rescan cadence.
Export the applied policy state — reports and links — as evidence, leaving the GPO backup to course 1.19.
steps: Consolidate the deviations from lesson 3 and the items lesson 4 resolved as deviations into one exception record, C:\Evidence\exception-record.csv — rule, setting, reason, compensating measure, risk note, owner and review date — and file a dated copy in C:\Evidence\hardened. Course 1.4's example belongs here — the rule expecting the PDC emulator to synchronize with an authorized external time source, which the course 1.3 design answers with a declared, checked clock. It stays a living record outside the sealed folder: later courses add their entries to it, and it travels into the authorization path as part of the Body of Evidence.

Set the standing cadence: review each quarterly DISA release for applicable updates, and rescan after any role addition or significant configuration change — course 1.6's closing rescan of both controllers, once its certificates and autoenrollment policy reach them, is the first change-driven run. When you adopt a new release, scan once with the new content before changing any policy, so the record separates what the content changed from what your policies changed.

Export the Group Policy reports and each GPO link into C:\Evidence\hardened: the reports make the applied policy state reviewable without a live console, and the link export records where each policy applies — the part a GPO backup never restores, since it brings back settings and permissions, not links. The backup itself belongs to course 1.19, which defines and schedules the backup of every GPO with the rest of the recovery set, so this course sets up no backup job.

Write the handoff a future administrator or assessor would need — where the evidence lives, which versions produced it, and what is intentionally open — and hash C:\Evidence\hardened into C:\Evidence\hardened-manifest.csv. Course 1.8 later moves SCC and STIG Viewer to AdminJumpBox01 and links these policies to the admin seats' OUs; until then the cadence runs at the controllers' consoles.
lessons.command:
# Seed the exception record from the findings resolved as deviations; add lesson 3's deviations and fill in every column
Import-Csv C:\Evidence\hardened\findings\findings-record.csv | Where-Object Resolution -eq 'deviation' | Select-Object Target, GroupId, StigId, Title, Setting, Reason, CompensatingMeasure, RiskNote, Owner, ReviewDate | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\exception-record.csv -NoTypeInformation -NoClobber
Copy-Item C:\Evidence\exception-record.csv "C:\Evidence\hardened\exception-record-$(Get-Date -Format yyyy-MM-dd).csv"   # once it is complete
# The applied state as records; course 1.19 schedules the GPO backup itself
Get-GPOReport -All -ReportType Html -Path C:\Evidence\hardened\gpo-report.html
'DC=sbd,DC=test', 'OU=Domain Controllers,DC=sbd,DC=test', 'OU=Servers,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' | ForEach-Object { (Get-GPInheritance -Target $_).GpoLinks } | Select-Object Target, Order, DisplayName, Enabled, Enforced | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\hardened\gpo-links.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\hardened -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\hardened-manifest.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\hardened-manifest.csv
lessons.check: The exception record has owners, compensating measures and review dates, with a dated copy filed, the GPO reports and link export are filed, the evidence folder is sealed in the manifest with its own hash recorded, and the rescan triggers are written where course 1.6 will meet them.
lessons.evidence: Finish the hardening checklist: the living exception record in C:\Evidence and its dated copy, the GPO report and link export, C:\Evidence\hardened-manifest.csv with its own hash, the cadence, and the named owner of the next review.

model.label: Offline backup facility
model.text: Where course 1.19 carries the recovery set, including the GPO backup it schedules, under media custody.

quizzes.question: What triggers a rescan before the next quarterly cycle?
answers: Only a calendar reminder
A role addition or significant configuration change
Nothing — quarterly is the only trigger
quizzes.explanation: Change is the other trigger. Course 1.6 ends with exactly such a rescan of the domain controllers it changed, and the build courses after it rescan what they change.

quizzes.question: Why export the GPO reports and links into the evidence?
answers: It makes gpupdate run faster
DISA requires reports inside SYSVOL
The applied policy state becomes reviewable without a live console, and the links are recorded — a GPO backup doesn't restore them
quizzes.explanation: Reports and the link export let anyone — including a future you — verify the applied state without trusting memory. With the GPO backup course 1.19 schedules, they also make it restorable, links included.

quizzes.question: Where does the exception list end up in the bigger arc?
answers: It is deleted after the course
In the Body of Evidence the authorization path organizes and assesses
Inside the offline root CA
quizzes.explanation: Deviations and POA&M candidates are authorization-package material; course 2.2 shows how artifacts like this list join the Body of Evidence.

recap: Exceptions have owners and review dates.
Rescans follow the DISA quarter and every meaningful change.
The applied GPO state is reported, its links exported, and both hashed; course 1.19 backs the GPOs up.
lessons.next: That completes Harden with Group Policy. Course 1.6 builds the two-tier PKI on this hardened base: its domain-joined servers join the Servers OU, where the member-server policies already apply, and its closing rescan of the controllers is this cadence's first change-driven run.

prerequisites: Complete courses 1.1–1.5: both domain controllers healthy and replicating, DNS (course 1.2) with the pki.sbd.test alias reserved, the domain time hierarchy (course 1.3), course 1.4's DISA media set and baseline method, and course 1.5's OU structure, member-server policies and exception record; verify domain health and internal name resolution.

Prepare separate Windows Server hosts: SBD-ROOTCA01, a disconnected workgroup machine in the offline vault, and two virtual machines with the hypervisor's time synchronization off, taking their time from the domain: SBD-SUBCA01 (10.0.30.20) joined to sbd.test, and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 (10.0.30.30) as a hardened member server, both joined straight into the Servers OU (course 1.8 moves them, with their administration, to a Tier 0 Servers OU).

Approve the CA names, cryptography, validity periods, publication URLs, administration, backups, and removable-media procedure before installation; confirm the network's service-path register permits HTTP to pki.sbd.test (rule F18) and carries a row for certificate enrollment from the domain controllers to SBD-SUBCA01, which lesson 10 relies on.
labNote: This course builds the whole PKI: a standalone offline Root CA, an enterprise subordinate/issuing CA, the pki.sbd.test publication site on SBD-PKI-MGMT01, template administration on its own seat, and certificates for both domain controllers. The root stays disconnected; approved removable media carries requests and public artifacts, and its clock is set from the approved reference at every session. Until course 1.8 builds AdminJumpBox01, work at each server's own console. Publication stays plain HTTP by design — clients must be able to fetch revocation data before they can validate any certificate.

Microsoft · Publish trust data and validate clients
NIST · SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5, Recommendation for key management
