lessons.title: Design the two-tier trust hierarchy
lessons.summary: The root establishes trust. The subordinate, also called the issuing CA in this design, handles approved end-entity certificates. Keeping these roles separate protects the root from daily network exposure.
steps: Draw the hierarchy: offline standalone root → enterprise issuing CA → approved server/client certificates. There is no network connection to the root.

Record final host and CA names, key provider, algorithm, key sizes, hashes, validity periods, renewal owners, and recovery arrangements. Start from this lab's example values in the next step and change any that your own policy requires: they are examples, not universal requirements.

Example values for this lab: the root CA uses an RSA 4096 key with SHA-256 and a 20-year certificate, and publishes a base CRL every 26 weeks with an overlap period and no delta CRL, refreshed at each offline ceremony. The issuing CA uses RSA 4096 (3072 at minimum) with SHA-256 and a 10-year certificate, a weekly base CRL, and a daily delta CRL. End-entity certificates last one to two years. NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 rates RSA 2048 at 112 bits of security, which it accepts for new signatures only through 2030, so a CA that will still be signing after 2030 uses at least 3072 bits (128 bits of security); the newest Windows Server release requires at least 2,048-bit RSA for TLS server authentication.

Know where each value is set. You choose the key, the hash, and the root's 20-year validity in the AD CS Configuration wizard. Each CA's CAPolicy.inf sets its CRL periods (CRLPeriod, CRLPeriodUnits, CRLDeltaPeriod, CRLDeltaPeriodUnits), which certutil -setreg can change later. The issuing CA's 10-year lifetime is set on the root (CA\ValidityPeriod and CA\ValidityPeriodUnits) before the signing ceremony, because a subordinate CA's lifetime comes from the CA that signs it.

Plan a stable internal publication name such as pki.sbd.test. The Authority Information Access (AIA) location supplies issuer certificates; the CRL Distribution Point (CDP) supplies certificate revocation lists.

Choose the publication host, paths, access rules, and refresh schedule before issuing certificates. Clients inside this air-gapped network must reach those locations without relying on the public internet.
lessons.command:
# Run on the future issuing CA, not the offline root.
Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object Name, Domain, PartOfDomain
Resolve-DnsName SBD-DC01.sbd.test
Resolve-DnsName SBD-DC02.sbd.test
lessons.check: The written plan separates trust, issuance, publication, and administration. It identifies who renews CRLs before they expire, and every key size, hash, lifetime, and CRL period has a recorded value and the setting that applies it.
lessons.evidence: Keep the approved hierarchy, the cryptography and lifetime table with the setting that applies each value, and a worksheet mapping every certificate/CRL URL to its actual publisher and file.

model.label: Offline trust
model.text: The root stays outside the live network; signing material is carried to it by hand and the results are carried back.

objectives: Explain why the root stays offline while the issuing CA handles enrollment.
Record the CA identities, cryptography, lifetimes, and CRL periods before installation, starting from this lab's example values.
Plan AIA and CDP publication locations that clients can reach inside the air gap.

quizzes.question: Which role issues routine server certificates in this design?
answers: The offline root for every request
The enterprise issuing CA
The DNS server
quizzes.explanation: The issuing CA handles end-entity enrollment while the offline root signs the approved subordinate CA certificate.

quizzes.question: What do the AIA and CDP locations supply?
answers: Private keys for backup
DNS zone transfers
Issuer certificates and certificate revocation lists
quizzes.explanation: Authority Information Access serves issuer certificates; CRL Distribution Points serve revocation lists. Clients must be able to reach both.

quizzes.question: Why is pki.sbd.test planned before any CA is installed?
answers: Issued certificates embed these URLs, so the publication name must be stable first
The root cannot be installed without it
DNS requires a CNAME before zones replicate
quizzes.explanation: Certificates keep the extensions they were issued with. A stable publication name avoids reissuing everything later.

quizzes.question: In this lab, where is the issuing CA's 10-year certificate lifetime set?
answers: In the issuing CA's own CAPolicy.inf
On the offline root, with CA\ValidityPeriod and CA\ValidityPeriodUnits, before the signing ceremony
In the certificate template for web servers
quizzes.explanation: A subordinate CA's lifetime is set by the CA that signs it. The root's issued-certificate validity settings decide how long the issuing CA's certificate lasts, so they are set and verified before the ceremony.

recap: Trust, issuance, publication, and administration are separated in writing.
Cryptography, names, lifetimes, and CRL periods are approved before installation, starting from this lab's example values.
CRL renewal has a named owner and a date.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 performs the controlled offline root installation.

lessons.title: Configure the offline Root CA
lessons.summary: Treat root installation as a controlled event. Its private key is the highest-value secret in the hierarchy, and its configuration shapes the subordinate certificate it will sign.
steps: Verify SBD-ROOTCA01 is in a workgroup with no active network path. Prepare approved installation media, protected administration, and backup storage, and set its clock from the approved reference that course 1.3 names, recording both readings: no network will ever correct this clock.

Place the reviewed CAPolicy.inf in %SystemRoot% before configuration. Tailor it to the root role: in this lab it sets CRLPeriod=Weeks and CRLPeriodUnits=26, and CRLDeltaPeriodUnits=0 so the root publishes no delta CRL. A self-signed root's own CDP/AIA choices differ from the extensions the root places into issued subordinate certificates.

Install the Certification Authority role with management tools. In the AD CS Configuration wizard choose Standalone CA, Root CA, and a new private key, then apply the approved provider, cryptography (RSA 4096 with SHA-256 in this lab), CA name, validity (20 years), database, and log settings.

Before signing anything, configure the root's issued-certificate AIA/CDP settings, the subordinate validity policy (CA\ValidityPeriod Years and CA\ValidityPeriodUnits 10 in this lab), and the base-CRL schedule (26 weeks with an overlap period, and no delta CRL). Hold requests for explicit approval. Produce and inspect a current root CRL, then capture a protected CA backup — a build-time step that stays inside this ceremony, and which course 1.19 accounts for in its recovery set without ever bringing it onto the network.
lessons.command:
# Inspect locally on SBD-ROOTCA01 during the approved root session.
Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object Name, Domain, PartOfDomain
Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff K'   # read against the approved reference; log both readings
Get-Service CertSvc
certutil -getreg CA\CRLPublicationURLs
certutil -getreg CA\CACertPublicationURLs
certutil -getreg CA\ValidityPeriodUnits
certutil -getreg CA\CRLPeriodUnits
lessons.check: The host remains disconnected, its clock matches the approved reference, the CA is standalone/root, requests require approval, and the planned subordinate URLs and 10-year subordinate validity are configured before signing.
lessons.evidence: Record the root certificate identity, policy file, publication settings, CRL dates, backup location, the clock check, and operator sign-off. Protect backups containing private keys.
objectives: Verify the disconnected workgroup host before installing the role.
Install a standalone root CA with the approved CAPolicy.inf and settings.
Configure publication URLs and the CRL schedule before signing anything.

quizzes.question: When must the root's issued-certificate publication URLs be configured?
answers: After clients have enrolled
Only after the first CRL expires
Before signing the subordinate CA certificate
quizzes.explanation: Issued certificates retain their extensions. Changing the CA configuration later does not rewrite existing certificates.

quizzes.question: Why is the root a standalone CA rather than an enterprise CA?
answers: Standalone CAs use stronger cryptography
It is not domain-joined and must work disconnected from the directory
Enterprise CAs cannot sign subordinate certificates
quizzes.explanation: An enterprise CA depends on Active Directory. The offline root lives in a workgroup with no network path, so it must be standalone.

quizzes.question: Where does CAPolicy.inf belong before configuration?
answers: The domain SYSVOL share
The removable media only
%SystemRoot% on the CA host
quizzes.explanation: Setup reads CAPolicy.inf from %SystemRoot% during configuration. Placing it afterward does not change the installed CA.

recap: The root host stays disconnected, with controlled media, administration, and time.
CAPolicy.inf is in place before the role is configured.
Publication URLs, validity policy, the CRL schedule, and a protected backup exist before any signing.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 prepares the online issuing CA and its certificate request.

lessons.title: Create the issuing CA request
lessons.summary: Prepare the online issuing server, but keep issuance paused until its CA certificate has been signed and installed. The request carries the public key; the private key stays protected on the issuing system or its approved key provider.
steps: Confirm SBD-SUBCA01 has its final hostname, domain membership, static address (10.0.30.20), internal DNS, and its time from the domain hierarchy, with the hypervisor's time synchronization off. Use a dedicated host and the privileges approved for enterprise CA configuration.

Prepare its role-specific CAPolicy.inf (in this lab: CRLPeriod=Weeks, CRLPeriodUnits=1, CRLDeltaPeriod=Days, CRLDeltaPeriodUnits=1, and LoadDefaultTemplates=0) and protected request directory. Decide which templates may later be published instead of enabling a broad default enrollment set.

Install the CA role and management tools. In the AD CS Configuration wizard choose Enterprise CA, Subordinate CA, and the approved new-key/provider settings (RSA 4096 with SHA-256 in this lab). Enter the planned CA identity and storage locations.
Choose Save a certificate request to file. Inspect the resulting request's subject, public key, and CA constraints; record its SHA-256 hash before handing it to the media custodian.
lessons.command:
w32tm /query /source   # a domain controller, never Local CMOS Clock or a hypervisor provider
# Use the actual request path chosen in the wizard.
certutil -dump C:\CAConfig\IssuingCA.req
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\CAConfig\IssuingCA.req
lessons.check: The request matches the approved issuing identity and key profile. The CA is waiting for its signed certificate; do not troubleshoot that expected state by installing another CA.
lessons.evidence: Retain the request, its reviewed fields and hash, and the request-transfer record. Do not place private keys in the transfer package.
objectives: Prepare the domain-joined issuing host with its final identity.
Generate the subordinate CA request without exposing the private key.
Verify and hash the request before it travels to the root.

quizzes.question: What moves to the offline root for signing?
answers: The issuing CA's certificate request
The issuing CA's private key
A network cable connected to the domain
quizzes.explanation: The signed request contains the public key. Root signing does not require exporting the issuing CA private key.

quizzes.question: Why record the request’s SHA-256 hash before the media transfer?
answers: So the root operator can confirm the file was not altered in transit
It encrypts the request
The configuration wizard requires it to continue
quizzes.explanation: An independently recorded hash lets the ceremony verify integrity. It does not encrypt anything — it proves the same file arrived.

quizzes.question: The new issuing CA is waiting with its service stopped. What is correct?
answers: Reinstall the role until the service starts
That is the expected state until the signed certificate is installed
Join the root to the domain to finish the setup
quizzes.explanation: A subordinate CA cannot run before its CA certificate exists. The waiting state is normal, not a failure to fix.

recap: The issuing host has its final name, addressing, DNS, and time before the role install.
The request file carries the public key only.
The request’s fields and hash are reviewed and recorded before transfer.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 walks the request through the offline signing ceremony.

lessons.title: Sign through the offline ceremony
lessons.summary: A signing ceremony connects an approved request to an approved CA identity. A matching filename alone is not proof that the root should trust the request.
steps: Use approved removable media and custody procedures to bring the request to the root. Before signing, read the root's clock against the approved reference and correct it by the measured difference if it has drifted: the certificate and CRL dates it signs come from that clock. Recalculate the request's hash, compare it with the independently recorded value, and inspect the request before submission.

Verify the root's issued-certificate validity policy and publication extensions. In Certification Authority, submit the request, review its pending entry, and issue it only after the required approval.

Export the subordinate certificate, root certificate, and current root CRL. Check identities, constraints, validity, signatures, URLs, and revocation data against the approved hierarchy. Record file hashes and the request ID.

Transfer only the approved public artifacts back to the connected environment. Match published filenames to the URLs embedded in certificates, retain the ceremony record and protected backup, then shut down and secure the root.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-ROOTCA01, first: read this against the approved reference and log both readings
Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff K'
# Inspect public artifacts; use your actual approved paths.
certutil -dump C:\CAConfig\IssuingCA.cer
certutil -dump C:\CAConfig\RootCA.crl
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\CAConfig\IssuingCA.cer, C:\CAConfig\RootCA.cer, C:\CAConfig\RootCA.crl
lessons.check: The root's clock matched the approved reference, and artifact identities, signatures, validity, and custody checks pass. The root remains offline; a field dump alone is not end-to-end trust validation.
lessons.evidence: Keep the clock check, approval, request ID, artifact hashes, verified certificate/CRL properties, media custody, and root shutdown evidence together.

model.label: Offline trust, step 2
model.text: The ceremony you perform in this lesson, shown as a custody walk with no network link to the root.

objectives: Verify the root's clock and the request's integrity before submission.
Issue the subordinate certificate under the approved validity policy.
Export and verify the public artifacts, then return the root to a secured state.

quizzes.question: Which transfer preserves the root boundary?
answers: An automated shared folder on the root
Approved removable media carrying the reviewed request and public artifacts
Temporary direct internet access
quizzes.explanation: This training architecture uses manual, human-controlled transfer. It never adds a live link to the root.

quizzes.question: What leaves the root environment after the ceremony?
answers: The root’s private-key backup
A live network share for future requests
Only approved public artifacts: the subordinate certificate, root certificate, and current CRL
quizzes.explanation: The boundary stays intact: public artifacts travel on approved media; keys and live connections never do.

quizzes.question: The request’s recalculated hash does not match the recorded value. What now?
answers: Stop and investigate; do not submit the request
Submit it anyway and compare afterward
Regenerate the hash until it matches
quizzes.explanation: A hash mismatch means the file is not the one that was approved. Submitting it would sign an unverified request.

recap: Integrity is verified before submission, and issuance follows explicit approval.
Artifact identities, validity, and URLs are checked against the plan.
The ceremony record, hashes, and root shutdown are all evidence.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 brings the issuing CA online and publishes the trust data.

lessons.title: Activate the issuing CA and distribute trust
lessons.summary: A signed certificate is not yet a working CA. Install it, start Certificate Services, set the AIA and CDP locations every issued certificate will carry, and distribute the approved root through managed domain policy.
steps: Verify the returned artifacts and add the approved root certificate and the current root CRL to the issuing server's local stores: the CA checks its own chain when it starts, before pki.sbd.test serves those files. Complete CA certificate installation through Certification Authority and start Certificate Services.

Configure the issuing CA's AIA and CDP settings before issuing any certificate, pointing them at the planned pki.sbd.test locations. Every certificate the CA signs carries these URLs, so they are fixed now and served exactly as written in lessons 6 and 7.
Distribute the approved root trust through the managed domain policy and arrange the required intermediate/directory publication with delegated administrators.
Hold off on certificate templates: lessons 8 and 9 give template administration its own seat and publish only the templates the plan needs.
lessons.command:
# Before installing the signed certificate: the ceremony's root certificate and CRL, into the local stores
certutil -addstore -f Root C:\CAConfig\RootCA.cer
certutil -addstore -f Root C:\CAConfig\RootCA.crl
# Inspect the issuing CA after installation and publication.
Get-Service CertSvc
certutil -getreg CA\CRLPublicationURLs
certutil -getreg CA\CACertPublicationURLs
certutil -store Root
certutil -store CA
lessons.check: Certificate Services is running, the AIA and CDP settings carry the planned pki.sbd.test URLs, and the approved root reaches domain clients through policy.
lessons.evidence: Keep the CA installation record, the AIA and CDP settings, and the trust-distribution policy.
objectives: Install the signed certificate and start Certificate Services.
Configure the AIA and CDP URLs before any certificate is issued.
Distribute root trust through managed domain policy.

quizzes.question: Why are the AIA and CDP URLs set before the issuing CA signs its first certificate?
answers: They can be edited on each certificate afterward
Every issued certificate carries them for its whole life, so a later change strands the certificates already in use
Certificate Services will not start until they are published
quizzes.explanation: Extensions are fixed at issuance. Setting the locations first means every certificate points at the pki.sbd.test paths lessons 6 and 7 will serve.

quizzes.question: Why must published filenames match the URLs embedded in certificates?
answers: The CA service will not start otherwise
Clients fetch exactly those URLs; a renamed file breaks chain building and revocation checks
Filenames control template permissions
quizzes.explanation: Chain building and revocation checking follow the embedded AIA and CDP URLs literally. Publication must serve those names.

quizzes.question: How does the approved root certificate reach domain clients?
answers: Each user imports it manually from email
It replicates automatically through DNS
Through the managed domain policy trust distribution
quizzes.explanation: Group Policy distributes the trusted root deliberately and reversibly, which keeps trust decisions managed.

recap: The issuing CA is running with its signed certificate.
AIA and CDP URLs are set before the first certificate is issued.
Root trust distributes through managed domain policy.
lessons.next: Lesson 6 gives those embedded URLs a real home: the pki.sbd.test publication site.

lessons.title: Build the pki.sbd.test publication site
lessons.summary: Every certificate the issuing CA has signed carries the pki.sbd.test URLs inside it. This lesson gives those URLs a real home: a small web site on SBD-PKI-MGMT01 serving certificates and revocation lists to the whole network.
objectives: Stand up the HTTP publication site on SBD-PKI-MGMT01.
Confirm the DNS alias from course 1.2 points at the publication host.
Explain why CDP and AIA publication uses HTTP, not HTTPS.
steps: On SBD-PKI-MGMT01, install the Web Server role and create a site (or virtual directory) whose folder will hold the published certificates and revocation lists. Serve .cer, .crt, and .crl files, and allow double escaping in that site's request filtering only, because delta CRL file names carry a + that IIS otherwise refuses; nothing else belongs in this directory.
From SBD-DC01 in VLAN 10, outside VLAN 30, confirm the pki.sbd.test alias from course 1.2 resolves to 10.0.30.30 and that rule F18 in the service-path register permits HTTP to the site.

Leave the site on plain HTTP. Revocation checking has to work before any certificate can be trusted — putting the CRL behind HTTPS creates a loop where validating the site needs the very file it serves.
Restrict who can write to the publication folder: the CA's publishing process and the PKI administrators, nobody else. Clients read; they never write.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-DC01 (VLAN 10): the name and the path from outside VLAN 30
Resolve-DnsName pki.sbd.test
Test-NetConnection pki.sbd.test -Port 80
# On SBD-PKI-MGMT01: the site, and double escaping allowed there for delta CRL names
Get-Website | Select-Object Name, State, PhysicalPath
Get-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'IIS:\Sites\<PKI site>' -Filter system.webServer/security/requestFiltering -Name allowDoubleEscaping
lessons.check: pki.sbd.test resolves to the publication host from outside VLAN 30, the site answers on port 80 with double escaping allowed only there, and the publication folder's permissions separate writers from readers.
lessons.evidence: Record the site configuration, folder permissions, the DNS resolution output from SBD-DC01, and rule F18, the register row that permits the path.

quizzes.question: Why does the publication site stay on plain HTTP?
answers: HTTPS licenses cost money
Clients need the CRL to validate certificates — serving it over HTTPS creates a dependency loop
HTTP is faster than HTTPS in every case
quizzes.explanation: Revocation data must be reachable before trust can be evaluated. The files are public and signed; integrity comes from the signatures, not the transport.

quizzes.question: What belongs in the publication directory?
answers: Public CA certificates and CRLs only
The issuing CA's private key backup
Administrator scripts and passwords
quizzes.explanation: The same rule that runs through the whole PKI: clients need the public trust artifacts; secrets never enter a client-readable path.

quizzes.question: Which earlier work made this lesson a one-page job?
answers: Nothing — it stands alone
Course 1.1's domain controller promotion
The DNS alias reserved in 1.2 and the HTTP row in the service-path register
quizzes.explanation: pki.sbd.test was reserved in course 1.2 and the path through the boundary is already in the register — the sequence pays off here.

recap: pki.sbd.test now answers from SBD-PKI-MGMT01 over HTTP.
Only public artifacts live in the folder; only PKI processes write to it.
The transport is HTTP on purpose — revocation precedes trust.
lessons.next: Lesson 7 fills the site with the real trust data and proves the embedded URLs work.

lessons.title: Publish the trust data at its advertised URLs
lessons.summary: A publication site is only correct when the filenames it serves match the URLs the certificates already carry. Copy the current certificates and CRLs into place, wire the issuing CA to keep them fresh, and prove retrieval from a client that has never cached anything.
objectives: Publish the root and issuing certificates and current CRLs at the exact embedded URLs.
Configure the issuing CA to refresh its published files automatically.
Prove live retrieval and chain building from outside VLAN 30.
steps: Compare the issuing CA's configured AIA and CDP URLs against the publication folder's layout. Every embedded URL must map to a real file path on the site — the filenames are not yours to improve.

Copy the current root certificate, root CRL, issuing certificate, and issuing CRL into the folder. The root's files still arrive by approved media; the issuing CA's can be written directly by its publishing process.
Configure the issuing CA's CRL publication to write into the site's folder on its schedule, so each new CRL replaces the old file at the same name before it expires.

From SBD-DC01, outside VLAN 30, clear the URL cache and verify the issuing CA's certificate with live retrieval: the chain must build to the root and the root's CRL must come from the live site, not a cache. Fetch the issuing CA's own base and delta CRLs at their URLs too; the certificates it issues from lesson 9 on point clients at them.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-DC01 (VLAN 10), with nothing cached; IssuingCA.cer is the ceremony's public certificate
certutil -urlcache * delete
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\pki\IssuingCA.cer
'<issuing CA CRL name>.crl', '<issuing CA CRL name>+.crl' | ForEach-Object { (Invoke-WebRequest "http://pki.sbd.test/$_" -UseBasicParsing).StatusCode }   # 200 for the base and the delta CRL
# On SBD-PKI-MGMT01: what the site serves, with timestamps
Get-ChildItem C:\inetpub\pkiroot | Select-Object Name, LastWriteTime
lessons.check: Every AIA and CDP URL the issuing CA's certificate carries returns the current file, urlfetch verification passes from SBD-DC01 outside VLAN 30, the issuing CA's base and delta CRLs answer at their URLs, and the CRL refresh lands at the same filename automatically.
lessons.evidence: Keep the URL-to-file mapping table, the folder listing with timestamps, and the urlfetch and CRL retrieval output from SBD-DC01.

model.label: Use a web app, step 3
model.text: A client checks revocation at the URL you publish on pki.sbd.test.

quizzes.question: Why can't the published filenames be renamed to something tidier?
answers: The web server forbids renames
Issued certificates already embed the exact URLs; clients fetch those literally
The hardening baseline assigns the filenames
quizzes.explanation: The same lesson this course taught at signing time: extensions are fixed at issuance, so publication conforms to them, never the reverse.

quizzes.question: How do new root CRLs reach the site in this lab?
answers: By approved removable media from the offline ceremony
Over a direct network share from the root
They never need refreshing
quizzes.explanation: The root has no network path. Its refreshed CRL travels like everything else that crosses that boundary — reviewed, hashed, carried.

quizzes.question: What does certutil -verify -urlfetch add over opening the certificate?
answers: It prints the certificate in color
Nothing
It follows the embedded URLs live, proving publication and reachability rather than cached trust
quizzes.explanation: The -urlfetch option is the end-to-end test: chain building plus live AIA and CDP retrieval through the routed network.

recap: Published filenames mirror the embedded URLs exactly.
The issuing CA refreshes its files on schedule; the root's arrive by media.
A cache-cleared check from outside VLAN 30 proves the chain and live revocation.
lessons.next: Lesson 8 moves template administration off the CA and onto its own seat.

lessons.title: Separate template administration
lessons.summary: Certificate templates are directory objects, and whoever edits them decides what the PKI will sign. Give that power its own seat — SBD-PKI-MGMT01 — with named administrators, instead of leaving it wherever a CA console happens to be open.
objectives: Establish SBD-PKI-MGMT01 as the only administration seat for templates.
Delegate template permissions to a named PKI administrators group.
Record the template change process before any template changes.
steps: Install the certificate management tools on SBD-PKI-MGMT01 and confirm the Certificate Templates console can read the directory's template store from there.

Create the SBD PKI Admins group in the directory, place it in the Admin OU from course 1.5, and delegate the template permissions to that group — membership is the record of who may change what the CA signs.

Remove day-to-day template editing from everywhere else: the issuing CA's console stays for CA operations, not template design, and no Domain Admins or Enterprise Admins account edits templates as routine work.

Write the change process: a template change names its requester, its reviewer, the versioning action (edit, duplicate, or supersede), and lands in the evidence record like any other configuration change.
lessons.command:
Get-ADGroup 'SBD PKI Admins' -Properties Members | Select-Object Name, Members
certutil -template | Select-String 'TemplatePropCommonName' | Select-Object -First 10
lessons.check: The templates console works from SBD-PKI-MGMT01, the PKI administrators group holds the delegated permissions, and the written change process names requester, reviewer, and versioning action.
lessons.evidence: Keep the delegation record, the group membership listing, and the signed-off template change process.

quizzes.question: Why do certificate templates deserve their own administration seat?
answers: Templates are directory objects that define what the CA will sign — editing them is a trust decision
The CA console cannot display templates
Templates take too much disk space on the CA
quizzes.explanation: A template edit changes what enrollment can produce. Separating the seat and naming the editors makes that power visible and auditable.

quizzes.question: Where does the PKI administrators group live?
answers: The default Users container
Under the Admin OU from course 1.5, with the other privileged groups
On the offline root
quizzes.explanation: The OU design already has a home for privileged identity — this group joins it so delegation and policy follow the same structure.

quizzes.question: A template needs a change. What is the first artifact?
answers: The edited template itself
A restart of Certificate Services
The change record: requester, reviewer, and the versioning action
quizzes.explanation: The record precedes the change, the same discipline as the network's service-path register — configuration follows documentation, not the other way around.

recap: SBD-PKI-MGMT01 is the template administration seat.
A named group in the Admin OU holds the delegated power.
Template changes have a written process before they have edits.
lessons.next: Lesson 9 uses that process to publish the lab's first working templates.

lessons.title: Publish the first working templates
lessons.summary: The default template set is a menu, not a deployment. Duplicate the three templates this network actually needs — domain controller, computer and server authentication — set their cryptography deliberately, and publish only those.
objectives: Duplicate and configure the domain controller, computer and web server templates against the approved plan.
Set key sizes and validity that meet the Windows Server minimums.
Publish only the needed templates, with autoenrollment limited to the domain controllers and a pilot group.
steps: From the administration seat, duplicate Kerberos Authentication, the template Microsoft designates for domain controllers, as SBD Domain Controller Authentication: subject name format None with the DNS name in the alternative name, a key storage provider with RSA keys of at least 2,048 bits and SHA-256, a validity within lesson 1's one-to-two-year example, and the Domain Controller, Domain Controller Authentication and Kerberos Authentication templates on its Superseded Templates tab. Confirm Domain Controllers and Enterprise Domain Controllers hold Read, Enroll and Autoenroll: this is the PKI server certificate the STIG expects on every domain controller, course 1.4's POA&M candidate.

Duplicate the Computer template as SBD Computer Authentication. Set the approved key provider, a key size of at least 2,048 bits, a validity period within the same example, subject built from directory information, and autoenrollment permission for a pilot computer group only — SBD-PKI-MGMT01 for now, until the fleet arrives in course 1.13.

Duplicate the Web Server template as SBD Server Authentication for the TLS services later courses build — the collector (course 1.10), SBD-SPLUNK01 (1.12), SBD-WSUS01 (1.14) and the business services (1.18): the subject supplied in the request, Enroll for the server administrators (a Linux host's request is made on the host and submitted from their seat) and for an SBD TLS Servers computer group (a Windows server requesting into its own computer store is checked against its computer account, so each later course adds its server to that group first), no autoenrollment, and exportable keys only if the course 1.19 recovery plan explicitly says so.
Record each template's version, settings, and justification through the lesson 8 change process before publishing.
Publish exactly these three templates on the issuing CA and remove any default template the plan does not call for — an unpublished template cannot be mis-enrolled.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-PKI-MGMT01: the templates the CA publishes (use your CA's host\name configuration string)
certutil -CATemplates -config 'SBD-SUBCA01\SBD Issuing CA'
# Each SBD template's minimum key size and subject-name flags, read from the directory
Get-ADObject -SearchBase 'CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Filter "Name -like 'SBD*'" -Properties displayName, msPKI-Minimal-Key-Size, msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag | Select-Object Name, displayName, msPKI-Minimal-Key-Size, msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag
lessons.check: The CA publishes exactly the three planned templates, each shows the approved key size and permissions, and each carries a completed change record.
lessons.evidence: Keep each template's configuration export, its change record, and the CA's published-template listing.

quizzes.question: Why duplicate the built-in templates instead of editing them?
answers: Built-ins cannot be published at all
Duplication preserves the originals and gives your version its own name, version, and record
Duplicates issue faster
quizzes.explanation: Working on a named copy keeps the baseline intact and makes your settings — and their history — unmistakably yours.

quizzes.question: What floor applies to the template key sizes on this network?
answers: 512 bits for speed
1,024 bits
2,048-bit RSA at minimum — the newest Windows Server release enforces it for TLS server authentication
quizzes.explanation: The newest Windows Server release requires at least 2,048-bit RSA keys for TLS server authentication, so a plan below that produces certificates the platform itself will reject.

quizzes.question: Why publish to a pilot group before the whole domain?
answers: A small blast radius proves the template before autoenrollment touches fifty machines in course 1.13
Pilots are a licensing requirement
Templates expire if unused
quizzes.explanation: The fleet course will turn autoenrollment loose at scale. Proving the template on a pilot first is the same test-then-widen habit as the Group Policy work.

quizzes.question: Why do the domain controllers get a duplicate of Kerberos Authentication rather than of the Computer template?
answers: Computer certificates cannot be autoenrolled
Domain controllers cannot use RSA keys
It is the template Microsoft designates for domain controllers: it adds KDC Authentication to client and server authentication
quizzes.explanation: Kerberos Authentication is the current domain controller template, with the KDC Authentication usage that certificate-based Kerberos expects. A named duplicate with its own permissions gives the controllers their PKI server certificate through autoenrollment.

recap: Three named templates exist, configured on purpose, nothing else published.
Key sizes meet the platform's 2,048-bit floor; autoenrollment reaches only the domain controllers and the pilot group.
Every template carries its change record.
lessons.next: The final lesson proves enrollment and revocation end to end, closes the domain controller certificate finding, and runs the closing scans.

lessons.title: Validate enrollment, revocation, and renewal
lessons.summary: Finish the way relying systems see it: both domain controllers and a pilot machine enroll on their own, validate against the live publication site, and reject a certificate you revoke — then the closing scans record what this course changed and close course 1.4's domain controller certificate finding.
steps: Turn on autoenrollment: create SBD Certificate Autoenrollment, a GPO that enables Certificate Services Client - Auto-Enrollment with renewal and template updates, and link it at the domain root, so each member enrolls only for the templates whose permissions name it. The controllers' requests reach SBD-SUBCA01 over RPC across the core from VLAN 10, so confirm the register's enrollment row first. Refresh policy: both controllers receive SBD Domain Controller Authentication certificates and the pilot, SBD-PKI-MGMT01, an SBD Computer Authentication certificate, without a human touching a request.

On SBD-DC01, outside VLAN 30, export its new certificate and the pilot's, clear the URL cache, and run the full verification on each: the chain must reach the approved root and every AIA and CDP URL must answer from pki.sbd.test with current CRL dates — cached success is not evidence of publication.

Enroll a disposable test certificate, revoke only that one, publish an updated issuing CRL, and verify on SBD-DC01, with the cache cleared again, that a fresh evaluation detects the revocation. Diagnose retrieval or stale-publication problems rather than turning off revocation checks.

Record owners and reminders for root and issuing CRL publication and certificate renewal. Schedule offline root ceremonies early enough to transfer and publish replacement CRLs before expiry, and start each one by setting the root's clock against the approved reference. Backups are not set up here: course 1.19 defines and schedules the issuing CA's backup — database, key and configuration — with the rest of the network's, accounts for the root's ceremony backup from lesson 2, and rehearses recovery, so list those items for it in the record.

Take the first SCAP baselines of SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 the course 1.4 way: SCC and the Windows Server benchmark from the course 1.4 media set, checked against its hashes, at the same versions and profile, run locally, with each session hashed and carried to C:\Evidence\pki\<host name> on SBD-DC01, where its hashes must match again, as SBD-DC02's did in course 1.4. List the IIS STIGs the publication site now falls under with an owner and a review date, then rescan both controllers the same way, because their certificates, root trust and autoenrollment policy are this course's change.

Close what this course fixed: in copies of the course 1.5 checklists in C:\Evidence\pki\checklists on SBD-DC01, answer the rule that every domain controller has a PKI server certificate Not A Finding, with each controller's certificate as the observation, and record course 1.4's POA&M candidate as closed. The companion rule, that those certificates come from the DoD PKI or an approved External Certificate Authority, stays open: record it in C:\Evidence\exception-record.csv if it is not there yet, because this lab's own hierarchy stands in for DoD's. Export the new GPOs' reports and links for the change record (course 1.19 backs the GPOs up), file the enrollment, urlfetch, revocation, template and owner records with the scans, and seal C:\Evidence\pki.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-DC01, SBD-DC02 and the pilot, SBD-PKI-MGMT01, once SBD Certificate Autoenrollment is linked at the domain root
gpupdate /force
certutil -pulse
Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My | Select-Object @{n='Template';e={ $x = $_.Extensions | Where-Object { $_.Oid.Value -eq '1.3.6.1.4.1.311.21.7' }; if ($x) { $x.Format($false) } }}, DnsNameList, NotAfter, Thumbprint
# On SBD-DC01 (outside VLAN 30): export its certificate, then verify it and the pilot's with nothing cached
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\pki -Force | Out-Null
$dc = Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My | Where-Object { $_.EnhancedKeyUsageList.ObjectId -contains '1.3.6.1.5.2.3.5' } | Select-Object -First 1   # KDC Authentication
Export-Certificate -Cert $dc -FilePath C:\Evidence\pki\SBD-DC01-dc.cer
certutil -urlcache * delete
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\pki\SBD-DC01-dc.cer
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\pki\pilot.cer   # the pilot's certificate, exported on SBD-PKI-MGMT01 with Export-Certificate
# On SBD-SUBCA01: revoke only the disposable test certificate, then publish a new CRL
certutil -revoke '<test certificate serial number>' 5   # 5 = cessation of operation
certutil -crl
# Back on SBD-DC01: the test certificate must now fail as revoked
certutil -urlcache * delete
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\pki\test.cer
# After the scans (each carried to C:\Evidence\pki\<host name> on SBD-DC01) and the checklist updates: record the new GPOs (course 1.19 backs them up), then seal the evidence
Get-GPOReport -Name 'SBD Certificate Autoenrollment' -ReportType Html -Path C:\Evidence\pki\gpo-report-autoenrollment.html   # and any root-trust GPO from lesson 5
(Get-GPInheritance -Target 'DC=sbd,DC=test').GpoLinks | Select-Object Target, Order, DisplayName, Enabled, Enforced | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\pki\gpo-links.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\pki -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\pki-manifest.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\pki-manifest.csv
lessons.check: Both controllers and the pilot enroll hands-free and verify with live retrieval from pki.sbd.test; after revocation and publication the test certificate is rejected for the expected reason; SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 have first baselines and both controllers a rescan; and the domain controller certificate rule is answered with its evidence, its DoD companion recorded as an exception.
lessons.evidence: Finish the PKI checklist with each controller's and the pilot's certificate details, urlfetch and revocation results, renewal dates and owners, the items handed to course 1.19 for backup, the first baselines of SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01, the controllers' rescans, the updated checklist copies, the exception-record row, the GPO report and link export, and C:\Evidence\pki-manifest.csv with its own hash.

model.label: Use a web app, step 2

objectives: Prove hands-free autoenrollment of the domain controller and pilot certificates through the published templates.

Schedule the renewals that keep the PKI alive, run the closing scans, close the domain controller certificate finding, and file the evidence.

quizzes.question: What does a hands-free pilot enrollment prove?
answers: Template permissions, autoenrollment policy, the CA, DNS, and the network path all agree — the whole chain works
Only that Group Policy refreshed
That the root CA is online
quizzes.explanation: Autoenrollment succeeds only when every layer this path has built cooperates — which is exactly why it is the closing test.

quizzes.question: A valid certificate fails because its CRL cannot be retrieved. What is the next step?
answers: Fix and retest the publication or reachability problem
Disable revocation checking for all clients
Copy the root private key to the client
quizzes.explanation: Reliable revocation publication is part of the service. Bypassing the check conceals the failed dependency.

quizzes.question: Why schedule offline root ceremonies ahead of CRL expiry?
answers: A replacement CRL must be transferred and published before the old one expires
The root certificate expires monthly
Clients delete their trust store on expiry
quizzes.explanation: If the root CRL lapses, revocation checking fails across the hierarchy. Manual transfer takes lead time, so it is scheduled early.

quizzes.question: Which hosts get scanned at the end of this course?
answers: Only the pilot machine
SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 for their first baselines, and both domain controllers, which this course changed
The offline root over the network
quizzes.explanation: The cadence is change-triggered: two new servers joined the domain and the controllers took new certificates, trust and policy, so two first baselines and two rescans.

recap: Both controllers and the pilot enroll hands-free, with live revocation retrieval from pki.sbd.test.
A revoked test certificate is rejected for the expected reason.
CRL publication and renewal each have an owner and a date, backup and recovery are handed to course 1.19, and the closing scans and the closed controller finding finish the PKI chapter.

prerequisites: Complete courses 1.1–1.6: both domain controllers with DNS (course 1.2) and the domain time hierarchy (course 1.3), course 1.4's DISA media set and baseline method, course 1.5's OU structure with the member-server STIG policies on the Servers OU, and course 1.6's PKI. The network's routing, default-deny segmentation and service-path register are already in place, including the core's DHCP relay for VLAN 80.

Provision a Windows Server virtual machine for SBD-DHCP01 (10.0.20.10, VLAN 20) with a second volume for its audit-log copies (D: in this sample), and a disposable Windows client virtual machine on VLAN 80 for testing, named SBD-TEST80 in this sample, with sbd.test as its primary DNS suffix and left out of the domain. Turn off the hypervisor's time synchronization on both, as course 1.3 requires of every virtual machine.

Until course 1.8 builds the administration seats, Tier 0 steps (the directory, DNS, and authorizing the server, which takes an Enterprise Admins member) happen at SBD-DC01's console, and SBD-DHCP01 is built and run at its own console with the server-administration accounts lesson 2 creates.
labNote: SBD-DHCP01 hands the workstation VLAN its addresses, and with them the gateway, the DNS servers, and the domain name every client will trust. This course designs that service, builds it on a member server, registers client names under one dedicated low-privilege account, keeps its lease trail, writes the restore note that course 1.19's backup of the server relies on, and proves it with a test client. It runs before the tiered administration plane exists: Tier 0 steps happen at SBD-DC01's console, and SBD-DHCP01 is run at its own console by a server-administration group that course 1.8 adopts as Tier 1. The core's DHCP relay is part of the network's build, so this course verifies it and never changes the router. Evidence goes in C:\Evidence\dhcp — on SBD-DHCP01 for the server's own records, and on SBD-DC01 for the Tier 0 steps — and course 1.8 carries each to its tier's seat. Scope values are sample values from Inside the Network.
