Red Hat · Using shared system certificates
DISA · Security Content Automation Protocol (SCC and SCAP benchmarks)
DISA · SRG/STIG tools (SCC and STIG Viewer)

lessons.title: Design the repository and its trust
lessons.summary: Before anything is mirrored, decide what SBD-REPO01 is for: the one approved source of operating-system packages for the domain-joined Linux servers, fed by dated snapshots whose upstream signing keys you verified first. Then place it on VLAN 70 and write its rows into the register.
objectives: Define the repository's job, its consumers, and the one-source rule for Linux packages.
Choose what is mirrored and verify the upstream signing keys that make it trustworthy.
Place SBD-REPO01 and register every path it uses.
steps: Write the repository's job: the only source of operating-system packages for the domain-joined Linux servers (SBD-SPLUNK01 in course 1.12, SBD-WEB01 in course 1.18, and SBD-NESSUS01 when course 1.17, coming soon, arrives) and for SBD-REPO01 itself. Application software, such as Splunk in course 1.12 and SCC for Linux in lesson 5, still arrives as hashed vendor media; anything else is a documented exception, never a second source.

Choose one Red Hat Enterprise Linux–family distribution and major release for every Linux server, one with a published DISA STIG and a SCAP benchmark that SCC for Linux supports, so there is one mirror to feed and one benchmark to scan against. Mirror only its operating-system repositories for one architecture: BaseOS and AppStream. Third-party repositories stay out.

Decide the trust anchor: the vendor's signing keys. Get each key file, read its fingerprint, and compare it with the vendor's published value through a second channel before anything is published; the fingerprints go into the snapshot catalog. Each published mirror is a dated snapshot, and that date is the repository's version.

Place it as Inside the Network does: SBD-REPO01 at 10.0.70.20 on VLAN 70, not domain-joined, administered over SSH 22 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 only (rule A02, Tier 1). Confirm the register rows: the Linux servers to REPO01 on HTTP 80 (F19), REPO01 to both domain controllers for DNS (F01), and REPO01's syslog over TLS to the collector (F07, enabled when course 1.10 builds it). Rule F09 lists only domain members for time, so add SBD-REPO01's own time row, to both controllers on UDP 123, with an owner and a reason, as course 1.3 planned.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: start the evidence folder and confirm no record exists yet
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force C:\Evidence\linux-repository | Out-Null
Resolve-DnsName SBD-REPO01.sbd.test -Server 10.0.10.10 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue   # expected: no answer yet
# On the approved connected system: read each upstream signing key's fingerprint
gpg --show-keys --with-fingerprint /etc/pki/rpm-gpg/RPM-GPG-KEY-redhat-release   # or the distribution's own key file
lessons.check: The design names the consumers, the one distribution and the repositories mirrored; each upstream key's fingerprint matches the vendor's published value; and the register carries F19, F01, F07 and SBD-REPO01's added time row, each with an owner.
lessons.evidence: Keep the repository design (job, consumers, distribution, repositories, snapshot naming), the verified key fingerprints with where you checked them, and the register rows that name SBD-REPO01.

model.label: SBD-REPO01
model.text: The Linux repository's address, its package path (F19) and its syslog path (F07).

quizzes.question: Why does this course come before any Linux server is built?
answers: Linux servers cannot be installed without a repository
So every Linux server takes its packages from the approved source from its first day, with no earlier source to explain
Because the collector must be built from it
quizzes.explanation: SBD-SPLUNK01, the first Linux server, arrives in course 1.12. With REPO01 already running, its first update and every one after come from the reviewed snapshot.

quizzes.question: What makes a mirrored package trustworthy in this design?
answers: SBD-REPO01 served it
It came from a well-known mirror
Its upstream signature verifies against a signing key whose fingerprint you checked against the vendor's published value
quizzes.explanation: The repository is only a carrier. Trust comes from the vendor's signature, checked against a key you verified once, deliberately, and recorded.

quizzes.question: SBD-REPO01 is not domain-joined. What follows from that?
answers: It uses local named accounts and a DNS record the DNS owner creates, and patching does not depend on the directory being up
It needs no register rows
It needs no time source
quizzes.explanation: Keeping the package source outside the domain removes a dependency, but nothing registers it automatically: its accounts, DNS record and time row are deliberate decisions.

recap: One distribution, one mirror, one source of Linux packages.
Verified upstream keys are the trust anchor; the dated snapshot is the version.
REPO01's place and every path it uses are in the register, including its time row.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 builds and hardens SBD-REPO01 in its place.

lessons.title: Build and harden SBD-REPO01
lessons.summary: Build SBD-REPO01 as a minimal Linux server that does one job: answer package requests on TCP 80 and accept administration on SSH from one seat. Every other service, listener and account is left out.
objectives: Install the server with its static address and DNS record, course 1.3's chrony file, and the course 1.6 root in its trust store.
Restrict administration to named local accounts over SSH from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01.
Serve only the repository directory from a minimal web server behind a host firewall that mirrors the register.
steps: Install the chosen distribution's minimal server profile from install media whose hash matches the vendor's published checksum, with a separate file system mounted at /srv, sized for at least two snapshots plus growth: /srv/repo is the web root, /srv/incoming receives each crossing, and /srv/repo-records holds the catalog. Set the name SBD-REPO01.sbd.test and the static address 10.0.70.20/24, with the core's VLAN 70 interface (10.0.70.1 in this sample) as gateway and both domain controllers as DNS servers. Because REPO01 cannot register itself in DNS, the DNS owner adds its A record (and PTR, if the reverse zone exists) from AdminJumpBox01. Install only from that verified media until SBD-REPO01 serves its own snapshot; if the image lacks a package this lesson needs, such as chrony or the web server, bring it signature-checked with the first crossing (lesson 3) and install it from that copy.

Apply course 1.3's chrony file before the first package update, and turn off the hypervisor's time synchronization for the VM, so the domain controllers are its only clock: /etc/chrony.conf names only the two controllers, server SBD-DC01.sbd.test iburst and server SBD-DC02.sbd.test iburst, with maxdistance 16 and no pool, other server, sourcedir or allow line, and reaches both controllers over the time row added in lesson 1. Check that chronyc sources shows one controller selected (^*) and the other usable, with a small, steady offset; the maxdistance line is what admits controllers that serve their own clock, as course 1.3 explains.

Create a named local account for each administrator in one admin group with sudo, lock root's password, and copy each administrator's SSH public key from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01. In a drop-in that sorts before the distribution's own (for example /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-sbd.conf, because the first value read wins), set PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no and AllowGroups to that group. Over your first SSH session, add the course 1.6 root certificate to the system trust store, because a server outside the domain gets it from no Group Policy: export it from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01's Trusted Root store, check its SHA-256 against the hash course 1.6 recorded, copy it across, place it in /etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors and run update-ca-trust, ready for course 1.10's syslog over TLS.

Install Apache (httpd) and give it one site: Listen 10.0.70.20:80, DocumentRoot /srv/repo, Options FollowSymLinks with no Indexes, AllowOverride None, only GET and HEAD allowed, everything outside /srv/repo denied, ServerTokens Prod, ServerSignature Off and TraceEnable Off. Remove the welcome page, autoindex and user directories; with SELinux enforcing, label /srv/repo httpd_sys_content_t with semanage fcontext so restorecon keeps it. The repository files stay owned by root and read-only to the web server.

Make the host firewall the register's copy. With firewalld, create a zone for 10.0.60.20 that allows only ssh and a zone for SBD-SPLUNK01, SBD-NESSUS01 and SBD-WEB01 (10.0.50.10, 10.0.50.20, 10.0.40.40) that allows only http, with no services left in the default zone. Adding those consumers now, before they exist, is safe because F19 already approves them.
lessons.command:
hostnamectl; ip -4 addr show
grep -E '^(pool|server|sourcedir|allow|maxdistance)' /etc/chrony.conf   # both controllers and maxdistance 16, nothing else
chronyc sources -v; chronyc tracking   # ^* one controller, ^+ or ^- the other; System time offset small and steady
sshd -T | grep -Ei '^(permitrootlogin|passwordauthentication|allowgroups) '
# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: export the course 1.6 root and compare its hash with course 1.6's record, then copy it over
Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\Root | Where-Object Subject -like '*<root CA name>*' | Export-Certificate -FilePath C:\Evidence\linux-repository\sbd-root.cer
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\linux-repository\sbd-root.cer
scp C:\Evidence\linux-repository\sbd-root.cer <your-account>@SBD-REPO01.sbd.test:/tmp/
# On SBD-REPO01: the same fingerprint, then the system trust store
openssl x509 -inform der -in /tmp/sbd-root.cer -noout -fingerprint -sha256
sudo cp /tmp/sbd-root.cer /etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors/ && sudo update-ca-trust
trust list --filter=ca-anchors | grep -i '<root CA name>'   # expected: the SBD root
apachectl -S        # expected: one site on 10.0.70.20:80
ss -tlnp            # expected: 22 and 80, plus loopback-only listeners, if any
firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
firewall-cmd --list-all --zone=public   # expected: no services
curl -sI http://SBD-REPO01.sbd.test/ | head -1   # expected: 403, no directory listing
lessons.check: SBD-REPO01 resolves to 10.0.70.20 and, with course 1.3's chrony file and the hypervisor's time synchronization off, syncs from a domain controller with a small, stable offset; sshd refuses root and passwords and admits only the admin group; the system trust store holds the course 1.6 root, its hash matching course 1.6's record; only TCP 22 and 80 listen; the firewall admits SSH from 10.0.60.20 alone and HTTP from the three registered consumers alone; and the web root returns 403 instead of a listing.
lessons.evidence: Keep the install media hash, the chrony file with its sources and tracking output, the root certificate's hash compared with course 1.6's record, the effective sshd settings, the Apache site and listener output, the firewall zones, and the administrator account list (names only, no keys or passwords).

quizzes.question: Why does chrony on SBD-REPO01 point at both domain controllers?
answers: chrony needs exactly two servers
Only SBD-DC02 answers Linux clients
They carry the domain's time; two sources keep REPO01 on time if one controller is down, so its log timestamps line up with every other system's
quizzes.explanation: REPO01 is outside the domain but not outside the time design. Its log timestamps are evidence, and evidence must line up.

quizzes.question: Why is plain HTTP on TCP 80 acceptable for this repository?
answers: Integrity comes from the GPG signatures every client checks, the packages are public, and F19 registers exactly this path
HTTPS cannot be configured on Linux
Nothing else on the network uses HTTP
quizzes.explanation: A tampered package fails its signature check whatever the transport. HTTP also keeps patching independent of the PKI's certificate lifecycle.

quizzes.question: The firewall allows SSH only from 10.0.60.20. Why that one address?
answers: It is the core router
It is SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, the Tier 1 seat rule A02 names for REPO01's administration
Every VLAN 60 host needs SSH everywhere
quizzes.explanation: The tier model names the seat that administers each target. The host firewall enforces the same rule, so a path the router would allow still ends at REPO01.

recap: A minimal install: static address, DNS record, and time from both controllers through course 1.3's chrony file.
Named accounts, keys only, SSH from one seat, and the SBD root trusted.
One web site, one directory, and a firewall that matches the register.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 fills it with the first mirrored, verified, dated snapshot.

lessons.title: Mirror, verify, and publish a snapshot
lessons.summary: The repository's content crosses the boundary like everything else: mirrored on the connected side, hashed, carried across, and checked twice on arrival, once against the hash manifest and once against the vendor's signatures. Only then is it published as a dated snapshot and entered in the catalog.
objectives: Mirror the approved repositories with their signatures checked on the connected side.
Carry the set across and verify both its hashes and its signatures before publishing.
Publish a dated snapshot and record it in the snapshot catalog.
steps: On the approved connected system, mirror into a dated directory. From a registered system of the same release, run dnf reposync with --download-metadata, which keeps the vendor's own repository metadata (including groups and modules) so the copy is usable as a repository as it stands, and --gpgcheck, which deletes any package whose signature fails and exits non-zero.

If you trim the set instead of mirroring it whole, the vendor metadata no longer matches the files: rebuild it with createrepo_c (and add module metadata back with modifyrepo_c) and rely on gpgcheck on every client, because your rebuilt metadata carries no vendor signature. Then write a SHA-256 manifest of every file, hash the manifest itself, and carry both across under the course 1.4 media procedure.

On SBD-REPO01, copy the set and its manifest into /srv/incoming, outside the web root, and check the set against the manifest. Then verify signatures independently of the connected side: rpm -K on every package, against the keys verified in lesson 1 (rpm --import those key files first if rpm -q gpg-pubkey does not list them). One failure stops publication and becomes a finding.

Publish: move the set to /srv/repo/snapshots/<date> (a rename on the same file system), restore its SELinux labels, and switch the current link to it with an atomic rename so clients never see a half-copied mix. The previous snapshot stays in place for rollback.

Add the snapshot to the catalog in /srv/repo-records, outside the web root: date, repositories, upstream key fingerprints, manifest hash, transfer record, who published it, and its status (current, previous or retired). Copy the catalog and manifest to C:\Evidence\linux-repository on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 and hash them.
lessons.command:
# Connected side: keep vendor metadata, delete anything whose signature fails
dnf reposync --repoid=<baseos-repo-id> --repoid=<appstream-repo-id> --download-metadata --gpgcheck -p /srv/stage/2026-10-13
cd /srv/stage/2026-10-13 && find . -type f -print0 | sort -z | xargs -0 sha256sum > ../SHA256SUMS-2026-10-13.txt
# On SBD-REPO01, after the crossing:
cd /srv/incoming/2026-10-13 && sha256sum -c --quiet ../SHA256SUMS-2026-10-13.txt   # expected: no output
find . -name '*.rpm' -print0 | xargs -0 rpm -K | grep -v 'digests signatures OK'   # expected: no output
mv /srv/incoming/2026-10-13 /srv/repo/snapshots/ && restorecon -R /srv/repo/snapshots/2026-10-13
ln -sfn snapshots/2026-10-13 /srv/repo/current.new && mv -T /srv/repo/current.new /srv/repo/current
lessons.check: The manifest check and the signature check both pass with no exceptions, /srv/repo/current points at the new dated snapshot, the previous snapshot (if any) is untouched, and the catalog entry carries the fingerprints and manifest hash.
lessons.evidence: Keep the manifest and its hash, the transfer record, the clean signature-check output, the catalog entry, and the hashes of the copies filed on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01.

model.label: SBD-REPO01
model.text: The Linux package repository and the rule (F19) that lets the domain-joined Linux servers patch from it.

quizzes.question: What is the repository's version, for evidence purposes?
answers: The hashed snapshot date of its mirrored content
The server's uptime
The newest package's name
quizzes.explanation: A mirror is a moment in time. The dated, hashed snapshot is what lets anyone say exactly which content the lab could install.

quizzes.question: The manifest check passes on SBD-REPO01, but rpm -K reports one package with a bad signature. What does that mean?
answers: The media was damaged in transit
Nothing; the manifest already proved the content
The package was already bad before it crossed: the manifest proves the copy is identical, not that the original is genuine, so the snapshot is not published and the package is a finding
quizzes.explanation: Hashes and signatures answer different questions. The manifest proves nothing changed in transit; the signature proves the vendor produced it. Both have to pass.

quizzes.question: Why switch the current snapshot with a link and an atomic rename instead of copying over the old files?
answers: It saves disk space
Clients see either the old snapshot or the new one, never a half-copied mix, and the previous snapshot stays whole for rollback
Apache can only serve symbolic links
quizzes.explanation: Publishing is a change, and a change should be all or nothing and reversible. The rename gives you both.

recap: Mirror with signature checks on, then hash the whole set.
On arrival, check the hashes and the signatures; either failure stops publication.
A dated snapshot goes live by atomic switch and enters the catalog.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 writes the client configuration every Linux server will use.

lessons.title: Configure the Linux clients
lessons.summary: Write the one client configuration every Linux server will use: a single source definition pointing at SBD-REPO01, the verified signing keys, and no other source. No consumer exists yet, so prove it on SBD-REPO01's own package manager and hand the files to courses 1.12 and 1.18.
objectives: Write the dnf source definition and signature settings for the chosen release.
Trust only the verified keys and remove every other package source.
Prove the configuration on SBD-REPO01 and package it for the later Linux servers.
steps: Write one source definition that names SBD-REPO01.sbd.test, so DNS carries it (F01): /etc/yum.repos.d/sbd-repo01.repo has one section per repository with baseurl=http://SBD-REPO01.sbd.test/current/<repo-id>/, gpgcheck=1 and gpgkey=file:///etc/pki/rpm-gpg/<vendor key>.

Trust only the keys verified in lesson 1, installed from local files and never fetched from the repository at install time: whoever could change the repository could then change the key too. List the trusted keys (rpm -q gpg-pubkey) and remove any key nothing needs with rpm -e.

Remove or disable every other source: set enabled=0 in every other .repo file, including any install-media entry, and where subscription-manager is installed, stop it managing repositories (subscription-manager config --rhsm.manage_repos=0), so it cannot write its own definitions back.

Prove it on SBD-REPO01 itself, which follows the same rule: apply the files, refresh the metadata with no errors or warnings, and confirm that a package you will need in course 1.10, rsyslog-gnutls, resolves from the SBD-REPO01 source. A Failed to fetch line or a missing package is a gap in the mirror to fix before any server depends on it.

Package the source file, the key files and a short apply-and-verify sheet in /srv/repo-records/client, hash them, and file them as the configuration every Linux server applies, courses 1.12 and 1.18 when they build SBD-SPLUNK01 and SBD-WEB01: after course 1.3's chrony file and before the server's first package update.
lessons.command:
dnf repolist --all                 # expected: only the sbd-repo01 repositories enabled
rpm -q gpg-pubkey --qf '%{NAME}-%{VERSION}-%{RELEASE}\t%{SUMMARY}\n'
dnf makecache && dnf info rsyslog-gnutls | grep -Ei '^(repository|from repo)'   # expected: from the sbd-repo01 repositories
# Hash the client package for the later courses
sha256sum /srv/repo-records/client/*
lessons.check: On SBD-REPO01 the package manager lists SBD-REPO01 as its only source, trusts only the verified keys, refreshes without errors, and resolves rsyslog-gnutls from the snapshot; the client package is hashed and filed.
lessons.evidence: Keep the source listing, the trusted key list, the refresh output, the package's source line, and the client package with its hashes.

quizzes.question: How is the one-source rule enforced on a Linux consumer?
answers: By asking administrators nicely
External source definitions are removed or disabled — the configuration itself allows only the internal repository
By firewall rules alone
quizzes.explanation: Both layers help, but the consumer's own configuration is the primary control — and the thing the scan or config review verifies.

quizzes.question: Why install the signing key from a local, verified file rather than from SBD-REPO01?
answers: Anyone who could change the repository could then change the key as well, and the signature check would prove nothing
HTTP cannot carry key files
Keys expire when downloaded
quizzes.explanation: The key is the trust anchor, so it must come through a channel the repository cannot influence. That is why lesson 1 verified it separately.

quizzes.question: What does gpgcheck=1 do at install time?
answers: Encrypts the download
Makes metadata refresh faster
Refuses any package whose signature does not verify against a trusted key
quizzes.explanation: dnf checks each package's signature before installing it. Your job is to make sure the key they check against is the right one, and the only one.

recap: One source definition, by name, with signature checks on.
Only verified keys are trusted, and no other source remains.
Proven on SBD-REPO01, packaged for courses 1.12 and 1.18.
lessons.next: The final lesson keeps the repository current, rehearses rollback, and baselines SBD-REPO01.

lessons.title: Keep it current and prove it
lessons.summary: A repository is only as good as its last snapshot. Set the cadence that keeps it current, rehearse promoting a new snapshot and rolling back, stage SCC for Linux for every Linux server and take SBD-REPO01's first SCAP baseline with it, and close the course with a record an assessor can check.
objectives: Set the update cadence for snapshots across the air gap.
Promote a new snapshot and roll back to the previous one, on record.
Stage SCC for Linux and the STIG benchmark for every Linux server, baseline SBD-REPO01 with them, and hand off to course 1.10.
steps: Write the cadence: a new snapshot crosses on a fixed schedule (monthly is a common sample value), plus an expedited crossing when the vendor publishes a critical security fix. Keep the current and previous snapshots, retire older ones in the catalog, and name who approves each crossing. Course 1.14 later carries Windows updates on the same monthly run.

Rehearse change control with the next snapshot: publish it as in lesson 3, refresh SBD-REPO01's own client and confirm it sees the new content, then switch current back to the previous snapshot and confirm the client follows. Rolling back stops a bad snapshot from spreading, but it does not uninstall anything; a server that already updated needs dnf history undo or dnf downgrade there. Record both switches in the catalog.

Stage the Linux assessment set once, for every Linux server: SCC for Linux for your distribution and architecture, the DISA STIG SCAP benchmark for the distribution, and, for the manual items, the distribution's STIG and the Apache Server 2.4 UNIX STIGs. Check SCC against DISA's published checksum on the connected side, hash every file into connected-side-hashes.csv, carry the set under the course 1.4 media procedure, and check it again into C:\Staging\DISA\linux on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: the Tier 1 copy that courses 1.12 and 1.18 scan their Linux servers with.

Scan every Linux server the same way, starting with SBD-REPO01: copy SCC and the benchmark over your Tier 1 SSH session, check their hashes there, install SCC as its readme directs, and run it as root with the benchmark and the profile course 1.4 recorded. Copy the session back to C:\Evidence\linux-repository\baseline\SBD-REPO01, answer the manual items, Apache's included, in a STIG Viewer checklist for SBD-REPO01 on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, and classify every open item as in course 1.4: fix now, deviation candidate or POA&M candidate. Plain HTTP on F19 is a deviation candidate, justified by signed content.

File the assessable record in C:\Evidence\linux-repository with hashes: the design, the snapshot catalog, the client package, the baseline results and checklist, and the administration record of who changed what. Write the handoff to course 1.10: SBD-REPO01 is running, rsyslog-gnutls is in its snapshot, the SBD root is in its trust store, and its syslog over TLS (F07) is waiting for the collector.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-REPO01: promote the next snapshot, then rehearse rollback
readlink /srv/repo/current
ln -sfn snapshots/2026-11-10 /srv/repo/current.new && mv -T /srv/repo/current.new /srv/repo/current
ln -sfn snapshots/2026-10-13 /srv/repo/current.new && mv -T /srv/repo/current.new /srv/repo/current   # rollback
# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: no output means every staged file is on the connected-side list
(Get-ChildItem C:\Staging\DISA\linux\* -File -Exclude *.csv | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256).Hash | Where-Object { $_ -notin (Import-Csv C:\Staging\DISA\linux\connected-side-hashes.csv).Hash }
scp C:\Staging\DISA\linux\<SCC for Linux package> C:\Staging\DISA\linux\<STIG benchmark> <your-account>@SBD-REPO01.sbd.test:/tmp/
# On SBD-REPO01: the same hashes, then SCC's command-line scanner as root (path and options from the SCC readme)
sha256sum /tmp/<SCC for Linux package> /tmp/<STIG benchmark>
sudo <SCC install directory>/cscc
# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: collect the session and the record, then hash everything
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force C:\Evidence\linux-repository\baseline | Out-Null
scp -r <your-account>@SBD-REPO01.sbd.test:<SCC session folder> C:\Evidence\linux-repository\baseline\SBD-REPO01
scp -r <your-account>@SBD-REPO01.sbd.test:/srv/repo-records/* C:\Evidence\linux-repository\
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\linux-repository -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\linux-repository-hashes.csv -NoTypeInformation
lessons.check: The cadence is written with an approver, the promotion and the rollback both show in the catalog and in the client's view, the Linux assessment set sits checked in C:\Staging\DISA\linux on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, SBD-REPO01 has a first baseline with every open item classified, and the record and handoff are filed with hashes.
lessons.evidence: Keep the cadence, the catalog showing promotion and rollback, the Linux assessment set's hash check, the SCC results and STIG Viewer checklist, the classified findings, the administration record, the hash list, and the handoff note to course 1.10.

quizzes.question: You roll the repository back to the previous snapshot. What happens to servers that already installed the newer packages?
answers: They keep them until you undo or downgrade on each server; rollback stops the spread, it does not reverse installs
They revert automatically on the next refresh
They stop working until they are rebuilt
quizzes.explanation: The repository decides what can be installed next, not what is installed now. Undoing an installed update is a separate, recorded change on each server.

quizzes.question: How is SBD-REPO01 baselined?
answers: It is exempt because it only serves files
With the Windows Server benchmark
With SCC and the DISA STIG benchmark for its distribution, plus the manual checklist items such as the Apache web server STIGs
quizzes.explanation: A Linux server is held to its own DISA STIG on the same cadence as every other server. The web server's items are manual, so they are answered in STIG Viewer.

quizzes.question: A STIG item expects the web server to use TLS, but F19 is plain HTTP. How do you record it?
answers: Mark it not a finding
As a deviation candidate with its justification — signed content on a registered path — decided in the exception record
Turn off the web server
quizzes.explanation: A deliberate design choice that differs from a STIG value is neither hidden nor fixed by default. It is written down, justified, and decided by the right person.

recap: Snapshots cross on a written cadence, with an expedited path for critical fixes.
Promotion and rollback are rehearsed, and rollback's limits are known.
SCC for Linux is staged for every Linux server, SBD-REPO01 has its first baseline, and course 1.10 inherits a running source.
lessons.next: That completes course 1.9. Course 1.10 builds the collector, SBD-SYSLOG01, and enrolls SBD-REPO01 as its first Linux syslog-over-TLS source.

prerequisites: Complete courses 1.1–1.9: every Windows system they built — both DCs, SBD-SUBCA01, SBD-PKI-MGMT01, SBD-DHCP01, and the three admin seats — becomes a source; the tiered admin plane (course 1.8) means the collector is administered only from VLAN 60 (SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, Tier 1); and SBD-REPO01 (10.0.70.20, course 1.9) is running and becomes this course's first Linux source.

Provision SBD-SYSLOG01 (10.0.20.20) as Windows Server joined to sbd.test in the Servers OU, so course 1.5's member-server STIG policies apply from first boot, with a separate data volume (D: in this sample) for the logs. Turn off the hypervisor's time synchronization and check that w32tm /query /source names a domain controller (course 1.3).

Have the network's service-path register, the course 1.6 SBD Server Authentication template, and an approved syslog receiver for Windows (staged across the air gap and hashed, as in course 1.4) ready: Windows has no built-in syslog listener.
labNote: This is the first of three logging courses. Course 1.10 designs the whole collect → protect → analyze pipeline and builds the collect stage on SBD-SYSLOG01; course 1.11 protects the record on SBD-AUDIT01, and course 1.12 analyzes it in SBD-SPLUNK01. Collection is configuration you can show: a subscription, a listener, and events with the right source names and times.

sources.title: Microsoft · Use Windows Event Forwarding to help with intrusion detection
Microsoft · Setting up a source initiated subscription
Red Hat · Configuring a remote logging solution
RFC 5425 · Transport Layer Security (TLS) Transport Mapping for Syslog
DISA · SRG/STIG tools (SCC and STIG Viewer)
NIST · SP 800-53 Rev. 5 security controls (AU family)

lessons.title: Design collect, protect, analyze
lessons.summary: Three systems, three distinct jobs: SBD-SYSLOG01 gathers, SBD-AUDIT01 preserves, SBD-SPLUNK01 answers questions. This course builds the first; courses 1.11 and 1.12 build the other two — so decide now, for all three, what is collected, how long it lives, who may touch it, and where each stream is picked up.
objectives: Assign the three roles, the course that builds each, and the first collection scope.
Decide retention, readers, and the no-delete rule per stage, recording the period chosen for your environment.
Name the streams and register every pipeline path.
steps: Write the role sentence for each host and the course that builds it: SBD-SYSLOG01 (course 1.10) receives Windows events and syslog; SBD-AUDIT01 (course 1.11) holds the protected copy for the full retention period; SBD-SPLUNK01 (course 1.12) indexes a working copy for search and alerting. One copy to keep, one copy to question.

Scope the first collection to what already produces evidence: the Security log and the Windows Time events course 1.3 keeps from every Windows system that exists — both DCs, SBD-SUBCA01, SBD-PKI-MGMT01, SBD-DHCP01, and the three admin seats — plus the core router's deny log and SBD-REPO01's syslog. The fleet joins in course 1.13, and every later server in the course that builds it.

Decide the AU answers per stage. How long each stage keeps its records is dependent on your environment and your records policy, so write down the period you chose for each and why: the collector keeps a local buffer long enough for the downstream pickups to catch up after an outage, administered by Tier 1 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01; the repository keeps the protected record for the whole period your policy requires, written only by a write-only archival account, read by a named auditors group, and deleted by nobody outside the custodian's logged retention process, with independent approval (rule A04); analysis keeps as much searchable history as investigations need, read by analysts.

Name the two streams and where they are picked up: Windows events land in the ForwardedEvents log (file on D:\Logs\ForwardedEvents) and syslog in daily files per sender under D:\Logs\Syslog. Course 1.11's archival job and course 1.12's forwarder both read from these two places; nothing else writes there.

Add the register rows with owners: Windows sources to the collector (F17, WinRM 5985, source-initiated), Linux syslog over TLS (F07, TCP 6514), the core router's deny log (rule F24, UDP 514, owned by the network owner: the router already sends it to the collector's address as part of the network's existing configuration, and this course only receives it), the archive path (F11, SMB 3 with encryption) and the forwarder path (F10, TCP 9997 with TLS). The last two stay unused until courses 1.11 and 1.12.
lessons.command:
# From AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): what the DCs audit today.
Invoke-Command SBD-DC01, SBD-DC02 { auditpol /get /category:* /r } | Out-File C:\Evidence\logging-pipeline\DCs-auditpol-before.csv
# From SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (Tier 1): no collector runs yet.
Invoke-Command SBD-SYSLOG01 { Get-Service Wecsvc | Select-Object Status, StartType }
lessons.check: The design names each stage's job, building course, scope, chosen retention period with its reason, and readers; the no-delete rule is written; the two streams and their pickup folders are named; and the register carries the five pipeline paths with owners, F24 for the router's deny log included.
lessons.evidence: Keep the pipeline design sheet, the retention and access table, the stream and pickup definitions, and the new register rows.

model.label: Follow a log
model.text: Follow one event from a domain controller to the collector, then to Splunk and the audit copy.

quizzes.question: Why separate the repository from the analysis system?
answers: The protected record and the working copy have different jobs — tampering with searches must never mean tampering with evidence
Splunk cannot store data
Two systems are cheaper than one
quizzes.explanation: Analysis needs flexibility; the record needs integrity. Splitting them means a compromised search tier still leaves the evidence intact.

quizzes.question: What is in the first collection scope?
answers: Every system, including the fleet that does not exist yet
The sources that already produce evidence: every existing Windows system's Security log and time events, the router's deny log, and SBD-REPO01
Only the collector's own log
quizzes.explanation: Collect what exists and matters most. The fleet widens the scope in course 1.13 — into a pipeline already proven.

quizzes.question: Who may delete from SBD-AUDIT01?
answers: Any Domain Admin
The analysis system automatically
Nobody outside the written retention process — that restriction is the protection control
quizzes.explanation: AU-9 in one sentence: the record survives its administrators. Deletion happens only by the documented retention process, which course 1.11 builds.

recap: Collector gathers (1.10), repository preserves (1.11), analysis answers (1.12).
Retention, readers, and the no-delete rule are written for every stage.
Two named streams, their pickup folders, and five registered paths.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 makes sure the right events exist before anything forwards them.

lessons.title: Turn on the right auditing
lessons.summary: Forwarding garbage faster is not monitoring. Set the advanced audit policy so the events that tell the network's story — sign-ins, account changes, directory changes, policy changes — actually get written, at or above the STIG values course 1.4 measured.
objectives: Apply the advanced audit policy subcategories the design needs.
Reconcile audit settings with the course 1.5 STIG Group Policy objects.
Verify effective auditing on the DCs and admin hosts.
steps: Review what the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Group Policy objects (GPOs) linked in course 1.5 already audit — most of the advanced audit policy arrived with the STIGs, including the setting that makes subcategories override the old category policy. This lesson reconciles and fills gaps rather than starting over.

Confirm the subcategories the design depends on are at least at the STIG values on the DCs: Credential Validation, Logon, Special Logon, User Account Management, Security Group Management, Directory Service Changes, Audit Policy Change, and Security State Change, which writes event 4616 for every clock change course 1.3 records — success and failure where the design says so. Directory Service Changes writes event 5136 only for objects whose auditing entries ask for it, so check the domain's auditing entries too.

Extend the same policy to the Admin OU's computer sub-OUs from course 1.8, so privileged sessions on the admin hosts write their sign-in trail, and confirm that SBD-SUBCA01, SBD-PKI-MGMT01, and SBD-DHCP01 already carry the member-server STIG values.

Make every addition a separate, documented GPO linked above the STIG GPO, never an auditpol /set on one server. Advanced audit settings merge across GPOs per subcategory, and only a conflicting subcategory is decided by precedence — record each addition in the course 1.5 exception record, kept on AdminJumpBox01.
lessons.command:
# From AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): effective audit policy and the policy result on a DC.
Invoke-Command SBD-DC01 { auditpol /get /category:* /r } | Out-File C:\Evidence\logging-pipeline\SBD-DC01-auditpol.csv
Invoke-Command SBD-DC01 { auditpol /get /subcategory:"Directory Service Changes,Security State Change" }
gpresult /s SBD-DC01 /scope computer /h C:\Evidence\logging-pipeline\SBD-DC01-gpresult.html
lessons.check: Effective audit policy on the DCs and admin hosts covers the designed subcategories at or above the STIG values, applied through GPO, with every addition documented.
lessons.evidence: Keep the auditpol output per host class, the GPO report, and the documented additions.

quizzes.question: Why start from the course 1.5 STIG GPOs instead of a fresh audit policy?
answers: Fresh policies are forbidden
The STIGs already set most of it — reconciling avoids conflicts and double maintenance
auditpol cannot show existing settings
quizzes.explanation: The hardening baseline was the first word on auditing. This lesson's job is alignment and gaps, not a rival policy.

quizzes.question: Where do audit-policy additions get made?
answers: In the GPO structure, documented — never as local tweaks
Directly in each server's local policy
In the collector's configuration
quizzes.explanation: Local tweaks drift and hide, and Group Policy can overwrite them. Policy through GPO keeps the audit posture visible, scanned, and reproducible.

quizzes.question: Which event families does the design treat as the core story?
answers: Print spooler events
Disk defragmentation logs
Sign-ins, account management, directory changes, and policy changes
quizzes.explanation: Who authenticated, who changed an account, who touched the directory, who altered policy — that is the identity network's narrative.

recap: Audit policy is reconciled with the STIG baseline, not reinvented.
DCs and admin hosts write the designed event families.
Additions are GPO-visible and documented.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 builds the collector those events will flow to.

lessons.title: Build the collector
lessons.summary: SBD-SYSLOG01 becomes the funnel: Windows Event Forwarding brings in the events of every Windows system that exists by source-initiated subscription, and a syslog receiver takes the core router's denies and, from lesson 5, the Linux servers over TLS — one host where the network's record first lands.
objectives: Configure the Windows Event Collector service and a source-initiated subscription.
Enroll the sources by GPO with read access to their Security logs.
Stand up the syslog intake for UDP 514 and TLS on TCP 6514.
steps: On SBD-SYSLOG01, run wecutil qc /q, move the ForwardedEvents log file to D:\Logs\ForwardedEvents, and create the subscription SBD-ForwardedSecurity from an XML file: SourceInitiated, MinLatency delivery (push, 30-second batches), into ForwardedEvents, with two queries — the whole Security log (event 4616 included), and the Microsoft-Windows-Time-Service events 12, 35, 36, 37, 129, and 142 from the System log that course 1.3 keeps. Allow one computer group, SBD Event Sources, created from AdminJumpBox01 and holding every Windows system that exists now: both DCs, SBD-SUBCA01, SBD-PKI-MGMT01, SBD-DHCP01, and the three admin seats. The default allows Domain Computers, which does not include domain controllers.

From AdminJumpBox01, enroll the sources with one GPO linked to the Domain Controllers, Tier 0 Servers, Servers, and Admin sub-OUs and security-filtered to SBD Event Sources (Authenticated Users keep read), so the collector and later servers stay out until a course adds them: the subscription manager Server=http://SBD-SYSLOG01.sbd.test:5985/wsman/SubscriptionManager/WEC,Refresh=60, the WinRM service set to automatic, and NETWORK SERVICE in Event Log Readers — on the DCs through the domain's built-in group, on the other sources as a local group preference. Restart each source so the group changes apply; the sources push, the collector reads nothing.

Allow WinRM 5985 inbound on the collector only from the enrolled sources: VLANs 10 and 60, SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 (10.0.30.20 and 10.0.30.30), and SBD-DHCP01 (10.0.20.10), which shares VLAN 20, so only this host firewall scopes it. Rule F17 covers every Windows member; each later course widens this scope when it enrolls new sources. Kerberos authenticates both ends and encrypts the forwarded events, even over HTTP.

Install the approved syslog receiver as a service: UDP 514 for the core router, which already sends its deny log to this address (rule F24), and TCP 6514 with TLS using an SBD Server Authentication certificate for SBD-SYSLOG01.sbd.test, requested from the course 1.6 issuing CA through its process after adding SBD-SYSLOG01 to the SBD TLS Servers group. Write daily files per sender under D:\Logs\Syslog, and allow each port only from its registered senders.
Confirm the register rows are the only paths in use: WinRM from the enrolled sources (F17), syslog from the core (F24), and nothing listening that the design didn't ask for.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-SYSLOG01 (Tier 1 session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01): the subscription, the first events, and the listeners.
wecutil es
wecutil gs SBD-ForwardedSecurity
Get-WinEvent -LogName ForwardedEvents -MaxEvents 20 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, MachineName
Get-NetUDPEndpoint -LocalPort 514
Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 6514,5985 -State Listen
# On each source, from its tier's seat: Network Service is in Event Log Readers, and the forwarder connected (events 104 and 100).
net localgroup "Event Log Readers"
Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-Forwarding/Operational' -MaxEvents 5 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, Message
lessons.check: The subscription is enabled, events from every member of SBD Event Sources — Security and Time-Service — appear in ForwardedEvents with correct source machine names, router deny entries arrive in the syslog files, and only the registered ports listen.
lessons.evidence: Record the subscription XML and wecutil gs output, the enrolling GPO report, the first forwarded event per source, a received router deny line, and the listener list.

model.label: Follow a log, step 1
model.text: SBD-DC01 pushes its subscribed security events to the collector under rule F17.

quizzes.question: Why source-initiated subscriptions rather than the collector pulling?
answers: Pulling is impossible on Windows
Sources push to one known collector, so no account with read-everything rights roams the network
Push is the only mode GPO supports
quizzes.explanation: Collector-initiated collection needs a credential that can read every source's logs — exactly the kind of credential tiering just eliminated.

quizzes.question: The admin seats forward, but neither DC appears in the subscription. What is the likely cause?
answers: The subscription still allows only Domain Computers, which does not include domain controllers
Domain controllers cannot forward events
The DCs need UDP 514 open
quizzes.explanation: Domain controllers belong to the Domain Controllers group, not Domain Computers. Naming a group that holds every intended source fixes it and keeps the allowed list explicit.

quizzes.question: How do you know a forwarded event really came from DC02?
answers: All events look identical
The collector renames events randomly
The MachineName on the event record in ForwardedEvents
quizzes.explanation: Forwarded events keep their source identity — which is what makes the central copy usable as a record at all.

recap: Sources push by subscription; the collector reaches into nothing.
Windows sources and router records land in two named streams.
Only registered paths carry the pipeline.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 keeps the collector trustworthy once it is running.

lessons.title: Keep the collector trustworthy
lessons.summary: A collector that silently stops is worse than none, because everyone assumes it works. Watch the subscription's runtime status, the sources that went quiet, the log's size and overwrite behavior, the disk, and the syslog intake — and decide who is told when collection fails.
objectives: Read subscription runtime status and find silent sources.
Size the ForwardedEvents log and data volume for the design's buffer.
Define what a collection failure is and who responds.
steps: Read wecutil gr SBD-ForwardedSecurity: each source shows a runtime status and its last heartbeat. A source that is inactive, or whose last heartbeat is older than the subscription's heartbeat interval (wecutil gs shows it), has gone silent — check its Microsoft-Windows-Forwarding/Operational log first.

Set the ForwardedEvents log's size and behavior with wevtutil sl: overwrite the oldest events (/rt:false) so new events are never refused, sized so the oldest event is always older than the buffer period you chose in lesson 1. Overwriting is safe only while courses 1.11 and 1.12 pick events up well inside that window; a full log in retain mode would drop new events instead.
Check the data volume and the syslog intake: free space on D:, both listeners up, and today's file growing for every registered sender. A sender with no file today is a silent source too.

Write the failure response (AU-5): a stopped Windows Event Collector service, an inactive source, the oldest event younger than the buffer, a data volume past the fill level you set (dependent on your environment; record the value you chose), or a silent syslog sender. The logging owner is told the same day, restores collection, and records the gap window. Until course 1.12 turns these into alerts, run the check daily and keep each result.
lessons.command:
wecutil gr SBD-ForwardedSecurity
wevtutil sl ForwardedEvents /ms:4294967296 /rt:false   # 4 GB in this sample: size it to hold your chosen buffer
wevtutil gl ForwardedEvents
Get-WinEvent -LogName ForwardedEvents -Oldest -MaxEvents 1 | Select-Object TimeCreated
Get-Volume -DriveLetter D | Select-Object SizeRemaining, Size
Get-ChildItem D:\Logs\Syslog -Recurse -File | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 FullName, LastWriteTime
lessons.check: Every enrolled source is active with a recent heartbeat, ForwardedEvents overwrites oldest-first and holds more than the chosen buffer period, the data volume has headroom, every registered syslog sender wrote today, and the failure response names its owner.
lessons.evidence: Keep the runtime status output, the log configuration, the oldest-event time, the volume figures, and the written failure response with its first daily check.

model.label: SBD-SYSLOG01
model.text: The collector's listeners and its two downstream paths, F10 and F11.

quizzes.question: A DC stopped forwarding last night. Where does it first show on the collector?
answers: Nowhere — WEF has no status
In the subscription's runtime status: the source is inactive or its last heartbeat is old
As an error on the DC's desktop
quizzes.explanation: The collector keeps each source's heartbeat and bookmark. wecutil gr is the first place a silent source becomes visible.

quizzes.question: Why overwrite the oldest events instead of retaining them when the log fills?
answers: Retain mode refuses new events once the log is full, so the newest record — usually the one you need — would be lost
Overwrite mode encrypts the log
Retain mode deletes the whole log
quizzes.explanation: The collector is a buffer, not the archive. Size it larger than the pickup window so overwriting only ever removes events already copied downstream.

quizzes.question: What makes a collection failure a control rather than a surprise?
answers: A larger disk
Restarting the collector weekly
A defined failure condition, a named owner who is told, and a recorded gap window
quizzes.explanation: AU-5 asks for an alert to named people and a defined response. The daily check is that response until course 1.12 automates it.

recap: Runtime status and heartbeats show silent sources.
The log is sized past the buffer and overwrites oldest-first.
Collection failures have a definition, an owner, and a record.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 proves collection with real events and closes the course.

lessons.title: Prove collection and hand off
lessons.summary: Prove the collector with events you cause on purpose: a failed sign-in, a denied probe, and a test message from SBD-REPO01, the first Linux source. Each must land with the right source name and time — then the cadence scans close the course.
objectives: Trace a failed sign-in and a router deny to the collector.
Enroll SBD-REPO01 as the first syslog-over-TLS source.
Baseline SBD-SYSLOG01, rescan the DCs, and write the handoff.
steps: Generate one failed sign-in on SBD-DC01 with a wrong password for a tier admin account. Find event 4625 in the DC's Security log, then in ForwardedEvents with MachineName SBD-DC01 and the same time; compare the delay with the 30-second delivery setting.

Probe one unregistered port across the core — from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, TCP 23 on SBD-DHCP01 — and find the router's deny line (rule F24) in the syslog files with the right source, destination, port, and time. Attempt and deny now form an evidence pair.

Enroll SBD-REPO01 (rule F07): install rsyslog's TLS driver, rsyslog-gnutls, with dnf from REPO01's own repository; in a file under /etc/rsyslog.d, point the driver's CA file at the system trust bundle, which holds the course 1.6 root that course 1.9 placed there, and forward to SBD-SYSLOG01.sbd.test on TCP 6514 with x509/name authentication, so the collector's certificate name is checked; then check the configuration and restart rsyslog. Add REPO01 to the 6514 sender list, send a test message with logger, and find it in REPO01's daily file.

Run the cadence: SBD-SYSLOG01's first SCAP baseline with the course 1.4 benchmark and tool versions, run locally in a Tier 1 session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 with SCC copied from that seat's course 1.8 copy over PowerShell remoting and its hash checked, and a rescan of both DCs from AdminJumpBox01, attributing the deltas to lesson 2's audit policy.

Write the handoff to course 1.11: the two streams, their pickup folders, the buffer period you chose, which the archive job must stay inside, the gap windows the daily check records (those days need re-exporting once a source replays its backlog), and the F11 row waiting for SBD-AUDIT01.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-SYSLOG01 (Tier 1 session): the failed sign-in, and the router's deny of the probe to SBD-DHCP01.
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='ForwardedEvents'; Id=4625; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} | Select-Object TimeCreated, MachineName
Select-String -Path D:\Logs\Syslog\*\*.log -Pattern '10\.0\.20\.10' | Select-Object -Last 3
# On SBD-REPO01: the TLS driver, then /etc/rsyslog.d/sbd-forward.conf:
sudo dnf install rsyslog-gnutls
#   global(DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile="/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt")
#   *.* action(type="omfwd" target="SBD-SYSLOG01.sbd.test" port="6514" protocol="tcp"
#          StreamDriver="gtls" StreamDriverMode="1" StreamDriverAuthMode="x509/name"
#          StreamDriverPermittedPeers="SBD-SYSLOG01.sbd.test")
# Check the configuration, restart, confirm the TLS session, then send the test message.
sudo rsyslogd -N1
sudo systemctl restart rsyslog
ss -tn 'dport = :6514'
logger -t sbd-collector-proof 'SBD-REPO01 syslog over TLS test'
# Back on SBD-SYSLOG01: the test message in REPO01's daily file.
Select-String -Path D:\Logs\Syslog\*\*.log -Pattern 'sbd-collector-proof' | Select-Object -First 3
# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: this course's evidence, hashed.
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\logging-pipeline\*
lessons.check: The failed sign-in, the router deny, and REPO01's test message each appear on the collector with the right source and a time that matches the source; SBD-SYSLOG01 has its first baseline; and the DC rescan deltas are attributed to the audit policy.
lessons.evidence: Keep the three traces with their timestamps, REPO01's forwarding configuration, the scan set with hashes, and the handoff note to course 1.11.

model.label: Follow a log, step 2
model.text: SBD-REPO01 opens a syslog-over-TLS session to the collector under rule F07.

quizzes.question: What does a deliberately caused event prove that configuration checks don't?
answers: That event IDs exist
That the collector has a certificate
That a real record travels from source to collector with its source name and time intact
quizzes.explanation: Every setting can look right while nothing arrives. One known event, found where it should be, is the integration test.

quizzes.question: Why does SBD-REPO01 use syslog over TLS on TCP 6514 rather than UDP 514?
answers: TLS protects the messages in transit and lets REPO01 check it is talking to the real collector; UDP 514 has neither encryption nor delivery guarantees
UDP 514 does not work on Linux
TCP 6514 is faster
quizzes.explanation: RFC 5425 maps syslog onto TLS. The router's UDP 514 stream stays inside the register as rule F24, a known, recorded exception.

quizzes.question: Why scan the DCs again in a logging course?
answers: Scans are required weekly
Lesson 2 changed their audit policy, and a change triggers a rescan whose deltas are attributed to it
The collector cannot work without a scan
quizzes.explanation: Change-triggered rescans are the course 1.5 cadence. The deltas should match lesson 2's documented additions — nothing more.

recap: A failed sign-in, a deny, and a Linux message all landed with the right names and times.
SBD-REPO01 is the first syslog-over-TLS source.
Baselines, rescans, and the handoff to course 1.11 close the course.
lessons.next: That completes course 1.10. Course 1.11 gives the record its protected home on SBD-AUDIT01, picking up the two streams this course collects.

prerequisites: Complete course 1.10: SBD-SYSLOG01 collects Windows events into the ForwardedEvents log (on D:\Logs\ForwardedEvents, overwriting the oldest) and syslog into daily files per sender under D:\Logs\Syslog, keeps the buffer period course 1.10 recorded, and the register carries row F11 waiting for this course.

Provision SBD-AUDIT01 (10.0.50.40, VLAN 50) as Windows Server with a separate data volume (D: in this sample), ready to join sbd.test, with the hypervisor's time synchronization turned off; lesson 1 sizes the volume.

Have course 1.8's administration seats in place — the audit custodian's separate accounts in SBD Audit Custodians work from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (rule A04), and directory changes are Tier 0 work from AdminJumpBox01 — plus the Tier 1 SCC copy course 1.8 installed on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, at course 1.4's tool and benchmark versions, for the first baseline.
labNote: This is the second of three logging courses: course 1.10 collects the record on SBD-SYSLOG01, this course gives it a protected home on SBD-AUDIT01, and course 1.12 analyzes a working copy in SBD-SPLUNK01. Protection is something you can show: one write path, permissions that refuse even administrators, a hash for every archive, and retention that runs only as an approved, logged process. How long each stage keeps the record depends on your environment and policy: the course says what each stage keeps and why, and you record the periods you chose.

Microsoft · Advanced audit policy configuration (File System, Detailed File Share)

DISA · SRG/STIG tools (SCC and STIG Viewer)
