lessons.title: Design the repository and build SBD-AUDIT01
lessons.summary: The repository has one job: keep the collector's record intact for its whole retention period, even from its own administrators. Size it, fix the one way in, name every identity and what it may do, and build SBD-AUDIT01 where the model puts it — before a single archive arrives.
objectives: Size the repository for the retention period you record and the volume the collector actually receives.
Define the single write path and the identities that may write, read, and delete.
Build SBD-AUDIT01 in its own OU, administered only by the audit custodian.
steps: Write the repository's rules from course 1.10's design (AU-11): the collector buffers long enough to cover a missed archive night and a source replaying its backlog; the repository keeps the protected copy for the whole retention period your records policy requires; and analysis keeps a shorter searchable window for investigations. Each period depends on your environment and policy — record the values you chose and who approved them. The repository holds the protected copy and nothing else — it is not a search tool, and nothing is removed from it except by the custodian's approved, logged retention process.

Size it (AU-4): on SBD-SYSLOG01, export the last 24 hours of ForwardedEvents to a temporary file and add up the syslog files written in the same day. Multiply a typical day by the days in your recorded retention period, add headroom for growth (the fleet joins in course 1.13, so revisit the figure then), and record the D: size and a disk-space warning threshold set the way the collector's is — a value that depends on your environment, recorded with the reason.

Fix the one way in (rule F11): SBD-SYSLOG01 writes to the LogArchive share over SMB 3 with encryption as SBD-Archive$, a group managed service account (gMSA) whose password no person knows. Nothing else connects to the share; people work on SBD-AUDIT01 itself, in sessions opened from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 under rule A04.

Name every other identity and its one job: SBD-Catalog$ hashes arrivals, SBD-Retention$ is the only account the design lets delete, SBD Auditors read the record in remote sessions from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, and SBD Audit Custodians (course 1.8) — the custodian's separate admin accounts — run the server but can't delete records either. In a Tier 0 session from AdminJumpBox01, create SBD Auditors under the Groups OU, add it to SBD-ADMIN-SRV01's seat GPO beside SBD Tier 1 Admins and SBD Audit Custodians (Allow log on locally, a change to course 1.8's STIG value that its exception record notes), and run Get-KdsRootKey on SBD-DC01. If it returns nothing, create the forest's one KDS root key with Add-KdsRootKey -EffectiveImmediately now: domain controllers wait up to ten hours before gMSAs can be created and used, so lesson 2 creates the accounts.

Build SBD-AUDIT01 (10.0.50.40, VLAN 50) as Windows Server with its data volume, DNS on both domain controllers, and time from the domain hierarchy (course 1.3): hypervisor time synchronization off, and w32tm /query /source naming a domain controller. Join it into a new Audit Servers OU (OU=Audit Servers,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test, created from AdminJumpBox01 with deletion protection) that already carries course 1.5's member-server STIG GPOs and course 1.8's two deny GPOs (the tier logon GPO and the network-logon deny GPO, never its Servers administrators GPO), so nothing granted to ordinary server administrators through the Servers OU reaches it. By GPO on that OU, make SBD Audit Custodians the local Administrators in place of Domain Admins, as the STIG's member-server rule requires, put SBD Auditors in Remote Management Users, and scope Remote Desktop and Windows Remote Management to SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (10.0.60.20). Its Windows updates come through SBD-WSUS01 once course 1.14 builds it, in a group of their own: downloaded only, and installed when the custodian starts them, never by ordinary Tier 1 operators.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-SYSLOG01 (Tier 1 session): one day of each stream, for sizing.
wevtutil epl ForwardedEvents $env:TEMP\sizing.evtx "/q:*[System[TimeCreated[timediff(@SystemTime) <= 86400000]]]" /ow:true
(Get-Item $env:TEMP\sizing.evtx).Length / 1MB
(Get-ChildItem D:\Logs\Syslog -Recurse -File | Where-Object LastWriteTime -gt (Get-Date).AddDays(-1) | Measure-Object Length -Sum).Sum / 1MB
# From AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): the KDS root key's effective time, and where SBD-AUDIT01 landed.
Invoke-Command SBD-DC01 { Get-KdsRootKey | Select-Object KeyId, EffectiveTime }
Get-ADGroup 'SBD Auditors' | Select-Object DistinguishedName
Get-ADComputer SBD-AUDIT01 | Select-Object DistinguishedName
# From SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (custodian account): who administers SBD-AUDIT01.
Invoke-Command SBD-AUDIT01 { Get-LocalGroupMember Administrators; w32tm /query /source }
lessons.check: The rules with their recorded retention periods, the sizing, and the identity table are written; the KDS root key exists with its effective time recorded; and SBD-AUDIT01 sits in the Audit Servers OU with SBD Audit Custodians in place of Domain Admins and management allowed from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 alone, and its time comes from a domain controller.
lessons.evidence: Keep the repository rules and sizing sheet, the identity table (who writes, reads, deletes, and administers), the KDS root key's ID and effective time, and SBD-AUDIT01's OU placement and local Administrators list.

model.label: SBD-AUDIT01
model.text: The repository's one inbound path, rule F11, and the controls it carries.

quizzes.question: Why does SBD-AUDIT01 get its own OU instead of joining the Servers OU?
answers: Windows Server can't join an OU named Servers
So nothing granted to ordinary server administrators through the Servers OU — such as local administrator rights — reaches the repository
OUs make the archive share faster
quizzes.explanation: Policy follows links. A separate OU, with the STIG and tier policies linked to it, keeps the repository's administration with the custodian alone (rule A04).

quizzes.question: Why create the KDS root key at the start of this lesson?
answers: Domain controllers wait up to ten hours after it is created before gMSAs can be created and used
It encrypts the archive share
SBD-AUDIT01 can't join the domain without it
quizzes.explanation: The wait lets the key replicate to every domain controller first. A forest needs only one KDS root key; later courses reuse it.

quizzes.question: Which identity may delete records from the repository?
answers: Any member of SBD Audit Custodians
SBD-Archive$, because it wrote them
Only SBD-Retention$, running the approved, logged retention process
quizzes.explanation: Deletion is a process, not a person's privilege. The writer, the readers, and even the custodians' admin accounts hold no delete right on the record.

recap: The repository keeps the record for the whole recorded retention period; the collector and analysis keep shorter working copies.
One write path (F11), one writer, and one identity that can delete.
SBD-AUDIT01 is built in its own OU and run only by the custodian, who also installs its updates.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 builds the archive path: the managed accounts, the permissions, the encrypted share, and the tasks that write and catalog each day's record.

lessons.title: Archive, hash, and protect the record
lessons.summary: The repository is where the record outlives mistakes and attackers alike: daily archives from the collector over an encrypted share, hashed before they leave and again on arrival, readable by few, and deletable by process only.
objectives: Archive the collector's two streams to the repository every day.
Hash and catalog every archive on arrival.
Enforce create-without-delete, read-few, and delete-by-process-only permissions.
steps: From AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0), create the three gMSAs now that the KDS root key is in effect, each usable by one computer only: New-ADServiceAccount SBD-Archive -DNSHostName SBD-Archive.sbd.test -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword 'SBD-SYSLOG01$', then SBD-Catalog and SBD-Retention the same way for 'SBD-AUDIT01$'. That allowed-computer list is each account's real access list: an administrator of that computer can act as the account, so it names one host.

On SBD-AUDIT01, create D:\LogArchive with ForwardedEvents, Syslog, Catalog, and Retention folders, remove its inherited permissions (icacls D:\LogArchive /inheritance:r), and grant, inheritable to everything below: SYSTEM full control; read and execute (RX) to SBD Audit Custodians, SBD Auditors, SBD-Catalog$, and SBD-Retention$; and OWNER RIGHTS read permissions only on files, '*S-1-3-4:(OI)(IO)(RC)', which takes away a file owner's implicit right to rewrite its permissions. On each stream folder, give SBD-Archive$ create files on that folder only — icacls D:\LogArchive\ForwardedEvents /grant 'SBD\SBD-Archive$:(WD,RA,S)' — and SBD-Retention$ delete on its files, 'SBD\SBD-Retention$:(OI)(IO)(DE)'. A file's creator gets the access it asks for while creating it, then only what the file inherits, so the writer can add archives but never read, replace, or delete them.

Share it: New-SmbShare -Name LogArchive -Path D:\LogArchive -EncryptData $true -ChangeAccess 'SBD\SBD-Archive$'. Share permissions are only the outer gate for network access — effective access is the stricter of share and NTFS — so the share names its one writer, and Get-SmbShareAccess must show nobody else, not even Everyone. Leave RejectUnencryptedAccess at its default (True) with SMB 1 off, so only encrypted SMB 3 sessions reach the share, and scope every enabled inbound rule for TCP 445 to 10.0.20.20: VLAN 50 will also hold SBD-SPLUNK01 (course 1.12) and the other security servers Inside the Network places there, whose traffic to this server never crosses the core, so only this host firewall stops them.

On SBD-SYSLOG01 (Tier 1 work), register the archive task to run daily at 01:00 as SBD-Archive$: Register-ScheduledTask with New-ScheduledTaskPrincipal -UserId 'SBD\SBD-Archive$' -LogonType Password — no password is typed; Windows retrieves the managed one. Keep the script in a folder only administrators can change, because whoever can edit it acts as the writer. Through a GPO filtered to SBD-SYSLOG01 and linked above the STIG GPO, give SBD-Archive$ Log on as a batch job and add it to Event Log Readers with a Group Policy preference that adds a member rather than replacing the list (course 1.12 adds the Splunk forwarder's account to the same group the same way) — user rights don't merge across GPOs, so the list repeats any entries the STIG sets for that right — then grant it read on D:\Logs\Syslog and a staging folder of its own, and send the grants to the owner of the course 1.5 exception record on AdminJumpBox01.

Each run, the script exports every completed UTC day not yet archived from ForwardedEvents into its staging folder — wevtutil epl with a TimeCreated filter for that day — and zips that day's syslog files, so a missed night is caught up while the collector's buffer still holds the events. It writes each file's SHA-256 (Get-FileHash) into a .sha256 file, copies the archive and then its .sha256 to the share, and keeps its own list of what it sent, because the writer can't list the share. When course 1.10's health check records a gap window, re-export the affected days once the source has replayed its backlog, under a new name such as ForwardedEvents-2026-10-12-r1.evtx: forwarded events keep their source's times, so the late ones land in the right day, and the first archive stays as it was.

On SBD-AUDIT01, register the catalog task the same way, hourly as SBD-Catalog$, with Log on as a batch job through the Audit Servers OU's policy and write, but not delete, on the Catalog folder and the files in it. For each archive whose .sha256 has arrived, it computes the SHA-256, appends a line to catalog.csv (columns Arrived, File, Size, SentSHA256, SHA256, Result), and writes the same line as an event from the source SBD-Repository (registered once with New-EventLog): 1000 when the hashes match, 1001 when they don't or a .sha256 is still missing after the wait you set and recorded — a finding, not a file. Then fill in the AU table: where each stage's data lives, its retention clock, and who can touch it — the kind of artifact course 2.2 shows joining the Body of Evidence for the audit controls.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-AUDIT01 (custodian session): the share, its encryption, its one writer, and a stream folder's permissions.
Get-SmbShare -Name LogArchive | Select-Object Name, Path, EncryptData
Get-SmbShareAccess -Name LogArchive
Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select-Object RejectUnencryptedAccess, EnableSMB1Protocol
icacls D:\LogArchive\ForwardedEvents
# On SBD-SYSLOG01 (Tier 1 session): the task's identity and its last result (0 = success).
(Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'SBD Archive to AUDIT01').Principal | Select-Object UserId, LogonType
Get-ScheduledTaskInfo -TaskName 'SBD Archive to AUDIT01' | Select-Object LastRunTime, LastTaskResult
# Back on SBD-AUDIT01: who wrote the newest archives, and their catalog lines.
Get-ChildItem D:\LogArchive\ForwardedEvents | Sort-Object Name | Select-Object -Last 2 Name, Length, @{n='Owner';e={(Get-Acl $_.FullName).Owner}}
Import-Csv D:\LogArchive\Catalog\catalog.csv | Select-Object -Last 4
lessons.check: Daily archives and their .sha256 files arrive owned by SBD-Archive$ on a share that requires encryption and refuses unencrypted access, every catalog line shows matching hashes, Get-SmbShareAccess lists the writer alone, and icacls shows delete rights for SYSTEM and SBD-Retention$ only.
lessons.evidence: Keep the share, encryption, and permission listings, the two task definitions with their gMSA principals, the first catalog lines, and the completed AU table.

model.label: Follow a log, step 4
model.text: The collector writes a retained copy to SBD-AUDIT01 under rule F11.

quizzes.question: What does the hash catalog actually protect against?
answers: Disk space exhaustion
Silent modification — an archive that no longer matches its recorded hash announces itself as tampered or corrupted
Slow searches
quizzes.explanation: Integrity is only provable if you recorded what intact looked like. The catalog is that record.

quizzes.question: How does anything ever get deleted from the repository?
answers: Any administrator's right-click
The analysis system prunes it
Only the documented, logged retention process
quizzes.explanation: The point of the repository is surviving its administrators. Deletion exists — as a process with a log, never a privilege.

quizzes.question: Where does the AU table go after this course?
answers: Into the Body of Evidence for the audit controls — course 2.2 shows how artifacts like it are organized
Back into course 1.1, retroactively
Nowhere — it is decorative
quizzes.explanation: Where the records live, how long, and who reads them is precisely what the audit control family asks an assessor to verify.

recap: Archives arrive daily over one encrypted path, with two hashes that must agree.
Readers are named; deletion is a process, not a right.
The AU table is written for the authorization path.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 verifies the catalog every day and watches who touches the repository.

lessons.title: Verify the catalog and watch the repository
lessons.summary: A catalog nobody checks is a list of hopes. Re-hash every archive on a schedule, treat a mismatch as a finding, audit who reads or tries to change the repository, and keep the readers as few as the day they were approved.
objectives: Verify every archive against the catalog on a schedule and report the result.
Handle a mismatch as a finding, not a file to fix.
Audit access to the repository and review who may read and write it.
steps: Add a daily verification task on SBD-AUDIT01, running as SBD-Catalog$ like the catalog task: it re-hashes every archive and writes D:\LogArchive\Catalog\verify-<date>.csv with one row per file and its result — OK, MISMATCH, MISSING (cataloged but absent, or a day with no archive), or UNKNOWN (present but never cataloged). It then writes one event from SBD-Repository: 1100 when every row is OK, 1101 when any isn't.

Treat event 1101 as a finding: don't re-hash the file until it passes, edit its catalog line, or delete it. Record what failed and when it last verified, and read the repository's access events for that window. Re-export that day under a new name through the normal path while the collector's buffer still holds it — or, once course 1.19 has made them, recover an offline copy — keep the damaged file as evidence, and have the custodian report an incident.

Audit the repository itself: in a separate GPO linked to the Audit Servers OU, recorded as a documented addition with the exception record's owner, turn on Audit File System (success and failure) and Audit Detailed File Share (failure). On D:\LogArchive, add auditing entries for failed access of any kind by Everyone; successful delete, change permissions, and take ownership by Everyone; and successful reads by SBD Auditors and SBD Audit Custodians. File System auditing writes events only where those entries match, so the service accounts' routine work stays quiet.

Send that trail off the box: from AdminJumpBox01, add SBD-AUDIT01 to SBD Event Sources, link course 1.10's enrolling GPO to the Audit Servers OU, and restart SBD-AUDIT01 so both apply. On the collector, widen the WinRM 5985 scope to 10.0.50.40 (rule F17): its Security log, with events 4656, 4660, 4663, 4670, and 5145, now arrives through the subscription's Security query, so add only a query for its SBD-Repository events in the Application log, filtered to that computer. Someone who can alter SBD-AUDIT01's logs or its catalog still can't reach the copies on the collector, which other administrators run.

Review the people each quarter and after any change: compare SBD Auditors, SBD Audit Custodians, and SBD-AUDIT01's local Administrators with the approved list, and check that only SBD-SYSLOG01 may retrieve SBD-Archive$'s password — any computer added there could write as the archive job. Record the review with its date and reviewer.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-AUDIT01 (custodian session): the latest verification's exceptions, and the result events.
$report = Get-ChildItem D:\LogArchive\Catalog\verify-*.csv | Sort-Object Name | Select-Object -Last 1
Import-Csv $report.FullName | Where-Object Result -ne 'OK'
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Application'; ProviderName='SBD-Repository'; Id=1100,1101} -MaxEvents 3 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id
# The audit policy and the auditing entries on the repository.
auditpol /get /subcategory:"File System"
auditpol /get /subcategory:"Detailed File Share"
(Get-Acl D:\LogArchive -Audit).Audit | Format-Table IdentityReference, FileSystemRights, AuditFlags
# On SBD-SYSLOG01 (Tier 1 session): the repository's events arrive with their source name.
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='ForwardedEvents'; Id=4656,4663,1100,1101; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddDays(-1)} -MaxEvents 5 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, MachineName
# From AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): the readers, and the computers allowed to act as the writer.
Get-ADGroupMember 'SBD Auditors' | Select-Object Name, SamAccountName
(Get-ADServiceAccount SBD-Archive -Properties PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword).PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword
lessons.check: Today's report covers every archive and its event is 1100 (or an open 1101 is being handled as a finding), the audit policy and auditing entries are in place, the repository's events reach ForwardedEvents on the collector with MachineName SBD-AUDIT01, and the readers review is recorded.
lessons.evidence: Keep a verification report with its event, the audit policy and auditing-entry listings, one forwarded repository event, and the dated readers review.

quizzes.question: The daily verification reports a MISMATCH. What is the right first move?
answers: Re-hash the file until the result is OK
Update the catalog line to the new hash
Keep the file as evidence, record the finding, and read the access events since it last verified
quizzes.explanation: A mismatch is a finding, not a file. The catalog line records what intact looked like; changing it would erase the evidence that something happened.

quizzes.question: Why are the repository's own access events forwarded to the collector?
answers: So someone who can alter SBD-AUDIT01's logs still can't erase the copy that left the box
Forwarding makes the events smaller
SBD-AUDIT01 can't keep a Security log
quizzes.explanation: Audit information must be protected from the people it describes. The forwarded copy lives on another system with other administrators.

quizzes.question: Why must only SBD-SYSLOG01 be allowed to retrieve SBD-Archive$'s password?
answers: Otherwise the gMSA password stops rotating
Any computer allowed there could write archives as the archive job
SBD-AUDIT01 needs the password to read archives
quizzes.explanation: The allowed-computer list is the gMSA's real access list. Reviewing it is part of reviewing who can write to the record.

recap: Every archive is re-hashed daily, and the result is an event.
A mismatch is preserved and investigated, never re-hashed away.
Access to the repository is audited, forwarded, and reviewed.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 runs retention as a process and proves an old archive can still be read.

lessons.title: Run retention and prove retrieval
lessons.summary: Retention cuts both ways: records must last the full period, and they must go when it ends — by a process with a log, never by a person's right-click. Run retention the way the design says, then prove the other half: an archive from the past can be found, verified, and read.
objectives: Run retention through an approved, logged process under its own identity.
Show that nothing younger than the retention period can be removed.
Retrieve a past archive, verify its hash, and read its events.
steps: Build the retention task on SBD-AUDIT01 to run as SBD-Retention$ (batch logon, like SBD-Catalog$) with no trigger, so it runs only when the custodian starts it. It reads the newest approved list in D:\LogArchive\Retention, re-verifies each listed archive against the catalog, refuses any file younger than the recorded retention period by its catalog arrival date — whatever the list says — and deletes the rest with their .sha256 files. It appends one line per file to retention-log.csv (date, file, catalog hash, list hash, result), which the daily verification now reads, so a retired archive reports RETIRED rather than MISSING. SBD-Retention$ gets write on the Retention folder and the custodians create files there only, so a list can be added but not edited.

Run it as a two-person process, the independent approval rule A04 asks for (AU-9(5), dual authorization): the custodian prepares the list of archives past retention, an approver who is not a custodian approves it and records the list's SHA-256, and the custodian starts the task with Start-ScheduledTask. The log carries the same list hash, tying the run to the approval, and every deletion also writes events 4663 and 4660 naming SBD-Retention$, which reach the collector.

Prove the guard now: nothing in a new lab is past its retention period, so put one archive from lesson 2 on an approved list marked as a test. The run must refuse it, log the refusal, and leave the file and its catalog line untouched.

Prove retrieval: pick the oldest archive in the catalog, confirm its SHA-256 still matches its catalog line, and read it — Get-WinEvent -Path for a ForwardedEvents archive, or expand a syslog ZIP into D:\Retrieval, a working folder outside the archive, and search it. Security events render because SBD-AUDIT01 has the same Windows publishers; the event data itself is in the file either way.

Record the retrieval — the archive, both hashes, the events you read, who, and when — and repeat it each quarter with an older archive, so over time you prove retrieval across the whole retention period. Course 1.19 retrieves the offline copies the same way.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-AUDIT01 (custodian session): no trigger, so only a person starts a run.
(Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'SBD Repository Retention').Triggers.Count   # expected 0
(Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'SBD Repository Retention').Principal.UserId   # expected: the SBD-Retention$ account
Get-FileHash D:\LogArchive\Retention\approved-test-list.txt   # the hash the approver recorded
Start-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'SBD Repository Retention'
Import-Csv D:\LogArchive\Retention\retention-log.csv | Select-Object -Last 5
# Retrieval: the oldest archive's hash against its catalog line, then the events inside.
$file = Get-ChildItem D:\LogArchive\ForwardedEvents\*.evtx | Sort-Object Name | Select-Object -First 1
(Import-Csv D:\LogArchive\Catalog\catalog.csv | Where-Object File -eq $file.Name).SHA256 -eq (Get-FileHash $file.FullName).Hash
Get-WinEvent -Path $file.FullName -MaxEvents 5 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, MachineName
lessons.check: The retention task has no trigger and runs as SBD-Retention$, the approved test run refused the young archive and logged the refusal with the list's hash, and the retrieved archive's hash matches its catalog line and its events read correctly.
lessons.evidence: Keep the retention task definition, the approved test list with its hash and approval, the retention log, and the retrieval record with both hashes and a sample of the events read.

quizzes.question: Why does the retention task have no schedule?
answers: Scheduled tasks can't delete files
So deletion happens only when the custodian starts an approved run, never silently on a timer
Triggers would slow the server
quizzes.explanation: A timer deletes whether or not anyone looked. An approved, started, logged run makes every deletion a decision two people can account for.

quizzes.question: An approved list includes an archive younger than the retention period. What happens?
answers: The task refuses it, logs the refusal, and leaves the file and its catalog line in place
The task deletes it, because the list was approved
The catalog line is removed but the file stays
quizzes.explanation: The retention period is enforced by the process itself, not by the care of whoever wrote the list. An approval can't shorten the record's life.

quizzes.question: What does a successful retrieval prove that the daily verification doesn't?
answers: That the file still exists
That the hash algorithm is SHA-256
That someone can actually find, verify, and read the record when it is needed
quizzes.explanation: Verification proves the bytes are unchanged; retrieval proves the record is usable for an investigation, which is what retention is for.

recap: Retention runs only on an approved list, under its own identity, with a log.
The task refuses anything younger than the retention period.
A past archive was found, verified, and read — and will be again each quarter.
lessons.next: The final lesson tries to break the record on purpose, takes the first baseline, and hands off to analysis.

lessons.title: Prove the record survives and hand off
lessons.summary: Test the protection the way an attacker or a careless administrator would: try to delete an archive and tamper with a copy, and check that each attempt is refused or caught, and recorded. Then take SBD-AUDIT01's first baseline and hand the record to analysis.
objectives: Show that an administrator's delete attempt is refused and logged on and off the repository.
Show that a tampered copy fails verification against the catalog.
Baseline SBD-AUDIT01 and write the handoff to course 1.12.
steps: In a custodian session on SBD-AUDIT01 — an administrator of this server — try to delete the newest archive with Remove-Item. It must fail with access denied: administrators hold read only, and only SBD-Retention$ can delete. An administrator can still force their way in — by taking ownership, using backup and restore privileges, or running a process as SYSTEM — which is why only the custodians administer this server and those steps are audited too. Use the newest archive, so if the delete wrongly succeeds that day can be re-exported from the collector's buffer — and you have a finding to fix first.

Find the record of the attempt: event 4656, an audit failure naming your account, the archive, and DELETE, in SBD-AUDIT01's Security log — then the same event in ForwardedEvents on SBD-SYSLOG01 with MachineName SBD-AUDIT01. The attempt and its refusal now exist on two systems with different administrators.

Tamper with a copy, never the record: copy the newest archive to D:\Retrieval\tamper-test, append one byte to the copy, and compare its SHA-256 with the catalog line. The copy must fail while the record still matches — the same check that would catch an altered offline copy in course 1.19.

Take SBD-AUDIT01's first SCAP baseline with the course 1.4 SCC and benchmark versions, run locally in the custodian's session: this server refuses SMB from VLAN 60, so a remote scan can't reach it, and the installer arrives from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01's course 1.8 copy over PowerShell remoting (Copy-Item -ToSession) with its course 1.4 hash checked. Store the results under C:\Evidence\audit-repository with hashes, and classify open items as course 1.4 taught — fix by GPO, deviation candidate, or POA&M candidate — noting this course's documented additions: batch-logon rights and object-access auditing.

Write the handoff to course 1.12: the repository keeps the protected copy and stays out of the analysis flow, which takes its working copy from the collector over F10; a day's events reach the repository in the next morning's archive, which is where an end-to-end trace finds them; the repository's events — 1001 and 1101 findings, refused access, and retention deletions — are ready to become alerts; and course 1.19 sets up the backup of the archive and its catalog, which the audit custodian carries to the backup cabinet.
lessons.command:
# Custodian session on SBD-AUDIT01: try to delete the newest archive (expected: access denied).
$newest = Get-ChildItem D:\LogArchive\ForwardedEvents\*.evtx | Sort-Object Name | Select-Object -Last 1
Remove-Item $newest.FullName
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4656; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddMinutes(-15)} | Where-Object KeywordsDisplayNames -contains 'Audit Failure' | Select-Object -First 3 TimeCreated, Id
# On SBD-SYSLOG01 (Tier 1 session): the same refusal, forwarded.
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='ForwardedEvents'; Id=4656; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} | Select-Object TimeCreated, MachineName
# Back on SBD-AUDIT01: a tampered copy fails the catalog check while the record passes.
New-Item -ItemType Directory D:\Retrieval\tamper-test -Force | Out-Null
Copy-Item $newest.FullName D:\Retrieval\tamper-test\
Add-Content "D:\Retrieval\tamper-test\$($newest.Name)" -Value 'x' -NoNewline
$expected = (Import-Csv D:\LogArchive\Catalog\catalog.csv | Where-Object File -eq $newest.Name).SHA256
(Get-FileHash "D:\Retrieval\tamper-test\$($newest.Name)").Hash -eq $expected   # expected False
(Get-FileHash $newest.FullName).Hash -eq $expected   # expected True
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\audit-repository\*
lessons.check: The delete failed and appears as event 4656 on SBD-AUDIT01 and in ForwardedEvents on the collector, the tampered copy fails verification while the record passes, SBD-AUDIT01 has its first baseline, and the handoff names what course 1.12 inherits.
lessons.evidence: Keep the refused delete with both events, the tamper test's hash comparison, the scan set with hashes, and the handoff note to course 1.12.

model.label: Offline backup & recovery
model.text: In course 1.19 the audit custodian carries offline copies of the archive and its catalog here. There is no network path to the cabinet.

quizzes.question: The custodian administers SBD-AUDIT01. Why can't their admin account delete an archive?
answers: Administrators hold only read on the record; delete belongs to SBD-Retention$ alone, through the approved process
Windows never lets administrators delete files
The archive is open in another program
quizzes.explanation: Running the server and owning the record are separate rights. The permissions give the custodians read, and the attempt itself is recorded on two systems.

quizzes.question: Why tamper with a copy instead of the record?
answers: Copies are faster to hash
It proves detection without damaging evidence — the catalog catches a changed copy exactly as it would a changed record
The record can't be read
quizzes.explanation: The check compares bytes with the catalog wherever they sit. Testing on a copy proves the check and leaves the record intact.

quizzes.question: Where does analysis get its data after this course?
answers: From SBD-AUDIT01's archives
From the offline backup cabinet
From the collector over the forwarder path (F10); the repository stays out of the analysis flow
quizzes.explanation: One copy to keep, one copy to question. The protected record never depends on the search tier.

recap: An administrator's delete was refused and recorded on two systems.
A tampered copy failed verification; the record still passes.
SBD-AUDIT01 is baselined, and course 1.12 inherits a protected record.
lessons.next: That completes course 1.11. Course 1.12 builds analysis in SBD-SPLUNK01 on a working copy from the collector and turns the repository's findings into alerts.

prerequisites: Complete courses 1.10 and 1.11: SBD-SYSLOG01 collects the two streams — the ForwardedEvents log on D:\Logs\ForwardedEvents, sized for the buffer course 1.10 recorded, and daily syslog files per sender under D:\Logs\Syslog — SBD-AUDIT01 archives them every night, and the register carries row F10 waiting for this course.

Provision a virtual machine for SBD-SPLUNK01 on VLAN 50 (10.0.50.10) with a separate data volume for the indexes (/srv/splunk in this sample), and have course 1.9's client package for SBD-REPO01 and its Linux assessment set (SCC for Linux and the distribution's STIG benchmark in C:\Staging\DISA\linux on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01), course 1.3's chrony file, course 1.6's root certificate hash, SBD Server Authentication template, and domain controller certificates, and course 1.8's administration seats ready.

Stage across the air gap, hashed as in course 1.4: the Splunk Enterprise package for Linux (.tgz), the universal forwarder installer for Windows (.msi), the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows, an Enterprise license file, and DISA's Splunk Enterprise STIG for lessons 3 and 6 (the Linux scan reuses course 1.9's set).
labNote: This is the last of three logging courses: course 1.10 collects the record on SBD-SYSLOG01, course 1.11 protects it on SBD-AUDIT01, and this course analyzes a working copy in SBD-SPLUNK01, then traces one event through all three. SBD-SPLUNK01 is a single Splunk instance: one server holds every Splunk role this network needs. Analysis is a search someone actually runs and an alert someone owns. Linux commands are for the Red Hat Enterprise Linux–family release course 1.9 chose. Retention periods, alert thresholds and alert expirations depend on your environment and policy: the course says what each one is for, and you record the value you chose.

lessons.title: Plan analysis and build SBD-SPLUNK01
lessons.summary: Analysis works on a copy, not on the record: SBD-AUDIT01 keeps the evidence, and SBD-SPLUNK01 keeps a searchable working copy, for a period your environment sets, for the people who question them. Decide what the single instance holds, its indexes, retention, roles, and console paths first, then build the domain-joined Linux host that runs it — patched only from SBD-REPO01 and on domain time from its first boot.
objectives: Define what analysis is for, what the single instance holds, its indexes and the retention you choose, and who may do what from where.
Stage the Splunk media across the air gap with verified hashes.
Build SBD-SPLUNK01 as a domain-joined Linux server on domain time, patched only from SBD-REPO01.
steps: Decide the shape before the details: SBD-SPLUNK01 is a single instance, the design Splunk calls S1. One installation is the indexer that stores the events, the search head people sign in to, its own license manager, and its own Monitoring Console. There is no deployment server, because one forwarder is configured by hand, and no search peers. That fits this network: one forwarder, a few people searching, and a daily volume far below what one server indexes. Size the VM from Splunk's reference hardware for a single instance (12 physical cores or 24 vCPU, 12 GB of RAM, and at least 800 sustained IOPS on the volume Splunk writes to); a lab this size runs on less, so record what you allocated, and lesson 3's health report tells you when it isn't enough. A single instance has no second copy to switch to: while SBD-SPLUNK01 is down, searching waits, the forwarder picks up where it stopped once it is back, the record keeps reaching SBD-AUDIT01, and course 1.19 restores the configuration.

Write analysis's job and its limits: SBD-SPLUNK01 indexes a working copy of the collector's two streams (rule F10) for searches, dashboards, and alerts, while the protected record stays on SBD-AUDIT01 — when an investigation needs evidence, it retrieves the archive. Plan one index per stream, sbd_wineventlog for the forwarded Windows events and sbd_syslog for the syslog files, each searchable for as long as investigations in your environment need to look back and then deleted, because the repository already keeps the record for its own retention period. The period depends on your environment and policy; record the value you chose and why. Size each from a typical day times that period plus headroom, starting from course 1.11's daily figures until lesson 2 measures what Splunk actually stores, and cap its size above that, so age rather than size retires the data. Then size the volume for both caps, Splunk's own indexes (_internal, _audit), which live there too, and lesson 3's free-space reserve: per the current STIG, Splunk stops indexing once the volume is three-quarters full, so everything you plan to keep must fit in that three-quarters.

Decide who does what: analysts (sbd_analyst) search and review alerts but change nothing, administrators (sbd_admin) manage inputs, indexes, roles, and alerts, and no role used by people gets delete_by_keyword, so nothing in the working copy can be quietly removed. People sign in with domain accounts over LDAPS, their role set by group (SBD Splunk Analysts, SBD Splunk Admins), never with a Tier 0 account, whose password would cross a Tier 1 server's sign-in page. The install-time admin becomes the one local emergency account, sealed in lesson 3. Splunk listens on four ports: Splunk Web (TCP 8000), the receiving port (TCP 9997), splunkd's management port (TCP 8089), and the KV store (TCP 8191). Only Splunk Web and the receiving port, with SSH, are in the register: no other host calls the management port or the KV store in this design, so the host firewall never admits them. Splunk Web and SSH answer VLAN 60 only: analysts and the host's Tier 1 administrators work from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (rule A02), and the Tier 0 operators who own the alerts on the domain controllers, the model's DC-facing scope, from AdminJumpBox01 (rule A01). Splunk's roles can't fence one administrator's alerts from another's, and root on the host can change any Splunk file, so keep both groups small and every change on record.

Stage the media as course 1.4 taught: the Splunk Enterprise package for Linux (.tgz) and the universal forwarder installer for Windows (.msi), each checked on the connected side against the SHA-512 that Splunk publishes for it, plus the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows, your Enterprise license file, and DISA's Splunk Enterprise STIG. Hash the set for the transfer record and check it again on the lab side before anything is opened. Don't plan on the 60-day trial license: Splunk Free has no users, roles, or alerts, and an Enterprise license installs from its file with no connection to Splunk.

Build SBD-SPLUNK01 from hashed install media of the Red Hat Enterprise Linux–family release course 1.9 chose, with the VM's hypervisor time synchronization turned off so the domain controllers are its only clock: the name SBD-SPLUNK01.sbd.test, the static address 10.0.50.10/24 with the core's VLAN 50 interface as gateway (10.0.50.1 in this sample), both domain controllers as DNS servers, and the data volume mounted at /srv/splunk. Before its first update, apply course 1.9's client package, checked against its hashes, so SBD-REPO01 is its only package source (rule F19) and no other source remains; then update from the current snapshot.

Install course 1.3's chrony file, both domain controllers with maxdistance 16, and confirm a controller is selected with a small, steady offset before anything else: Kerberos refuses a clock that is too far from the domain's. Then join sbd.test with realm join --computer-ou='OU=Servers,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' and a Tier 1 account, which course 1.7 allowed to create computers there (rules F01, F02, and F03), permit sign-in only to SBD Tier 1 Admins with realm permit -g, and give that group sudo through a drop-in file; SSSD then registers the host's address in DNS.

Make the host firewall the register's copy, with firewalld: SSH from 10.0.60.20, Splunk Web on TCP 8000 from 10.0.60.10 and 10.0.60.20, and TCP 9997 from SBD-SYSLOG01 (10.0.20.20) alone, and nothing for TCP 8089 or 8191. Then send the host's own syslog, sudo use included, to the collector over TLS (rule F07) as course 1.10 enrolled SBD-REPO01: rsyslog-gnutls from the snapshot, the course 1.6 root placed in the system trust store by hand as course 1.9 placed it on SBD-REPO01 (exported on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 and its SHA-256 checked against course 1.6's record), the collector's certificate name checked, and SBD-SPLUNK01 added to the collector's TCP 6514 sender list.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-SPLUNK01 (Tier 1 SSH session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01)
cd /srv/media && sha256sum -c --quiet SHA256SUMS-splunk.txt   # expected: no output
dnf repolist --all              # expected: only the sbd-repo01 repositories enabled
chronyc sources -v; chronyc tracking   # ^* one controller, ^+ or ^- the other
realm list                      # sbd.test, kerberos-member, one permitted group
openssl x509 -inform der -in /tmp/sbd-root.cer -noout -fingerprint -sha256   # matches course 1.6's record
firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
firewall-cmd --list-all       # SSH, 8000, and 9997 from their sources only; no 8089 or 8191
logger -t sbd-splunk-proof 'SBD-SPLUNK01 syslog over TLS test'
# On SBD-SYSLOG01 (Tier 1 session): the test message in SBD-SPLUNK01's daily file
Select-String -Path D:\Logs\Syslog\*\*.log -Pattern 'sbd-splunk-proof' | Select-Object -First 1
lessons.check: The design names what the single instance holds and the VM's allocation, analysis's job, both indexes with their retention and sizing inside the free-space reserve, the roles and who holds them, and the console paths; the media matches its published and transfer hashes; and SBD-SPLUNK01 resolves to 10.0.50.10, lists SBD-REPO01 as its only package source, has a controller selected with a small, stable offset, is joined with one permitted group, trusts the course 1.6 root whose hash matches that course's record, admits only the registered paths, and its test message arrives on the collector.
lessons.evidence: Keep the analysis design (the single instance and its allocation, job, indexes, the retention period you chose and why, sizing with the reserve, roles, ports and console paths), the media hashes with the transfer record, and SBD-SPLUNK01's build record: package sources, chrony output, realm list, the root certificate's hash compared with course 1.6's record, firewall zones, and its first syslog line on the collector.

model.label: SBD-SPLUNK01
model.text: The analysis server on VLAN 50, its one ingestion path (rule F10), and the controls it carries.

quizzes.question: What is SBD-SPLUNK01's copy of the record for?
answers: Searches, dashboards, and alerts on a working copy — the protected record stays on SBD-AUDIT01
Replacing the repository's archive once Splunk's retention period has passed
Long-term evidence an assessor reads instead of the archive
quizzes.explanation: One copy to keep, one copy to question. When evidence matters, it comes from the repository's hashed archive; Splunk's copy exists to be searched freely.

quizzes.question: Which role may run Splunk's delete command on indexed events?
answers: sbd_admin, because it inherits the admin role
Any analyst who owns the search
None that people use — no role they hold carries delete_by_keyword, so nothing in the working copy can be quietly removed
quizzes.explanation: Splunk's admin role doesn't include delete_by_keyword by default. Keeping it off every role people use means no search can hide what happened.

quizzes.question: Why install an Enterprise license file rather than switching to Splunk Free when the 60-day trial ends?
answers: Splunk Free can't read Windows events
Splunk Free has no users, roles, or alerts, so the analyst role and every alert in this course would stop working
Free licenses need an internet connection
quizzes.explanation: The license decides which features exist. Named accounts, roles, and alerts are the controls this course builds, and the Enterprise license file installs offline.

recap: One single instance keeps a working copy for the period you chose; the record stays on SBD-AUDIT01.
Domain accounts in two roles by group, no delete, consoles on VLAN 60 only.
SBD-SPLUNK01 is joined, on domain time, and patched only from SBD-REPO01.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 prepares the host, installs Splunk, and brings in the collector's two streams over rule F10.

lessons.title: Prepare the host, install Splunk, and bring in the streams
lessons.summary: Prepare SBD-SPLUNK01's hardened Linux for Splunk, then install Splunk Enterprise with the indexes, roles, and TLS receiving port lesson 1 designed, its indexes hashing every event from the first. Put a universal forwarder on SBD-SYSLOG01 that reads the collector's two streams and sends them over rule F10, and finish by proving the copy is faithful: Splunk's counts and times must match the collector's.
objectives: Prepare the host for Splunk: Transparent Huge Pages off, SELinux enforcing, fapolicyd trust, and Splunk's resource limits.
Install Splunk Enterprise with HTTPS, integrity-checked indexes, the roles, and a TLS receiving port, and forward both of the collector's streams over rule F10.
Show that Splunk's event counts and timestamps match the collector's.
steps: Prepare the host before Splunk touches it. Splunk asks for Transparent Huge Pages (THP) to be off on Linux, because THP slows its indexing and searches: add transparent_hugepage=never to every kernel's command line with grubby, reboot, and check that /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled shows [never]. Leave SELinux enforcing, as the distribution's STIG set it. Check whether fapolicyd is running (systemctl is-active fapolicyd): where the STIG turned it on, it blocks programs it doesn't trust, and Splunk, installed from a .tgz rather than an RPM, isn't in its trust database until you add it in the next step.

As root on SBD-SPLUNK01, create the splunk account (the package doesn't), extract the package with tar -xzf into /opt, and give splunk ownership of /opt/splunk and /srv/splunk with mode 700, as the STIG asks for Splunk's directories. Where fapolicyd runs, trust what you extracted before the first start (fapolicyd-cli --file add /opt/splunk/ --trust-file splunk, then fapolicyd-cli --update): it trusts each file by its hash, so do the same for every add-on you install, and refresh it after every upgrade. Before the first start, add SPLUNK_DB=/srv/splunk to /opt/splunk/etc/splunk-launch.conf and, where your rules require FIPS mode, SPLUNK_FIPS=1: Splunk can enter FIPS mode only at its first start (it turns it on by itself if the Linux kernel already runs in FIPS mode), and an instance started without it can't gain it later, even by upgrading. Start it as splunk with --accept-license, create the admin account when prompted (lesson 3 seals it), install the license file, and enable boot-start under systemd (splunk enable boot-start -systemd-managed 1 -user splunk -group splunk). The unit it writes already allows 65,536 open files; add the process limits Splunk recommends in a drop-in (systemctl edit Splunkd: LimitNPROC=16000 and TasksMax=16000), restart, and look for SELinux denials.

Request one SBD Server Authentication certificate for SBD-SPLUNK01.sbd.test through the course 1.6 process, with the key and request made on the host with openssl and the name in both subject and subject alternative name, and keep the key readable by splunk alone. Turn on HTTPS for Splunk Web in web.conf (enableSplunkWebSSL, serverCert, privKeyPath) and install the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows, trusted by fapolicyd like the rest. In a small app of your own, create both indexes with frozenTimePeriodInSecs set to lesson 1's retention period in seconds, the sized maxTotalDataSizeMB, and enableDataIntegrityControl = true, which the STIG asks for and which Splunk applies only to data indexed after it is on, so it goes in before the first event. Add the two roles: sbd_analyst inheriting the built-in user role, sbd_admin inheriting admin. People sign in once lesson 3 connects Splunk to Active Directory.

Open the receiving port in inputs.conf: a [splunktcp-ssl:9997] stanza and an [SSL] stanza whose serverCert is one PEM file holding the certificate, its key, and the SBD chain, with sslVersions = tls1.2. The forwarder checks the server's certificate, and requireClientCert stays false: as on the collector's syslog path in course 1.10, the sender is held to its address, by the host firewall's rule that admits 10.0.20.20 alone. A single instance keeps its own logs in its own indexes, so leave Forward data empty under Settings > Forwarding and receiving: an output that points back at itself would loop.

On SBD-SYSLOG01, in a Tier 1 session, install the forwarder with msiexec (AGREETOLICENSE=Yes LAUNCHSPLUNK=0 /quiet); by default it runs as a low-privilege virtual account, NT SERVICE\SplunkForwarder. The STIG's user-rights policy replaces any rights the installer grants, so give the account what it needs explicitly: Event Log Readers membership, added beside SBD-Archive$ in the course 1.11 GPO as a second add-member preference item so neither account replaces the other, and read on D:\Logs\Syslog, both recorded in the course 1.5 exception record. Copy the Windows add-on into the forwarder's apps folder and enable two inputs in its local inputs.conf: [WinEventLog://ForwardedEvents] with renderXml = true and index = sbd_wineventlog, and [monitor://D:\Logs\Syslog] with sourcetype = syslog, index = sbd_syslog, and host_segment = 3, so each line's host is its sender, not the collector.

Point it at rule F10 in outputs.conf: server = SBD-SPLUNK01.sbd.test:9997, useSSL = true, sslVerifyServerCert = true, sslAltNameToCheck = SBD-SPLUNK01.sbd.test, and useACK = true, so the forwarder keeps each block until the indexer confirms it. In server.conf, set sslRootCAPath to the SBD chain and turn off the forwarder's own management port ([httpServer] disableDefaultPort = true): nothing manages it remotely, and course 1.10 allows no listener the design didn't ask for. Start the service; on its first run the forwarder reads ForwardedEvents from the oldest event, so the whole buffer arrives, and its size on disk, divided by the days it covers, replaces lesson 1's sizing estimate.

Prove the copy is faithful. Pick one closed hour, count it on the collector with Get-WinEvent and in Splunk over the same window, and compare one event on both sides: the counts must match, and the event's time in Splunk must be when its source wrote it, not when it arrived. Do the same for yesterday's syslog file from each sender, check that host names each source system rather than SBD-SYSLOG01, and confirm in the indexer's own metrics that the forwarder's connection is TLS (connectionType cookedSSL).
lessons.command:
# On SBD-SPLUNK01 (Tier 1 SSH session): the host prepared for Splunk
sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="transparent_hugepage=never"   # then reboot
cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled   # expected: always madvise [never]
getenforce; systemctl is-active fapolicyd         # Enforcing; active where the STIG turned it on
sudo fapolicyd-cli --file add /opt/splunk/ --trust-file splunk && sudo fapolicyd-cli --update
stat -c '%U %a %n' /opt/splunk /srv/splunk         # splunk 700
systemctl show Splunkd -p User -p LimitNOFILE -p LimitNPROC -p TasksMax
sudo ausearch -m AVC,USER_AVC,SELINUX_ERR,USER_SELINUX_ERR -ts recent   # expected: <no matches>
# On SBD-SPLUNK01 (Tier 1 SSH session): the first-start decisions, an index, and the TLS port
grep -E '^SPLUNK_(DB|FIPS)' /opt/splunk/etc/splunk-launch.conf
sudo -u splunk /opt/splunk/bin/splunk btool indexes list sbd_wineventlog | grep -E 'frozenTimePeriodInSecs|maxTotalDataSizeMB|enableDataIntegrityControl'
sudo -u splunk /opt/splunk/bin/splunk btool inputs list splunktcp-ssl:9997 --debug
openssl s_client -connect SBD-SPLUNK01.sbd.test:9997 -CAfile /opt/splunk/etc/auth/sbd/sbd-chain.pem </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'Verify return code|Protocol'
# On SBD-SYSLOG01 (Tier 1 session): the forwarder's account and connection, and one closed hour
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='SplunkForwarder'" | Select-Object StartName, State
Select-String 'C:\Program Files\SplunkUniversalForwarder\var\log\splunk\splunkd.log' -Pattern 'Connected to idx' | Select-Object -Last 1
$start = (Get-Date).Date.AddHours((Get-Date).Hour - 2); $end = $start.AddHours(1)
(Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='ForwardedEvents'; StartTime=$start; EndTime=$end}).Count
# In Splunk Web (Search), as admin (lesson 3 connects the domain accounts): the same hour, the forwarder's connection, and the stored size
index=sbd_wineventlog earliest=-2h@h latest=-1h@h | stats count
index=_internal source=*metrics.log group=tcpin_connections | stats latest(connectionType) AS type, latest(version) AS version BY hostname, sourceIp
| dbinspect index=sbd_wineventlog index=sbd_syslog | stats sum(sizeOnDiskMB) AS MB BY index
lessons.check: THP shows [never], SELinux is enforcing with no denials from Splunk, and fapolicyd, where it runs, trusts /opt/splunk; Splunk runs as splunk under systemd with its directories at mode 700 and the recommended process limits; the indexes carry integrity control and the designed retention; Splunk Web answers over HTTPS, TCP 9997 presents the SBD-SPLUNK01 certificate over TLS 1.2, the forwarder runs as NT SERVICE\SplunkForwarder with a TLS connection to the indexer, and a closed hour's count and one event's time match the collector for both streams.
lessons.evidence: Keep the THP, SELinux, and fapolicyd state, the unit's account and limits, the first-start settings and the FIPS decision, the btool listings for the indexes and the receiving port, the TLS handshake result, the forwarder's inputs and outputs files and its service account, the measured daily size, and the count-and-time comparison for both streams.

model.label: Follow a log, step 3
model.text: The forwarder on the collector sends the Windows events and syslog intake to SBD-SPLUNK01 under rule F10.

quizzes.question: Why do SPLUNK_DB and the FIPS decision go into splunk-launch.conf before the first start?
answers: Splunk ignores splunk-launch.conf after the first start
FIPS mode can only be turned on at the first start, and the index location is simplest to set before any index exists
The license file overwrites them
quizzes.explanation: An instance first started without FIPS mode can't gain it, even by upgrading, and moving every index later is a project of its own. Two lines, decided once.

quizzes.question: The forwarder connects, but every Windows event shows host SBD-SYSLOG01. What is missing?
answers: The Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows on the forwarder and on SBD-SPLUNK01, which reports each forwarded event's source computer in host
A forwarder on each domain controller
UDP 514 on the indexer
quizzes.explanation: Forwarded events are read on the collector, so without the add-on they look as if the collector wrote them. With it, host names the system each event came from — which every search relies on.

quizzes.question: How do you show that Splunk's copy is faithful to the collector?
answers: Splunk Web shows a green status
The forwarder's log shows no errors
Count a closed hour on both sides and compare one event's time — both must match
quizzes.explanation: A copy that loses events or shifts their times would mislead every search built on it. A closed window, counted twice, is the simplest proof that nothing was dropped or retimed.

recap: The host runs with THP off, SELinux enforcing, and Splunk trusted by fapolicyd.
Splunk runs as its own account, with HTTPS and integrity-checked indexes that keep the period you chose; both streams cross rule F10 over TLS.
Counts and times in Splunk match the collector's.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 hardens Splunk to DISA's Splunk Enterprise STIG before anyone else signs in.

lessons.title: Harden Splunk to the STIG
lessons.summary: Splunk now holds the network's working copy, and DISA's Splunk Enterprise STIG says how it should behave. Before anyone else signs in, put the settings in place: the notice and session limits at the front door, sign-in with domain accounts over LDAPS, a free-space reserve the health report watches, and Splunk's audit trail under review. Then seal the install-time admin as the one local account, and record every STIG item this network meets another way.
objectives: Set the login notice, session timeout, TLS versions, and banner, and connect sign-in to Active Directory over LDAPS.
Reserve free space, watch it in the health report, and confirm the indexes' integrity and the installation's permissions.
Seal the install-time admin as the one local account, review Splunk's audit trail, and record each STIG item met another way.
steps: Work from the Splunk Enterprise STIG you staged in lesson 1, open in STIG Viewer on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, and put every setting in the small app that already holds the indexes and roles, so one folder carries the hardening and course 1.19's backup of /opt/splunk/etc keeps it. Splunk reads system/local ahead of every app, so check with btool --debug that each value comes from your app and nothing in system/local overrides it. The values below follow the STIG's text; check each against the release you staged, and record any difference.

Set the front door. In web.conf, put the notice and consent text your organization requires in login_content, so it shows before anyone signs in. Splunk Web counts idle time in two parts: the browser's ui_inactivity_timeout (60 minutes by default) runs first, then the shorter of web.conf's tools.sessions.timeout and server.conf's sessionTimeout. Set ui_inactivity_timeout = 1 and both session timeouts to 14 minutes, so an idle session ends within the STIG's 15 minutes. Allow TLS 1.2 only, with sslVersions = tls1.2 in web.conf and in server.conf's [sslConfig] stanza, sslVersionsForClient = tls1.2 there too, and the cipher suites the STIG lists. Add a global banner ([BANNER_MESSAGE_SINGLETON] in global-banner.conf) with the system's name and the marking your environment requires, so every page says where you are.

Connect sign-in to Active Directory, as the STIG asks for people's accounts. In a Tier 0 session from AdminJumpBox01, create SBD Splunk Analysts and SBD Splunk Admins under the Groups OU and add each person's account, a Tier 1 or standard account and never a Tier 0 one, and create svc-splunk-ldap, a bind account that is only a Domain User, with a long random password. On SBD-SPLUNK01, point Splunk's LDAP client at the SBD chain in /opt/splunk/etc/openldap/ldap.conf (TLS_CACERT, TLS_REQCERT demand, TLS_PROTOCOL_MIN 3.3 for TLS 1.2). In your app's authentication.conf, set authType = LDAP with one strategy: host sbd.test on port 636 with SSLEnabled = 1, so it reaches either domain controller over rule F03 and checks the certificate course 1.6 enrolled; the bind account; userNameAttribute = sAMAccountName; groupBaseDN at the Groups OU with groupMemberAttribute = member; anonymous_referrals = 0; and a role map: sbd_analyst = SBD Splunk Analysts, sbd_admin = SBD Splunk Admins. Splunk encrypts the bind password when it restarts.

Keep one local account and hold it to the STIG. Domain accounts follow the domain's password and lockout policy from course 1.5, while authentication.conf's [splunk_auth] stanza governs Splunk's own accounts, so give it the STIG's values: minPasswordLength = 15; minPasswordUppercase, minPasswordLowercase, minPasswordDigit, and minPasswordSpecial = 1; expirePasswordDays = 60; enablePasswordHistory = true with passwordHistoryCount = 5; and lockoutUsers = true, lockoutAttempts = 3, and lockoutThresholdMins = 15. Sign in once with a domain account from each group to prove the mapping, then give the install-time admin a long random password, seal it as course 1.8 seals the break-glass account, and sign out: it is the one local emergency account, and lesson 5 alerts on any use of it. Record, as course 1.4 taught, every item this network meets differently: email notice (there is no mail server, so the health report and lesson 5's Triggered Alerts carry it), Common Criteria mode, and CAC sign-in.

Reserve free space and watch it. In server.conf's [diskUsage] stanza, set minFreeSpace to a quarter of the index volume in megabytes, so Splunk stops indexing once the volume is three-quarters full (per the current STIG). A pause loses nothing here: the forwarder waits and resumes where it stopped, as long as the collector's buffer still holds the events. In Settings > Health report manager, set the Disk Space feature's red and yellow thresholds to the STIG's values, and put the Monitoring Console in standalone mode, so its dashboards show one instance holding every role. Then confirm what lesson 2 set: both indexes report enableDataIntegrityControl, splunk check-integrity passes on their warm buckets (a bucket gets its final hash when it rolls from hot to warm), and /opt/splunk and /srv/splunk are still splunk's with mode 700.

Watch Splunk itself. The _audit index records every sign-in and sign-out, account and role change, change under /opt/splunk/etc, capability used, and each start and stop, whatever else you configure. Signed in with your sbd_admin account, search it for the domain accounts signing in, one wrong password you type on purpose for your own account, and the settings you changed in this lesson, and keep the results: lesson 5 alerts on the sealed admin account, and the weekly review reads these events. Finish the record for lesson 6's checklist: each setting, the STIG item it answers, the btool line that shows it, and every item met another way with its reason.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-SPLUNK01 (Tier 1 SSH session): each value, and the file it comes from
sudo -u splunk /opt/splunk/bin/splunk btool web list settings --debug | grep -E 'login_content|sessions.timeout|ui_inactivity_timeout|sslVersions|enableSplunkWebSSL'
sudo -u splunk /opt/splunk/bin/splunk btool server list --debug | grep -E 'sessionTimeout|sslVersions|minFreeSpace'
sudo -u splunk /opt/splunk/bin/splunk btool authentication list --debug | grep -E 'authType|authSettings|host|port|SSLEnabled|bindDN |roleMap|sbd_|minPassword|lockout'
grep -E '^TLS_' /opt/splunk/etc/openldap/ldap.conf
openssl s_client -connect sbd.test:636 -CAfile /opt/splunk/etc/auth/sbd/sbd-chain.pem </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'Verify return code|Protocol'
sudo -u splunk /opt/splunk/bin/splunk btool global-banner list --debug
df -m /srv/splunk                                   # minFreeSpace = a quarter of this volume's size
sudo -u splunk /opt/splunk/bin/splunk btool indexes list sbd_syslog | grep enableDataIntegrityControl
sudo -u splunk /opt/splunk/bin/splunk check-integrity -index sbd_wineventlog
stat -c '%U %a %n' /opt/splunk /srv/splunk          # splunk 700
# In Splunk Web (Search), signed in with your sbd_admin account
| rest /services/authentication/users splunk_server=local | table title type roles
index=_audit action="login attempt" earliest=-24h | stats count BY user, info
index=_audit sourcetype=audittrail earliest=-24h | stats count BY action, info
lessons.check: The login page shows the notice, an idle session ends within 15 minutes, Splunk Web and splunkd accept TLS 1.2 only, and the banner names the system; Splunk reaches the domain controllers over LDAPS with a verified certificate, a domain account from each group signs in with the mapped role, and no Tier 0 account is in either group; [splunk_auth] carries the STIG's password and lockout values and the install-time admin is the one sealed local account; minFreeSpace is a quarter of the index volume, Disk Space is in the health report, and the Monitoring Console is in standalone mode; both indexes have integrity control and pass check-integrity; /opt/splunk and /srv/splunk are splunk's with mode 700; _audit shows the domain sign-ins, the failed sign-in, and the changes; and every STIG item met another way has its reason recorded.
lessons.evidence: Keep the btool listings with the file each value comes from, the LDAPS handshake result, the two groups' membership and the bind account's group list, the account list with types and roles, the sealed-admin record, the minFreeSpace calculation, the health report and Monitoring Console mode, the check-integrity results, the permissions, the _audit results, and the record of STIG items met another way.

model.label: SBD-SPLUNK01
model.text: The analysis server on VLAN 50 and the controls it carries.

quizzes.question: Why does enableDataIntegrityControl go on when lesson 2 creates the indexes, rather than now?
answers: Splunk hashes only data indexed after the setting is on, so the events already indexed would never be covered
An index's settings can't change once it holds data
It slows searching, so it has to be on before any analyst signs in
quizzes.explanation: Integrity hashes are computed as data is written. Turned on later, they protect only what arrives afterwards, so lesson 2's first events, the ones compared with the collector, would have none.

quizzes.question: Free space on /srv/splunk falls below minFreeSpace. What happens to the events on their way?
answers: They are dropped until an administrator frees space
Indexing pauses; the forwarder waits and resumes where it stopped while the collector's buffer still holds them, and the record on SBD-AUDIT01 never depended on Splunk
Splunk deletes the oldest buckets to make room
quizzes.explanation: minFreeSpace protects the volume: Splunk stops writing rather than fill it. The forwarder catches up afterwards, and the health report shows the condition before it gets there.

quizzes.question: Why do the two Splunk groups never hold a Tier 0 account?
answers: Splunk can't read Tier 0 accounts over LDAP
The password crosses the sign-in page of SBD-SPLUNK01, a Tier 1 server, and a Tier 0 credential must never be exposed to a lower tier
Tier 0 accounts are in Protected Users, which blocks web sign-in
quizzes.explanation: Tiering is about where a credential is typed. Anyone who controls SBD-SPLUNK01 could capture what crosses its sign-in page, so Tier 0 operators use their Tier 1 account for Splunk.

recap: The console shows the notice, ends idle sessions within 15 minutes, and speaks TLS 1.2 only.
People sign in with their domain accounts over LDAPS, mapped to roles by group; the install-time admin is the one sealed local account.
Free space, integrity, permissions, and Splunk's audit trail are watched, and every item met another way is on record.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 asks the network its first questions.

lessons.title: Build the working searches
lessons.summary: Analysis earns its place with three working searches: failed privileged sign-ins, the boundary's denies, and the health of time — questions this network can already answer about itself. Build them as an analyst, prove each against an event you caused, and save them for the alerts in lesson 5.
objectives: Search as an analyst and read the shape of the indexed data.
Build the first three searches against real events.
Save each with its owner and a known test event.
steps: Sign in from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 as an analyst and check what the role allows: | rest /services/authentication/current-context lists your roles and capabilities, and delete_by_keyword is not among them. Then read the shape of the data with | tstats count where index=sbd_* by index, host, sourcetype: every source system should appear, the Windows events with their source computer in host and their event ID in EventCode, and the syslog lines with their sender in host.

Build search one: failed sign-ins (event 4625) involving the tier admin accounts, grouped by source host — the tiering course's denials now have a dashboard. Take the accounts from course 1.8's tier groups (SBD Tier 0 Admins, SBD Tier 1 Admins, and SBD Tier 2 Admins), not from a naming pattern: from AdminJumpBox01, a Tier 0 operator exports the groups' members to sbd_tier_admins.csv (TargetUserName and tier), uploads it as a lookup the analysts can read, and refreshes it after every membership change.

Build search two: router denies by source VLAN and destination port — the network boundary, now trending. Extract src_ip, dest_ip, and dest_port from the core's deny lines (its deny log reaches the collector as syslog on UDP 514 under rule F24, part of the network's existing configuration) once with the field extractor, and derive each VLAN from an address's third octet, since every segment is 10.0.<VLAN>.0/24.

Build search three: time-service events, so clock drift surfaces before Kerberos complains. Course 1.10's SBD-ForwardedSecurity already carries Security event 4616 and the System log's Microsoft-Windows-Time-Service events course 1.3 keeps (12, 35, 36, 37, 129, and 142); event 12 on SBD-DC01 is expected, because the PDC emulator serves its own clock. The Linux servers report through chronyd in the syslog stream: which source they selected, or that none was selectable.

Save each as a report with its question, owner, the events it depends on, and a known event it must find, and have an sbd_admin share it with the analysts read-only: a wrong password for your Tier 1 account at SBD-ADMIN-SRV01's sign-in screen for search one, a probe of an unregistered port for search two, and a chronyd restart on SBD-SPLUNK01 for search three. Cause each, run each search, and keep the result: lesson 5 turns them into alerts.
lessons.command:
# In Splunk Web (Search), signed in as an analyst from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01
| rest /services/authentication/current-context splunk_server=local | table username roles capabilities
| tstats count where index=sbd_* by index, host, sourcetype
index=sbd_wineventlog EventCode=4625 [| inputlookup sbd_tier_admins.csv | fields TargetUserName] | stats count, values(IpAddress) AS sources, latest(_time) AS last BY host, TargetUserName | convert ctime(last)
index=sbd_syslog host=<core> src_ip=* | eval src_vlan="VLAN ".mvindex(split(src_ip, "."), 2) | stats count BY src_vlan, dest_port
(index=sbd_wineventlog "Microsoft-Windows-Time-Service") OR (index=sbd_syslog chronyd) | fillnull value="-" EventCode | stats count, latest(_time) AS last BY host, EventCode | convert ctime(last)
# On SBD-SYSLOG01 (Tier 1 session): course 1.10's subscription carries the Time-Service query
wecutil gs SBD-ForwardedSecurity /f:xml | Select-String 'Time-Service'
lessons.check: The analyst role searches both indexes and carries no delete capability, every source system appears with the right host and source type, the subscription carries the Time-Service query, and each saved search finds its known test event.
lessons.evidence: Record your role listing, the data-shape table, each saved search with its question, owner, and a result showing its test event, the lookup's source and date, and the subscription's Time-Service query.

quizzes.question: Why does the repository stay out of the analysis flow?
answers: The protected copy's integrity never depends on the search tier — analysis reads the working stream, not the record
Splunk cannot read archives
Repositories are read-only hardware
quizzes.explanation: The separation from lesson 1, built into lesson 2's plumbing: question the working copy freely; the record stays untouched.

quizzes.question: Why does search one take the tier accounts from a lookup of course 1.8's groups?
answers: Lookups make every search faster
The groups decide who is privileged, so a refreshed lookup follows their membership — a naming pattern misses any account that doesn't follow it
Splunk can't read account names from Windows events
quizzes.explanation: The tier groups are the source of truth for privilege. Exporting them keeps the search honest, and refreshing the lookup after each membership change keeps it current.

quizzes.question: Why is a time-health search in the first three?
answers: Clocks are easy to chart
Dashboards need a third panel
Drift breaks Kerberos quietly — course 1.3 set up the clock, this search watches it
quizzes.explanation: The pipeline watches the dependencies the network actually has. Time is one failure that looks like everything else until you chart it.

recap: Analysts question the working copy; the protected record stays untouched.
Three searches answer real questions from day one.
Each search has an owner and a test event it must find.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 turns these searches, and the pipeline's own failures, into alerts someone owns.

lessons.title: Own the alerts
lessons.summary: An alert nobody owns is a log entry with extra steps. Turn the working searches and the pipeline's own failure conditions into scheduled alerts, each with a threshold set for your environment, a named responder, and a written first response; test each one by causing it, tune the noise, and set the review cadence AU-6 asks for.
objectives: Write each alert's threshold, schedule, named responder, and first response, recording the values you chose.
Alert on the pipeline's own failures and the repository's findings.
Test and tune every alert, and review them on a set cadence.
steps: Write the alert register before building anything: for each alert, its search, threshold, schedule, severity, named responder with a deputy, and written first response. The threshold, schedule, throttle and expiration of each alert depend on your environment and policy, so record the value you chose and why. Start from lesson 4's searches: any failed sign-in for a tier account, since privileged sign-ins are few and each failure deserves a look; any deny from VLAN 80 toward VLAN 60 or from VLAN 60 itself, whose seats use only registered paths, or a burst of denies from one source above the count and window you record; and Time-Service events 36, 129, or 142, or chronyd finding no selectable source (never event 12, which SBD-DC01 writes by design). Add any use of a sealed account: course 1.8's break-glass account signing in anywhere, as that course promised, and Splunk's own admin account signing in to Splunk.

Add the conditions course 1.10's daily check has watched by hand (AU-5): no Windows events at all for longer than the silence threshold you record, which means the collector, its forwarder, or rule F10 has stopped, and a known source quiet past its own limit, taken from a lookup of expected sources (each host as Splunk shows it, with the longest quiet it may have). Add course 1.11's repository findings: SBD-Repository events 1001 and 1101 from SBD-AUDIT01, refused access to its archive (event 4656 with an audit failure), and any deletion (event 4660), which the responder matches to an approved retention run. Splunk sees missing data, not disks: the collector's free space and its buffer's oldest event stay in the daily check.

Build each as a scheduled alert owned by sbd_admin, the ones on the domain controllers from AdminJumpBox01: a cron schedule and a search window by index time, the window longer than the interval between runs (earliest=-24h _index_earliest=-<window>), so events that arrive late after an outage are still checked, a trigger when the number of results is greater than zero (so a missing-data search, such as the silence alert, is written to return a row only when its count is zero), throttling on the field that names one problem (the account, the source) for the period you record, a severity, and the Add to Triggered Alerts action. This network has no mail server, so the Triggered Alerts list is the responder's queue, and it keeps each entry for 24 hours by default: set each alert's expiration to cover the longest gap between reviews in your environment, so a weekend can't empty it, and record the value. Name every alert SBD - <condition>, so the register, the queue, and the scheduler's log use the same names.

Test each alert by causing its condition where that is safe, and record when you caused it, when it fired, and who saw it: one wrong password for your Tier 1 account at SBD-ADMIN-SRV01's sign-in screen, a probe of an unregistered port from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 across the core, and the SplunkForwarder service stopped on SBD-SYSLOG01 for longer than the silence threshold, which also shows the backlog arriving without a gap once it restarts. Where a condition can't be caused safely, such as a repository mismatch or a break-glass sign-in, run the alert's search over a window that holds a real or test example instead.

Tune before you trust: run each alert's search over the last seven days and count how often it would have fired. If that is more than the responder can act on, raise the threshold, widen the throttle, or exclude a known benign source, never just lower the severity, and record each change and its reason in the register.

Set the review cadence (AU-6; sample values): the responder works the queue at the start of each day and records every alert's outcome; once a week an analyst reviews each saved search's results and signs the review; and each month the register's thresholds, noise, and owners are reviewed, with both lookups refreshed after any change to the tier groups or the sources.
lessons.command:
# In Splunk Web (Search), as sbd_admin: the alerts as built
| rest /servicesNS/-/-/saved/searches splunk_server=local | search title="SBD - *" is_scheduled=1 | table title cron_schedule dispatch.earliest_time alert.severity alert.suppress.period alert.expires actions
# Each alert's runs and what it triggered, from the scheduler's own log
index=_internal sourcetype=scheduler savedsearch_name="SBD - *" | stats count, sum(result_count) AS results, values(alert_actions) AS actions BY savedsearch_name
# The silent-source alert's search: each expected source's last event against its limit
| inputlookup sbd_expected_sources.csv | join type=left host [| tstats max(_time) AS last where index=sbd_* earliest=-7d by host] | where isnull(last) OR last < relative_time(now(), "-" . max_quiet_minutes . "m")
# The pipeline test, on SBD-SYSLOG01 (Tier 1 session): stop the forwarder past the silence threshold
Stop-Service SplunkForwarder; Start-Sleep -Seconds <silence threshold plus one run interval, in seconds>; Start-Service SplunkForwarder
