lessons.check: Every alert in the register has a recorded threshold, schedule, expiration, severity, responder with deputy, and written first response; each safe condition fired its alert in a test, with the cause and the alert's time recorded; the forwarder stop fired the pipeline alert and its backlog arrived without a gap; and the first daily and weekly reviews are on record.
lessons.evidence: Keep the alert register, the listing of the alerts as built, each test's cause-and-fire record, the seven-day tuning counts with any changes, and the first review records.

quizzes.question: What makes an alert real rather than decorative?
answers: A red icon
A named responder and a written first step
Firing at least hourly
quizzes.explanation: Detection without ownership is noise. The responder and the first step are what turn a search into a control.

quizzes.question: No alert has fired for a whole day. Why doesn't that prove the pipeline works?
answers: Splunk holds alerts back on quiet days
Alerts only fire on weekdays
A stopped collector or forwarder looks exactly like a quiet network — only an alert on missing data tells them apart
quizzes.explanation: Silence is ambiguous. The pipeline and silent-source alerts turn missing data into an event someone has to answer, which is what AU-5 asks for.

quizzes.question: An alert fires forty times a day and the responder has started ignoring it. What is the right fix?
answers: Measure it against the last week, then raise the threshold, throttle it, or exclude a known benign source — and record the change
Lower its severity to informational
Turn it off until things calm down
quizzes.explanation: Tuning keeps the alert meaningful; hiding or disabling it removes the control. The register shows why each threshold is what it is.

recap: Every alert has a recorded threshold, an owner, and a written first response.
The pipeline's own failures and the repository's findings now raise alerts.
Each alert was caused, tuned, and put on a review cadence.
lessons.next: The final lesson traces one event through all three logging systems and closes the course.

lessons.title: Prove the chain and hand off
lessons.summary: One deliberate event, followed all the way: a failed privileged sign-in should appear on the source, the collector, the analyst's screen, and the repository's next-morning archive. That trace closes all three logging courses; SBD-SPLUNK01's first baseline and the handoff to the fleet close this one.
objectives: Trace a test event through all three systems, from source to analyst.
Verify the router-deny stream (rule F24) and its alert on the analysis side.
Baseline SBD-SPLUNK01 and file the evidence of all three logging courses.
steps: Generate the test event: one failed sign-in on SBD-DC01 with a wrong password for a tier admin account. From AdminJumpBox01, record its time, account, and event ID in the DC's Security log, then find the same event in ForwardedEvents on SBD-SYSLOG01 with MachineName SBD-DC01 and the same time, about 30 seconds after it happened.

Watch analysis catch it: the event appears in sbd_wineventlog with host SBD-DC01 and the same time, and the privileged sign-in alert fires on its next run. The responder sees it in the Triggered Alerts list and records the first response as written — the alert is part of the trace, not an extra.

The next morning, after course 1.11's 01:00 run has archived the event's completed UTC day, open that day's ForwardedEvents archive on SBD-AUDIT01 in an auditor's or the custodian's session, confirm its catalog line shows matching hashes, and read the event with Get-WinEvent -Path. Four places, one event, and the same source time in each: that is the chain working.

Repeat with the boundary on the analysis side: probe one unregistered port from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 as course 1.10 did, which already traced the deny to the collector over rule F24, and find it in search two with the boundary alert firing for a deny from VLAN 60. Attempt, deny, and alert now form one evidence set.

Run the cadence: take SBD-SPLUNK01's first SCAP baseline the way course 1.9 scans every Linux server. Over your Tier 1 SSH session, copy SCC for Linux and the distribution's STIG benchmark from C:\Staging\DISA\linux, check their hashes on the host, install SCC as its readme directs, and run it as root with the benchmark and the profile course 1.4 recorded. Answer DISA's Splunk Enterprise STIG for the application in a STIG Viewer checklist on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: lesson 3's record answers most items with the setting and the btool line that shows it, and carries the items met another way with their reasons. Classify every remaining open item as course 1.4 taught, adapted for Linux as in course 1.9 — fix now (no GPO applies to Linux), deviation candidate, or POA&M candidate — and store the session under C:\Evidence\splunk-analysis\baseline\SBD-SPLUNK01 with hashes.

Write SBD-SPLUNK01's upgrade procedure, because the STIG asks for a version the vendor still supports and Splunk doesn't arrive through SBD-REPO01. Record splunk version against Splunk's support policy. For each upgrade: stage the new .tgz, and the forwarder's .msi, hashed as in course 1.4; read Splunk's notes on upgrading to that version first; confirm course 1.19 holds a current copy of /opt/splunk/etc; stop Splunk, extract over /opt as the same owner, refresh fapolicyd's trust (fapolicyd-cli --file update, then --update), start with --accept-license --answer-yes, and repeat lesson 2's count check. Splunk has no downgrade: going back means reinstalling the old version and restoring its configuration. When endpoint protection reaches this host, exclude /opt/splunk, /srv/splunk, and Splunk's processes from on-access scanning, as Splunk advises.

File the end-to-end trace as the signature evidence of all three logging courses and write the handoff: the fleet course inherits a pipeline that will see its first domain join happen. When course 1.13 enrolls the workstations, their events arrive in sbd_wineventlog with no change in Splunk; add the ones that must never go quiet to the expected-sources lookup, and recheck the index sizing and the license's daily volume.
lessons.command:
# From AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): the test event on its source
Invoke-Command SBD-DC01 { Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, MachineName }
# On SBD-SYSLOG01 (Tier 1 session): the same event on the collector
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='ForwardedEvents'; Id=4625; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} | Select-Object TimeCreated, MachineName
# In Splunk Web (Search), as an analyst: the same event; its alert is in Triggered Alerts
index=sbd_wineventlog host=SBD-DC01* EventCode=4625 earliest=-1h | table _time host TargetUserName
# Next morning, in an auditor's or the custodian's session on SBD-AUDIT01: that UTC day's archive
Get-WinEvent -Path D:\LogArchive\ForwardedEvents\ForwardedEvents-<UTC date>.evtx -FilterXPath '*[System[EventID=4625]]' | Select-Object TimeCreated, MachineName
# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: copy course 1.9's Linux assessment set to the host
scp C:\Staging\DISA\linux\<SCC for Linux package> C:\Staging\DISA\linux\<STIG benchmark> <your-account>@SBD-SPLUNK01.sbd.test:/tmp/
# On SBD-SPLUNK01: the same hashes, then SCC's command-line scanner as root (path and options from the SCC readme)
sha256sum /tmp/<SCC for Linux package> /tmp/<STIG benchmark>
sudo <SCC install directory>/cscc
# The version the upgrade procedure starts from
sudo -u splunk /opt/splunk/bin/splunk version
# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: collect the session, then hash the course's evidence
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force C:\Evidence\splunk-analysis\baseline | Out-Null
scp -r <your-account>@SBD-SPLUNK01.sbd.test:<SCC session folder> C:\Evidence\splunk-analysis\baseline\SBD-SPLUNK01
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\splunk-analysis -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256
lessons.check: The test event appears on SBD-DC01, in ForwardedEvents, in Splunk with its alert fired, and in the next morning's archive with matching catalog hashes, all with the same source time; the probe's deny appears in search two and fired its alert; SBD-SPLUNK01 has its first baseline and a Splunk STIG checklist that answers lesson 3's items and classifies every open one; and the upgrade procedure is written, starting from a version the vendor supports.
lessons.evidence: Keep the four-place trace of the test event with its timestamps and the alert's record, the deny with its alert, SBD-SPLUNK01's scan set and checklist with hashes, the upgrade procedure with the current version, and the handoff note to course 1.13.

model.label: Follow a log
model.text: Follow the whole chain: an event leaves a domain controller, reaches the collector, then Splunk and the audit copy.

quizzes.question: What does the single traced event prove that stage-by-stage checks don't?
answers: That events have timestamps
That the stages connect — one real event surviving source to analyst is the pipeline working as a system
That 4625 exists
quizzes.explanation: Components can each pass while the chain fails. The traced event is the integration test.

quizzes.question: How is SBD-SPLUNK01, a domain-joined Linux server, scanned in this lab?
answers: It is exempt from evidence
With the Windows Server benchmark anyway
With the DISA STIG benchmark for its Linux distribution, on the same cadence as the Windows servers
quizzes.explanation: Linux distributions have their own DISA STIGs and Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) content, and Splunk Enterprise has a STIG of its own. A domain-joined Linux server is held to the same scan cadence as every other server.

quizzes.question: Why insist the pipeline exists before the fleet course?
answers: So fifty domain joins happen in view of the pipeline — observed from the first boot instead of retrofitted later
Fleets cannot join without Splunk
DHCP requires a SIEM
quizzes.explanation: The ordering argument of this whole path: build the watcher, then the watched. Course 1.13 arrives to a network already paying attention.

recap: One event, four places, one source time — the chain is real.
Boundary denies assemble their own evidence, alert included.
SBD-SPLUNK01's baseline, STIG checklist, and upgrade procedure, and the handoff to course 1.13, close the logging courses.
lessons.next: That completes course 1.12 and the three logging courses. Course 1.13 brings in the fifty-workstation fleet — watched, addressed, and policy-managed from first boot.

prerequisites: Complete courses 1.6–1.12: the course 1.6 PKI with its SBD Computer Authentication template and the SBD Certificate Autoenrollment GPO at the domain root, SBD-DHCP01 (course 1.7), whose relay course 1.7 verified, the three administration seats (course 1.8), with SBD-ADMIN-PC01's own SCC copy and first baseline, and the logging pipeline (courses 1.10–1.12), on the network's routed, segmented VLANs.
Prepare a patched Windows client reference image (or template) for the fifty endpoints, obtained through the approved offline media process.

Confirm the Workstations OU and the computer redirect from course 1.5, and the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) Group Policy objects (GPOs) for your Windows client release, imported in course 1.5 from the package course 1.4 staged and still unlinked there. Lesson 7 reuses SBD-ADMIN-PC01's own SCC copy, which course 1.8 installed with the Windows client benchmark course 1.4 staged, and the checked installer and connected-side-hashes.csv course 1.8 kept in C:\Staging\DISA there.

Confirm the VLAN 80 access switch supports 802.1X port authentication, including a monitor (audit) mode that logs each result without blocking traffic. No new server is needed: the Network Policy Server (NPS) role goes on SBD-DHCP01.
labNote: Fifty endpoints join a network that is finally ready for them: addressed by DHCP, landed by OU redirect, hardened by policy at first boot, certified by autoenrollment, and watched by the pipeline from their first sign-in. Tier 0 steps run from AdminJumpBox01, Tier 1 steps on SBD-DHCP01 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, and Tier 2 steps inside SBD-ADMIN-PC01; each seat keeps its part of the record under C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet. The sample names run SBD-PC01 through SBD-PC50; match them to your own plan.

sources.title: Microsoft · Get started with Windows LAPS and Windows Server Active Directory
DISA · STIG Group Policy Objects package
Microsoft · Use Windows Event Forwarding to help with intrusion detection
Microsoft · Configure Windows Firewall rules with Group Policy
DISA · Security Content Automation Protocol (SCC and SCAP benchmarks)

lessons.title: Prepare the fleet rollout
lessons.summary: Fifty of anything needs a factory, not fifty craft projects. Settle the image, the names, the join account, and the policy links so every endpoint is born identical — then prove it on paper before proving it on metal.
objectives: Finalize the reference image and naming plan for fifty endpoints.
Create a least-privilege join account scoped to the Workstations OU.
Link the Windows client STIG policies and the local Administrators, firewall and DNS registration policies to the Workstations OU before any join, below course 1.8's tier logon GPO.
steps: Finalize the Windows client reference image: current patches via the approved media process, no preinstalled extras, one local administrator account for Windows LAPS to manage (the Windows client STIG disables the built-in Administrator), and a generalized state so each clone takes its own identity. Record the image version and hash — it is the fleet's common ancestor and belongs in evidence.
Write the naming and rollout plan: SBD-PC01–SBD-PC50, addressed by the course 1.7 DHCP scope, joined in waves (pilot of three, then batches) rather than all fifty at once.

From AdminJumpBox01, create a dedicated domain-join account delegated only Create Computer objects on the Workstations OU — no broader privilege rides along with fifty join operations — and record it beside the same delegation course 1.8 gave SBD Tier 2 Admins for its test client. The course 1.5 redirect already guarantees machines land in that OU. Add a GPO, linked only to the Workstations OU, that makes SBD Tier 2 Admins the managing group in each PC's local Administrators (Group Policy Preferences, Local Users and Groups), as course 1.8 did by hand on its test client; course 1.8's tier logon GPO already denies sign-ins there to SBD Tier 0 Admins, SBD Tier 1 Admins and SBD Audit Custodians.

Link the DISA Windows client policies that course 1.5 imported and left unlinked to the Workstations OU now — the computer policy, the user policy, and course 1.5's loopback (Merge) GPO, as course 1.8 did for Admin Workstations — so the very first pilot boots into the hardened state, and note that the Windows client's own secure defaults will already satisfy some checks, just as Windows Server's did. Link each of them below course 1.8's tier logon GPO, which keeps link order 1 on the Workstations OU: user rights don't merge across GPOs, so a STIG GPO linked above it would win and drop the denies for Tier 0, Tier 1 and SBD Audit Custodians. Every GPO this course links to the OU goes below it.

Create the workstation firewall GPO (SBD Workstation Firewall in this sample) on the Workstations OU: Windows Defender Firewall on for every profile with inbound traffic blocked by default, and inbound rules that allow Remote Desktop (TCP 3389) and remote management (TCP 5985–5986) only from SBD-ADMIN-PC01 at 10.0.60.30 — the ports its register row, A03, carries. No rule allows SMB or Remote Desktop between workstations: traffic inside VLAN 80 never reaches the router, so this policy, not the core router's rules, enforces the register's peer denies. Then turn off the PCs' own DNS registration in a separate GPO on the same OU (SBD Workstation DNS in this sample): Computer Configuration > Policies > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client > Dynamic update, Disabled. Record the reason with the GPO: SBD-DHCP01 already registers each PC's A and PTR records under svc-dhcp-dns (course 1.7), and a client that registers its own record can take it over, so the DHCP server's account can no longer update it — one owner per record.
lessons.command:
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Staging\Windows-client-reference.vhdx
# On AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): the join account's delegation (svc-fleet-join in this sample) and the OU's links
(Get-Acl 'AD:\OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test').Access | Where-Object IdentityReference -match 'svc-fleet-join|SBD Tier 2 Admins' | Select-Object IdentityReference, ActiveDirectoryRights, ObjectType
(Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test').GpoLinks | Select-Object Order, DisplayName   # course 1.8's tier logon GPO stays at order 1
Get-GPOReport -Name 'SBD Workstation Firewall' -ReportType Html -Path C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet\workstation-firewall.html
Get-GPOReport -Name 'SBD Workstation DNS' -ReportType Html -Path C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet\workstation-dns.html
lessons.check: The image is hashed and recorded, the join account holds only Create Computer objects on the Workstations OU, and the client STIG, loopback, local Administrators, firewall and DNS registration GPO links show on that OU below course 1.8's tier logon GPO, still at link order 1, before any machine exists in it.
lessons.evidence: Keep the image record with its hash, the naming and wave plan, the delegation output for the join account and SBD Tier 2 Admins, the OU's GPO links in order, and the firewall and DNS registration GPO reports with the recorded reason.

quizzes.question: Why does the join account get only create-computer rights on one OU?
answers: Join operations fail with more rights
Fifty joins should carry the least privilege possible — a stolen join credential then creates computer objects, nothing more
Delegation is faster than Domain Admin
quizzes.explanation: Scale multiplies exposure. Scoping the account bounds what the rollout's most-used credential is worth to an attacker.

quizzes.question: Why link the STIG policies before the first machine joins?
answers: So every endpoint's first boot is already the hardened state — no window where an unmanaged machine exists
GPO links expire if unused
The OU cannot be created otherwise
quizzes.explanation: The redirect lands them in the OU, and the pre-linked policy means compliance from minute one — the course 1.5 design, now paying off at scale.

quizzes.question: What makes the reference image part of the evidence?
answers: Images are always evidence
It contains the domain password
Its recorded version and hash are what make fifty 'identical' endpoints a claim you can verify
quizzes.explanation: A configuration record for the fleet starts with the common ancestor. The hash is how an assessor — or future you — confirms descent.

quizzes.question: What stops one workstation from opening SMB or Remote Desktop to another?
answers: The router's access control lists
Each PC's own firewall, set by the workstation firewall GPO — traffic inside VLAN 80 never reaches the router
SBD-DHCP01, which refuses leases to a PC that tries it
quizzes.explanation: Two PCs in VLAN 80 talk through the access switch, so the router never sees their traffic. Each PC's Windows Defender Firewall enforces the register's peer denies, which Inside the Network shows as rules D01 and D02; DHCP only hands out addresses.

quizzes.question: Why does the Workstations OU turn off the PCs' own DNS registration?
answers: Workstations don't need DNS records
SBD-DHCP01 registers each PC's records under svc-dhcp-dns; a PC that registers its own can take a record over so the DHCP server can no longer update it
Dynamic registration is blocked by the router
quizzes.explanation: One owner per record. Course 1.7 made SBD-DHCP01 the registrar for every lease, so the PCs leave registration to it, and the reason is recorded with the GPO.

recap: One hashed image, one naming plan, waves instead of a big bang.
The join credential can create computer objects and nothing else.
The Workstations OU is armed with policy, and its managers named, before it holds a machine — with course 1.8's tier denies still first.
Peer SMB and Remote Desktop are blocked by each PC's own firewall, set by policy before the first join.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 joins the pilot and inspects everything a first boot should bring.

lessons.title: Join the pilot and inspect first boot
lessons.summary: Three machines go first, and everything the path has built shows up at once: a DHCP lease through the relay, an OU landing, STIG policy, a DNS record — and the join itself appearing on the analyst's screen.
objectives: Join a three-machine pilot with the scoped account.
Verify lease, OU placement, policy, and DNS registration per machine.
Confirm the joins appear in the logging pipeline.
steps: Deploy SBD-PC01 through SBD-PC03 from the image into VLAN 80 — where the PCs are virtual machines, with the hypervisor's time synchronization turned off, as course 1.3 requires — let each take its DHCP lease, and join sbd.test with the delegated account; nothing about the join should require a privileged credential.

Per machine, verify the inheritance chain: the computer object sits in the Workstations OU (the course 1.5 redirect working), gpresult shows the STIG policies applied, w32tm /query /source names a domain controller, and the A and PTR records SBD-DHCP01 registered for it under svc-dhcp-dns (course 1.7) answer from both DCs — with the PC's own registration off, as lesson 1's DNS GPO set.

Confirm the deny side holds: a pilot machine cannot reach another pilot machine's SMB or RDP — the lesson 1 firewall policy refuses it on the destination PC, because traffic inside VLAN 80 never reaches the router — and cannot open anything toward VLAN 60, which the core router's rules deny at the boundary.

Find the three joins in the logging pipeline: the domain controllers' computer-account creation events (4741) should already be on the course 1.10 collector and searchable in SBD-SPLUNK01 (course 1.12) — the first machines this network has watched arrive. If the course 1.10 subscription doesn't carry 4741, add it and record the change.
lessons.command:
Get-ADComputer -SearchBase 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Filter * | Select-Object Name, DNSHostName
gpresult /r /scope:computer
w32tm /query /source   # a domain controller, never Local CMOS Clock or the hypervisor
Resolve-DnsName SBD-PC01.sbd.test -Server SBD-DC02.sbd.test
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\DNSClient' | Select-Object RegistrationEnabled   # 0: the PC leaves registration to SBD-DHCP01
Test-NetConnection SBD-PC02.sbd.test -Port 445   # expected: TcpTestSucceeded False
lessons.check: All three pilots sit in the Workstations OU with STIG policy applied, time from a domain controller and DNS registered by SBD-DHCP01 on both DCs with the PC's own registration off, peer SMB/RDP fails as designed, and the join events are visible in analysis.
lessons.evidence: Keep each pilot's placement, gpresult, time source and DNS proof; the peer-deny output; and the analysis search showing the three computer-account creations.

model.label: Sign in
model.text: A workstation gets its address, finds a domain controller, authenticates, and reads its policy.

quizzes.question: How does a brand-new machine end up hardened without anyone touching it?
answers: Windows hardens itself completely
Redirect lands it in the Workstations OU, where the pre-linked STIG policies apply at first boot
The DHCP server pushes the STIG
quizzes.explanation: Three courses cooperate in that one moment: the course 1.5 redirect, the client policies course 1.5 imported from course 1.4's package, and this course's pre-linked OU.

quizzes.question: Why test pilot-to-pilot SMB and expect failure?
answers: SMB is removed from Windows
The pilots are in different domains
Each PC's firewall policy denies peer SMB and Remote Desktop — lateral movement inside VLAN 80 is cut at the destination host
quizzes.explanation: Peer traffic is switched inside VLAN 80 and never reaches the router, so the register's peer denies (D01 and D02) are enforced by each PC's own firewall — the policy lesson 1 linked before any join.

quizzes.question: What does seeing the joins in analysis demonstrate?
answers: The ordering worked — the pipeline built in courses 1.10–1.12 observed the fleet's very first machines arriving
That Splunk licenses cover 50 hosts
Nothing; joins are not logged
quizzes.explanation: Build the watcher, then the watched. The pilot's appearance on the analyst's screen is the sequencing argument made visible.

recap: Three pilots: leased, landed, hardened, registered — untouched by hand.
Peer traffic fails by design; the denies are the fleet's first evidence.
The pipeline watched the fleet being born.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 gives every endpoint a managed local administrator.

lessons.title: Manage local administrators with Windows LAPS
lessons.summary: Fifty identical machines must not share one local administrator password. Windows Local Administrator Password Solution (Windows LAPS) gives each endpoint its own rotating secret, stored in the directory, readable by the people the tier model says may have it.
objectives: Prepare the directory schema and permissions for Windows LAPS.
Apply the LAPS policy to the Workstations OU.
Retrieve and rotate a managed password under the tier rules.
steps: From AdminJumpBox01, extend the directory schema for Windows LAPS (Update-LapsADSchema, which needs Schema Admins) and grant the Workstations OU's computers the right to update their own password attributes (Set-LapsADComputerSelfPermission) — a one-time Tier 0 action, recorded like any schema change.

Grant read access on the managed passwords to SBD Tier 2 Admins (Set-LapsADReadPasswordPermission) — exactly the people SBD-ADMIN-PC01 exists for. Domain Admins can read them by default; no other group gets the right, and Tier 0 accounts don't sign in on workstations to use one. The tier model decides who may know an endpoint's local secret.

Create the LAPS GPO on the Workstations OU: back up to Active Directory, manage the local administrator account the image carries (named in the policy, because Windows LAPS manages the built-in Administrator unless told otherwise and doesn't create accounts), encrypt the password with SBD Tier 2 Admins as its authorized decryptor (otherwise only Domain Admins can decrypt it), the complexity, length and age the plan sets, and post-authentication actions that reset the password and sign the account out after a short grace period, so a used password does not live on.

On a pilot, confirm the policy applied, retrieve the password from SBD-ADMIN-PC01, use it once, and watch rotation after the grace period — one cycle, fully observed, is the proof the other forty-nine inherit.
lessons.command:
# On AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): who holds the LAPS rights on the Workstations OU
Find-LapsADExtendedRights -Identity 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test'
# Inside SBD-ADMIN-PC01 (Tier 2)
# The LAPS cmdlets read the directory over LDAP; the AD module's web service (TCP 9389) is open only to AdminJumpBox01
Get-LapsADPassword -Identity SBD-PC01 -AsPlainText | Select-Object ComputerName, Account, ExpirationTimestamp
# On the pilot
gpresult /r /scope:computer
lessons.check: The schema holds the LAPS attributes, only SBD Tier 2 Admins (beside the default Domain Admins) can read and decrypt passwords, the policy shows on the pilots, and one retrieve-use-rotate cycle is recorded.
lessons.evidence: Keep the schema-change record, the permission delegation, the LAPS policy report, and the observed rotation cycle.

quizzes.question: What problem does LAPS remove from a fifty-machine fleet?
answers: Slow sign-ins
One shared local administrator password — where a single capture would open every endpoint
Password complexity rules
quizzes.explanation: Identical images tempt identical secrets. Per-machine rotating passwords make one compromised endpoint worth exactly one endpoint.

quizzes.question: Who may read a managed endpoint password?
answers: Any authenticated user
The machine's primary user
SBD Tier 2 Admins, from SBD-ADMIN-PC01 — the tier model decides
quizzes.explanation: LAPS storage is directory data; the reading right is a tiering decision, which course 1.8 already made.

quizzes.question: Why does post-authentication reset matter?
answers: A password that was just used stops being valid — whoever saw it holds an expired secret
It makes passwords longer
It disables the account
quizzes.explanation: The rotation on use closes the window between 'retrieved for support' and 'floating around in a notes file.'

recap: Every endpoint owns its own rotating local secret.
Reading and decrypting rights follow the tier model, from the Tier 2 seat.
One full cycle is observed and on record.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 hands the fleet its certificates.

lessons.title: Autoenroll the fleet's certificates
lessons.summary: Course 1.6 proved autoenrollment on both domain controllers and its pilot, SBD-PKI-MGMT01; this lesson turns it loose. Widen the template permission to a fleet computer group, let the autoenrollment GPO already linked at the domain root do the enrolling, and verify a machine certificate chains and checks revocation across the boundary.
objectives: Widen the computer template's autoenrollment to a fleet computer group.
Confirm hands-free enrollment at Group Policy refresh.
Verify chain and live revocation from an endpoint.
steps: Through the course 1.6 change process (its lesson 8), grant a new computer group — SBD Fleet Computers in this sample, created from AdminJumpBox01 — Read, Enroll and Autoenroll on the SBD Computer Authentication template, from SBD-PKI-MGMT01. Template permissions name groups, never an OU; the change record names the widening and its approver.

Confirm with gpresult that course 1.6's SBD Certificate Autoenrollment GPO, linked at the domain root, already reaches the Workstations OU, then add the pilots to SBD Fleet Computers and restart them so the membership reaches their Kerberos tickets. Watch certificates arrive with no human in the loop: the requests reach SBD-SUBCA01 over the enrollment row course 1.6 confirmed (F23 in this sample).

On an enrolled pilot, export its certificate, clear the URL cache, and run the full verification: the chain must reach the approved root, and the AIA and CDP fetches must answer live from pki.sbd.test through the register's publication row, F18.
Record the issuing CA's view: the issued-certificate log now shows the pilots enrolling — volume the CA was designed for, beginning to arrive, and itself a record worth sampling into evidence.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-PC01, after the restart
gpupdate /force
certutil -pulse
Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My | Select-Object Subject, NotAfter, Thumbprint
Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My | Where-Object { $_.EnhancedKeyUsageList.FriendlyName -contains 'Client Authentication' } | Select-Object -First 1 | Export-Certificate -FilePath C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet\SBD-PC01.cer
certutil -urlcache * delete
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet\SBD-PC01.cer   # carry the output to SBD-ADMIN-PC01's record
lessons.check: Pilot endpoints enroll hands-free once they are in SBD Fleet Computers, verification passes with live publication retrieval and nothing cached, and the CA's issued log shows their SBD Computer Authentication certificates.
lessons.evidence: Keep the template change record, the SBD Fleet Computers membership, an endpoint's certificate details, the urlfetch output, and a sample of the CA's issued log.

quizzes.question: What governs widening the template from pilot to fleet?
answers: The course 1.6 change process — requester, reviewer, versioning, record
A quick edit on the CA console
Nothing; templates are self-service
quizzes.explanation: The pilot-then-widen plan was written into the template's own record. Scaling it is a change like any other — documented, not improvised.

quizzes.question: What does the endpoint's urlfetch verification exercise, end to end?
answers: Only the local certificate store
Template, CA, DNS alias, publication site, and the registered HTTP path, all in one command
The DHCP relay
quizzes.explanation: One passing verification on a fleet machine is the integration test for everything the PKI path built: course 1.6's hierarchy and publication site, and course 1.2's pki.sbd.test alias.

quizzes.question: Why sample the CA's issued-certificate log into evidence?
answers: Logs expire otherwise
The CA deletes it weekly
What the CA actually signed — and under which template version — is the PKI's ground-truth record
quizzes.explanation: Enrollment at scale is where template mistakes would surface. The issued log is where you would see it, so it joins the record.

recap: The widening went through the change process, not around it.
Enrollment is hands-free for the fleet group and verified live across the boundary.
The CA's issued log joins the evidence.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 puts those certificates to work at the switch port, starting in monitor mode.

lessons.title: Admit only enrolled devices with 802.1X
lessons.summary: Until now, anything plugged into a VLAN 80 port got an address. With 802.1X, the switch asks each machine to prove who it is with the certificate it enrolled. This lesson turns that check on in monitor mode — every result is logged, nothing is blocked yet — because 47 PCs have no certificate until they join the domain; lesson 6 enforces it once the whole fleet has enrolled. No new server: the NPS role joins DHCP on SBD-DHCP01.
objectives: Add the Network Policy Server (NPS) role to SBD-DHCP01 for port authentication.
Configure Extensible Authentication Protocol–Transport Layer Security (EAP-TLS) with machine certificates on the VLAN 80 access ports, in monitor mode.
Prove the pilots authenticate and that NPS logs every result.
steps: Add the Network Policy Server role to SBD-DHCP01 in a Tier 1 session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, and register it in Active Directory from AdminJumpBox01 (a Tier 0 action: it adds the server to RAS and IAS Servers). Give it an SBD Server Authentication certificate (course 1.6) for SBD-DHCP01.sbd.test, adding SBD-DHCP01 to the SBD TLS Servers group before it requests. It handles port admission only; router logins stay named local accounts, so the server stays in the member-server tier.

Add the VLAN 80 access switch as a RADIUS client with a long, unique shared secret, then create the network policy: wired 802.1X, EAP-TLS only, machine certificates that chain to the approved root and carry the Client Authentication purpose, from the Domain Computers group — any domain-joined computer, servers included where one sits on an 802.1X port. Don't narrow it to SBD Fleet Computers: that group decides who enrolls the fleet's certificate, not who may connect.

Create quarantine VLAN 90 on the access switch with no gateway and no routes (the core gets no VLAN 90 interface) and set it as the ports' failure and guest VLAN, but enable 802.1X on the VLAN 80 access ports in monitor (audit) mode: the switch runs every authentication and reports the result, yet keeps forwarding on VLAN 80 whatever the outcome (vendors name this mode differently). The other 47 PCs have no machine certificate until they join the domain in lesson 6, so enforcing now would strand them in VLAN 90, with no route to a domain controller. Push the wired 802.1X client settings to the Workstations OU by Group Policy (Wired AutoConfig, EAP-TLS, the approved root as the trusted CA).

Turn on Audit Network Policy Server (success and failure) for SBD-DHCP01 in a separate GPO linked above the STIG GPO, recorded as course 1.10 records audit additions — the STIG's audit policy leaves it off. Then prove monitor mode with the pilots: each authenticates with EAP-TLS and NPS logs a grant (event 6272), while a failed attempt is logged — as event 6273 when the request reaches NPS — but still forwards on VLAN 80. Add register row F20 with its owner, as Inside the Network records it, and confirm the NPS events reach the course 1.10 collector, adding 6272 and 6273 to SBD-ForwardedSecurity's query if it doesn't carry them yet.
lessons.command:
# On an enrolled pilot: the wired interface authenticated with EAP-TLS.
netsh lan show interfaces
# On SBD-DHCP01 (Tier 1): NPS auditing is on, then recent grants (6272) and denials (6273).
auditpol /get /subcategory:"Network Policy Server"
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=6272,6273} -MaxEvents 5 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id
lessons.check: The network policy admits Domain Computers with EAP-TLS; NPS auditing records success and failure; every pilot authenticates with EAP-TLS and NPS logs the grant (6272); a failed authentication is logged but, in monitor mode, the port still forwards on VLAN 80; the ports name VLAN 90 as their failure VLAN; and the NPS events appear in the collector.
lessons.evidence: Keep the network policy export, the RADIUS client list (without the secret), the audit GPO report, the monitor-mode port configuration, the pilots' grant events and the failed test, and the F20 register row.

model.label: SBD-DHCP01
model.text: The NPS role for 802.1X runs here, on the existing DHCP server.

quizzes.question: Once 802.1X is enforced, what lets a workstation onto a VLAN 80 port?
answers: Knowing a shared password
Its machine certificate, checked by NPS through EAP-TLS
Being plugged in before the switch boots
quizzes.explanation: EAP-TLS proves the device holds the private key for a certificate the approved CA issued. No certificate, no access.

quizzes.question: Once enforcement is on in lesson 6, where does an unknown device end up?
answers: Quarantine VLAN 90, which has no routes
VLAN 80, with a warning
The domain controller VLAN, so it can enroll
quizzes.explanation: The failure VLAN gives an unknown device a place to be that leads nowhere: VLAN 90 has no gateway, so nothing it sends is routed.

quizzes.question: Why does NPS on SBD-DHCP01 handle port admission only, not router logins?
answers: NPS cannot authenticate people
Router logins need a separate license
If it authenticated the router's administrators, it could control Tier 0 and would have to be managed as Tier 0
quizzes.explanation: Anything that can control a Tier 0 system is Tier 0. Keeping NPS to port admission keeps SBD-DHCP01 in the member-server tier.

quizzes.question: Why does this lesson start 802.1X in monitor mode instead of enforcing it?
answers: Monitor mode is faster
The other 47 PCs have no machine certificate until they join the domain; enforcing now would strand them in VLAN 90, where they could never reach a domain controller
NPS cannot enforce on wired ports
quizzes.explanation: A PC enrolls its certificate only after it joins, and it can join only if the port lets it reach a domain controller. Monitor mode proves the configuration with the pilots without locking the rest of the fleet out.

recap: 802.1X runs on every VLAN 80 port in monitor mode: every result is logged, nothing is blocked yet.
The pilots authenticate with machine certificates; enforcement waits until the whole fleet has enrolled.
No new server: NPS runs on SBD-DHCP01, and its decisions are logged with everything else.
lessons.next: Lesson 6 scales from three machines to fifty, then switches the ports to enforcement.

lessons.title: Scale to fifty, enforce 802.1X, and prove by sample
lessons.summary: Roll the remaining waves while the ports are still in monitor mode, confirm every PC enrolled its machine certificate and authenticates, then switch the ports to enforcement — and prove the fleet the only honest way at scale: a defined sample, the same checks as the pilot, and a written rule for what a sample failure means.
objectives: Roll out the remaining endpoints in planned waves.
Confirm fleet-wide enrollment, then enforce 802.1X and prove an unenrolled device is quarantined.
Verify a defined sample against the pilot's full check set and enrol the fleet in event collection.
steps: Deploy the remaining machines in the planned waves while the VLAN 80 ports are still in monitor mode, adding each wave to SBD Fleet Computers from AdminJumpBox01 and restarting it so it enrolls, and watch the DHCP scope's utilization and the join events arriving in analysis as each wave lands — the pipeline is now the rollout's progress bar.

Confirm every PC enrolled its machine certificate and authenticates: compare the issuing CA's issued certificates and the NPS grant events (6272) against the fifty computer objects, and fix any machine that is missing before going further. Then retire course 1.7's temporary test client, SBD-TEST80, whose Tier 2 test role the pilots now carry: remove it from the domain, delete its computer object, lease and DNS records, and record the retirement.

Switch the VLAN 80 access ports from monitor mode to enforcement, and prove it both ways: an enrolled PC still authenticates and gets its normal lease, and an unenrolled test laptop lands in quarantine VLAN 90 and reaches nothing. Record the switch's port status and the NPS events for both.

Define the sample before checking it: for example one machine per wave plus any machine that logged an error — then run the pilot's full set on each sampled host (OU, policy, DNS, LAPS, certificate, 802.1X admission, peer-deny).
Write the sample rule down: one failed check in the sample widens the sample; a repeated failure stops the rollout and becomes a finding. A sample without a failure rule is a formality.

Enrol the fleet in course 1.10's collection: from AdminJumpBox01, add SBD Fleet Computers to SBD Event Sources and link course 1.10's enrolling GPO to the Workstations OU, below course 1.8's tier logon GPO; from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, widen the collector's WinRM 5985 scope to VLAN 80 (rule F17); restart the PCs so both apply — and confirm fleet sign-ins now appear in the analyst's searches.
lessons.command:
# On AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): the fleet's computer objects and its group
(Get-ADComputer -SearchBase 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Filter *).Count   # 50, once SBD-TEST80 is retired
(Get-ADGroupMember 'SBD Fleet Computers').Count   # 50
# On SBD-DHCP01: authentication results in the last hour (6272 granted, 6273 denied).
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=6272,6273; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} | Group-Object Id | Select-Object Name, Count
Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics -ScopeId 10.0.80.0 | Select-Object PercentageInUse, AddressesInUse
# On SBD-SYSLOG01: the fleet's events arriving
Get-WinEvent -LogName ForwardedEvents -MaxEvents 5 | Select-Object MachineName, Id
lessons.check: Fifty computer objects sit in the Workstations OU and in SBD Fleet Computers, SBD-TEST80 is retired, every PC enrolled and authenticates, the ports enforce 802.1X with the unenrolled laptop quarantined in VLAN 90, scope utilization matches the rollout, every sampled host passes the full check set, and fleet events flow through the pipeline.
lessons.evidence: Keep the wave log, the enrollment reconciliation, the SBD-TEST80 retirement record, the enforcement change with both admission results and their records, the sample definition with its failure rule, the per-sample check results, and the enrolment proof from the collector.

quizzes.question: Why prove the fleet by sample instead of checking all fifty by hand?
answers: A defined sample with a failure rule is verifiable and honest at scale — and identical provenance is what the image hash bought you
Checking is impossible on Windows
Only pilots can be checked
quizzes.explanation: The factory model earns the sampling model. The written failure rule is what keeps the sample from being theater.

quizzes.question: What turns a sampled failure into more than a shrug?
answers: Deleting the failed machine
The written rule: failures widen the sample, repeats stop the rollout and become findings
Rebooting twice
quizzes.explanation: The rule was written before the checks ran — which is exactly what makes acting on it defensible.

quizzes.question: What is the pipeline's role during the rollout itself?
answers: It pauses to save disk
It only matters after completion
Live progress and anomaly surface — each wave's joins and errors appear as they happen
quizzes.explanation: The investment of courses 1.10–1.12 turns deployment into something observed, not something reconstructed afterward.

quizzes.question: When is it safe to switch the VLAN 80 ports from monitor mode to enforcement?
answers: As soon as the first pilot authenticates
Once every PC has enrolled its machine certificate and authenticates in monitor mode
Never; monitor mode is enough
quizzes.explanation: Enforce only after the whole fleet has proven it authenticates. Then a missing certificate cannot strand a machine in VLAN 90, and every unknown device that appears later is quarantined.

recap: Fifty machines, rolled in waves, watched as they landed.
Every PC enrolled before enforcement; an unenrolled device now lands in VLAN 90.
A defined sample with a failure rule carried the proof, and the fleet reports into the pipeline.
lessons.next: The final lesson baselines the fleet and hands off to courses 1.14 and 1.15.

lessons.title: Delta scan the fleet and hand off
lessons.summary: The cadence meets its first population: the sampled endpoints get Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) baselines with the Windows client benchmark from SBD-ADMIN-PC01's own SCAP Compliance Checker (SCC) copy, installed in course 1.8, the infrastructure this course changed is rescanned, and the fleet inventory is handed to course 1.15.
objectives: Baseline the sampled endpoints with the Windows client STIG benchmark from SBD-ADMIN-PC01's existing SCC copy.
Rescan the infrastructure this course touched.
Hand the fleet to courses 1.14 and 1.15.
steps: Baseline the lesson 6 sample with the Windows client benchmark from SBD-ADMIN-PC01, reusing the SCC copy course 1.8 installed there and baselined the seat with — this course scans only the fleet sample. First check the installer course 1.8 kept in C:\Staging\DISA against connected-side-hashes.csv. Rule A03 carries remote management, not the file-sharing and RPC ports a remote SCC scan uses, so copy SCC to each sampled PC over PowerShell remoting, check its hash there, scan locally in a Tier 2 session, bring the results back to C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet\baseline, and remove SCC from the PC. Note how much the pre-linked policies and the OS defaults already satisfy, and classify open items the course 1.4 way.

Rescan what changed and attribute each delta to its lesson: the DCs (schema and LAPS attributes) and SBD-SUBCA01 (fleet enrollment volume) from AdminJumpBox01, and SBD-DHCP01 (the NPS role, its audit GPO and a scope in daily use) locally in a Tier 1 session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01. Send any new deviation to the exception record's owner on AdminJumpBox01.
Assemble the fleet inventory — names, image ancestry, certificate thumbprints, sample status — as the course's closing artifact; course 1.15 makes it a source of SBD-MGMT01's living inventory.

Write the handoff: the fleet exists, watched and hardened, but takes no updates yet — course 1.14 builds SBD-WSUS01, with SBD-PC01–SBD-PC03 as its pilot ring and the other 47 PCs as Ring 2, and course 1.15 keeps the inventory current.
lessons.command:
# Inside SBD-ADMIN-PC01 (Tier 2): the installer course 1.8 kept still matches the record (expected: True)
$scc = Get-Item 'C:\Staging\DISA\<SCC installer>'
(Get-FileHash $scc.FullName -Algorithm SHA256).Hash -in (Import-Csv C:\Staging\DISA\connected-side-hashes.csv).Hash
# Per sampled PC: carry the installer over remote management (A03), install and scan there, bring the results back
$s = New-PSSession SBD-PC07.sbd.test
Copy-Item $scc.FullName -ToSession $s -Destination C:\Windows\Temp\
Copy-Item '<SCC results folder on the PC>' -FromSession $s -Destination C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet\baseline\SBD-PC07 -Recurse
# After the scans: this seat's record, hashed
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet-manifest.csv -NoTypeInformation
lessons.check: The installer course 1.8 kept on SBD-ADMIN-PC01 still matches its recorded hash, the sampled endpoints hold dated Windows client baselines with SCC removed afterwards, the infrastructure rescans carry attributed deltas, and the fleet inventory is complete and filed.
lessons.evidence: Finish the checklist: the installer's hash check, the endpoint baselines, infrastructure rescans, the fleet inventory, the hashed manifest, and the handoff note to courses 1.14 and 1.15.

quizzes.question: Which benchmark do the endpoints get?
answers: The Windows Server benchmark, close enough
The router's config export
The Windows client STIG benchmark — the fleet's own standard from the same DISA package
quizzes.explanation: Course 1.4 staged the Windows client STIG and its SCAP benchmark beside the server content; the GPO package carries the client GPOs, which course 1.5 imported. The fleet is scanned against its own content.

quizzes.question: Why does the issuing CA get a rescan now?
answers: Fifty enrollments changed its operational posture — change-triggered means this too
CAs are rescanned weekly by rule
It was missed earlier
quizzes.explanation: The cadence follows change wherever it lands. Enrollment at fleet scale is a change worth measuring.

quizzes.question: What does the fleet still lack as this course closes?
answers: Certificates and policy
Updates — SBD-WSUS01 arrives in course 1.14 — and an inventory kept current by course 1.15
Network addresses
quizzes.explanation: Honest handoffs name the gap. Fifty hardened machines that never patch would drift out of the state just proven — which is why course 1.14 is next.

recap: The endpoints are baselined by sample from SBD-ADMIN-PC01's existing SCC copy.
Infrastructure deltas are attributed, and the fleet inventory is the closing artifact.
The gap — updates and a living inventory — is named for courses 1.14 and 1.15.
lessons.next: That completes course 1.13. Course 1.14 builds SBD-WSUS01 and delivers the fleet's first Windows updates, ring by ring, starting with SBD-PC01–SBD-PC03.

prerequisites: Complete courses 1.1–1.13: the domain with its DNS and time design, the STIG baselines and hardening policies, the PKI, DHCP, the tiered administration seats, SBD-REPO01, the logging pipeline with SBD-AUDIT01, run by its audit custodian (course 1.11), and the fleet of SBD-PC01–SBD-PC50 with its three pilot machines.
Provision SBD-WSUS01 (10.0.20.30, VLAN 20) as a Windows Server virtual machine with a separate data volume (D: in this sample) sized for the update files.
Outside the boundary, have an approved connected system that can run a second WSUS server with access to Microsoft Update, and the course 1.4 removable-media procedure for carrying its output across.
labNote: This course gives every Windows system one road for updates. SBD-WSUS01 never touches the internet: each month a WSUS server on the connected side synchronizes the same scope, and its metadata and update files cross on hashed media to be imported inside. Microsoft deprecated WSUS in September 2024 — it gets no new features — but it still ships in Windows Server and is supported for production use, with security and quality updates under the product lifecycle. Ring timings and dates are sample values for your patch owner to set. Linux packages already have their road, SBD-REPO01 (course 1.9); endpoint protection and credentialed scanning are coming soon, as courses 1.16 and 1.17, and nothing here depends on them.

lessons.title: Design the rings and the Windows update rule
lessons.summary: Decide how Windows updates reach the network before any arrive: one road through SBD-WSUS01, four rings that try every update on what the network can lose before what it can't, and a monthly crossing on the media procedure. Then confirm the register already carries the road.
objectives: Write the Windows update rule and its documented exceptions.
Place every Windows system in one of four rings, in order.
Set the timing and the crossing cadence, and confirm the register rows.
steps: Write the Windows update rule — the network's one-source-per-type rule, applied to Windows: every Windows system takes updates only from SBD-WSUS01, and anything else is a documented exception. SBD-ROOTCA01 is the standing one: it has no network, so any update it takes is carried by hand at its next ceremony and recorded. Linux packages already have their one source, SBD-REPO01 (course 1.9); protection and scanner content are outside this course.

Place every Windows system in one of four rings, in the order rule F06 names. Ring 1, the pilot: the three course 1.13 pilot PCs (SBD-PC01–SBD-PC03) and SBD-WSUS01 itself, the first server to take each server update and one whose loss stops only patching. Ring 2: the other 47 workstations. Ring 3: the member servers and the Tier 1 and Tier 2 seats — SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 and its SBD-ADMIN-PC01 virtual machine — so the seats that would fix a broken workstation update still run the proven one. SBD-AUDIT01 takes Ring 3's updates at Ring 3's time but in a computer group of its own, Ring 3 - Audit archive: they download only, and its audit custodian installs them, Ring 4-style, because the custodian alone administers that server (course 1.11) — never ordinary Tier 1 operators.

Ring 4 holds the domain controllers and the rest of Tier 0: SBD-SUBCA01, SBD-PKI-MGMT01 and AdminJumpBox01. It goes last and is Tier 0 work, approved and installed from AdminJumpBox01 with Tier 0 accounts, one system at a time. SBD-WSUS01 itself stays a Tier 1 member server run by the patch operators: Tier 0's hold on Ring 4 is a written procedure (lesson 2), and moving SBD-WSUS01 to Tier 0 is recorded as the target.

Write the timing as sample values your patch owner approves: a ring advances only after its machines have installed and reported cleanly for a set soak time — three days after Ring 1 and five after Rings 2 and 3 in this sample. A failed or harmful update stops promotion until it is understood, and nothing skips a ring.

Set the crossing cadence: one crossing a month, after Microsoft's monthly security release on the second Tuesday, through the course 1.4 media procedure and on the same run as SBD-REPO01's monthly snapshot (course 1.9) — one custody record, one approval. An urgent out-of-band fix gets an expedited crossing on the same procedure, with shorter soak times the owner approves in writing.

Confirm the register: F06 already lets every Windows system reach SBD-WSUS01 — metadata over HTTPS 8531, signed content over HTTP 8530 — with the patch owner as its owner, and A01 and A02 carry the two consoles. Nothing leads out of the network and no row is added for one: the content arrives on media.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: every Windows computer object and its OU, the input for the ring table
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force C:\Evidence\patch-protect | Out-Null
([adsisearcher]'(&(objectCategory=computer)(operatingSystem=Windows*))').FindAll() | ForEach-Object { $_.Properties.distinguishedname[0] } | Sort-Object | Set-Content C:\Evidence\patch-protect\windows-computers.txt
(Get-Content C:\Evidence\patch-protect\windows-computers.txt).Count
# On any member: no update policy yet, so no WSUS server is named (expected: no output)
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
lessons.check: The rule names its one source and its exceptions, the ring table places every Windows computer object in exactly one ring with the reason for its place, SBD-AUDIT01 in its custodian-installed group, the timing and crossing calendar are written with an approver, and F06, A01 and A02 are confirmed with owners.
lessons.evidence: Keep the Windows update rule, the computer list and the ring table built from it, the timing and crossing calendar, and the confirmed register rows.

model.label: SBD-WSUS01
model.text: The update service on VLAN 20, its metadata and content ports, and the controls the model maps to it.

quizzes.question: Why do domain controllers sit in the last ring?
answers: They update fastest
A bad update should burn a pilot machine, not the identity fabric — criticality decides order
DCs cannot be updated
quizzes.explanation: Rings are a blast-radius design: change proves itself on what the network can lose before touching what it cannot.

quizzes.question: What does one-approved-source-per-type actually buy?
answers: Cheaper licensing
Faster downloads
'Unauthorized software' becomes checkable — anything not from the named source is a finding by definition
quizzes.explanation: A rule you can test is a control; a preference you cannot is a hope. One source per type draws the testable line.

quizzes.question: An urgent out-of-band security fix is released mid-month. What does the rule say?
answers: An expedited crossing on the same media procedure, through every ring, with soak times the owner shortens in writing
Copy the fix to each server from a USB stick
Approve it for all computers at once to save time
quizzes.explanation: Urgency changes the timing, not the road: the same custody and the same ring order, compressed by a recorded decision.

recap: One road: Windows updates only from SBD-WSUS01, exceptions written down.
Four rings, pilot to Tier 0 — updates earn their way up.
One monthly crossing beside SBD-REPO01's, with an expedited path.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 builds SBD-WSUS01 as a disconnected update server.

lessons.title: Build SBD-WSUS01 as a disconnected server
lessons.summary: Build the server the network will take its updates from: a hardened member server on VLAN 20 that never synchronizes, serves metadata over TLS and signed files over HTTP, and is administered only from the two seats the tier model allows. Its scope is decided here, because what crosses each month is whatever that scope holds.
objectives: Install WSUS on a hardened member server configured never to synchronize.
Decide and record the update scope the monthly crossing will carry.
Protect its metadata with TLS and its administration with the tier model.
steps: Build SBD-WSUS01 as a Windows Server virtual machine at 10.0.20.30 on VLAN 20, with a separate data volume for the update files (D: in this sample), both domain controllers for DNS, and the hypervisor's time synchronization turned off, so it takes time from the domain hierarchy (course 1.3). Join it straight into the Servers OU, so course 1.5's member-server STIG policies, course 1.8's tier logon policies and course 1.10's enrolling GPO, linked to the Servers OU when course 1.10 enrolled SBD-DHCP01, apply from its first boot; confirm with w32tm /query /source that it takes time from a domain controller.

Install the role with its default database, the Windows Internal Database (WID), and run the post-installation step with the content folder on D:. Microsoft announced in September 2024 that WSUS is deprecated: it gets no new features, but it still ships in Windows Server and is supported for production use, with security and quality updates under the product lifecycle. WID is deprecated too — Microsoft suggests SQL Server for the roles that use it — so record the database choice as a decision to revisit before either is removed.

Configure it as a disconnected server: cancel the configuration wizard, which needs Microsoft Update to list products, then in Options store update files locally, enable only the languages your systems use, leave express installation files off (the default), and keep synchronization manual — and never run it. SBD-WSUS01 has no route out; its updates arrive only by import (lesson 3).

Decide the scope and record it: the Windows Server and Windows client products the network runs, security and critical updates and — if Microsoft Defender Antivirus protects the endpoints — its definition updates; no upgrades and no drivers, which are planned changes of their own. The connected-side server in lesson 3 synchronizes exactly this scope, because whatever it holds is what crosses.

Protect the metadata: add SBD-WSUS01 to the SBD TLS Servers group, then request an SBD Server Authentication certificate (course 1.6) for SBD-WSUS01.sbd.test, bind it to the WSUS Administration site's HTTPS port 8531, require TLS on the five web services Microsoft lists (APIRemoting30, ClientWebService, DSSAuthWebService, ServerSyncWebService and SimpleAuthWebService), and run wsusutil configuressl. Update files stay on HTTP 8530, as F06 says: each one is signed, and its hash reaches the client inside the TLS-protected metadata, so a changed file is refused.

Hold the administration to the tier model: scope the 8530 and 8531 inbound rules to the VLANs that hold F06's Windows systems, install the WSUS console on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 and AdminJumpBox01, and keep WSUS Administrators to the named patch operators and the Tier 0 task accounts that run Ring 4. From AdminJumpBox01, add SBD-WSUS01 to SBD Tier 0 Console Hosts (course 1.8's recorded network-logon exception for this console) and to SBD Event Sources (course 1.10), and restart it once the collector's WinRM scope includes 10.0.20.30 (F17). WSUS can't limit an administrator to some computer groups, so Ring 4's Tier 0 rule — like the audit custodian's separation for SBD-AUDIT01 — is a written procedure, not a technical boundary. Write the Ring 4 procedure — Ring 4 is approved and installed only by Tier 0 accounts from AdminJumpBox01, and every Ring 4 approval is checked by name before a controller installs (lesson 5) — and record in the exception record the residual risk that a Tier 1 operator could still approve for Ring 4, with the target that closes it: moving SBD-WSUS01 to Tier 0, administered only from AdminJumpBox01. Until then SBD-WSUS01 stays Tier 1.
lessons.command:
w32tm /query /source   # a domain controller, never the hypervisor's time provider
Install-WindowsFeature -Name UpdateServices -IncludeManagementTools
& "$env:ProgramFiles\Update Services\Tools\wsusutil.exe" postinstall CONTENT_DIR=D:\WSUS
$wsus = Get-WsusServer
$wsus.GetConfiguration() | Select-Object HostBinariesOnMicrosoftUpdate, DownloadExpressPackages, AllUpdateLanguagesEnabled   # expected after Options: False, False, False
$wsus.GetSubscription() | Select-Object SynchronizeAutomatically   # expected: False
# TLS for metadata: the certificate, the 8531 binding, the five services, then wsusutil
$cert = (Get-Certificate -Template SBDServerAuthentication -SubjectName 'CN=SBD-WSUS01.sbd.test' -DnsName SBD-WSUS01.sbd.test -CertStoreLocation Cert:\LocalMachine\My).Certificate
(Get-WebBinding -Name 'WSUS Administration' -Protocol https).AddSslCertificate($cert.Thumbprint, 'My')
'APIRemoting30', 'ClientWebService', 'DSSAuthWebService', 'ServerSyncWebService', 'SimpleAuthWebService' | ForEach-Object { Set-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'IIS:\' -Location "WSUS Administration/$_" -Filter system.webServer/security/access -Name sslFlags -Value Ssl }
& "$env:ProgramFiles\Update Services\Tools\wsusutil.exe" configuressl SBD-WSUS01.sbd.test
Get-WebBinding -Name 'WSUS Administration' | Select-Object protocol, bindingInformation   # http *:8530, https *:8531
Get-LocalGroupMember 'WSUS Administrators'
lessons.check: SBD-WSUS01 sits in the Servers OU, takes time from a domain controller, and runs WSUS on WID, stores files locally, never synchronizes, and answers metadata over TLS on 8531 with a certificate that chains to the SBD root; WSUS Administrators holds only the named operators and Tier 0 task accounts; the server is in SBD Tier 0 Console Hosts and forwards its events; and the scope, the database decision, the written Ring 4 procedure, and its residual risk with the Tier 0 target are recorded.
lessons.evidence: Keep the installation and configuration output, the scope and database decisions, the certificate and binding details, the WSUS Administrators list, the group memberships, the written Ring 4 procedure, and the exception-record entry for the residual risk and its Tier 0 target.

model.label: Get updates, step 3
model.text: Members pull signed update files over HTTP 8530, while their metadata travels over HTTPS 8531.

quizzes.question: How does update content reach this WSUS server?
answers: Direct from Microsoft Update over the internet
By the approved export and import process — hashed media across the air gap
It generates updates locally
quizzes.explanation: The air gap holds for updates too. SBD-WSUS01 never synchronizes: Microsoft's design for air-gapped networks pairs an outside WSUS server that exports with an inside one that imports.

quizzes.question: What gates an update's arrival at the domain controllers?
answers: The calendar date alone
The DC's own download speed
Survival in the earlier rings first — approval promotes ring by ring
quizzes.explanation: Ring 4 installs only what Rings 1 to 3 have proven, and only when Tier 0 starts it — which is why its approvals are Tier 0 work and are checked by name in lesson 5.

quizzes.question: Why scope products and classifications tightly?
answers: Unused content is imported, stored, and reviewed for nothing — and every artifact crossing the boundary should earn its trip
WSUS breaks above ten products
Licensing forbids more
quizzes.explanation: In an air-gapped lab, every megabyte is carried by hand. Scope is both hygiene and respect for the boundary process.

recap: A hardened member server that never synchronizes.
Metadata over TLS on 8531; signed files over HTTP on 8530.
Two consoles, named administrators, and a written Ring 4 procedure for the limit WSUS can't enforce, with Tier 0 as the recorded target.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 carries the first month's updates across the air gap.

lessons.title: Carry updates across the air gap
lessons.summary: SBD-WSUS01 never talks to Microsoft. Each month a second WSUS server on the connected side synchronizes the recorded scope and downloads its files; its metadata export and content folder cross on approved media, hashed on both sides, and SBD-WSUS01 imports them — the two-server path Microsoft describes for air-gapped networks.
objectives: Run the connected-side export server with SBD-WSUS01's recorded scope.
Export the metadata and the files, and carry both under the media procedure.
Verify the crossing on SBD-WSUS01 before importing, and file its record.
steps: On the approved connected system, run the export server: WSUS on the same Windows Server release as SBD-WSUS01, synchronizing from Microsoft Update with exactly the products, classifications and languages lesson 2 recorded, and storing files locally. It sits outside the boundary and never connects to the lab; its only output is media.

After each month's synchronization, approve the updates you need on the export server so it downloads their files, and wait until nothing is still downloading — those approvals only switch the downloads on, and they stay outside. Then, as a local administrator on the export server, run wsusutil export for the metadata package and copy the WsusContent folder: the package carries the update metadata, and the files travel beside it (after the first crossing, only those added since the last one).

Hash the package and every file into connected-side-hashes.csv, which travels with the media, and carry the set under the course 1.4 media procedure with its custody record, on the run that also carries SBD-REPO01's snapshot. Declining an update doesn't stop it from being exported, so the export server's scope is the real limit on what crosses.

On SBD-WSUS01, hash the media's contents into lab-side-hashes.csv and compare the two lists before opening anything: one mismatch stops the import and becomes a finding. Copy the files into D:\WSUS\WsusContent first, then run wsusutil import locally as a local administrator — Microsoft warns never to import an export from a source you don't trust, and the custody record and matching hashes are how this network earns that trust. A large import can run for hours.

Check the import log, confirm the month's updates now appear in the console, and file the crossing in C:\Evidence\patch-protect\transfer: dates, carrier, file count, the package hash, both hash lists and the import log. If WSUS later shows an approved update as still waiting for its files, wsusutil reset makes it re-check its content folder against the database.
lessons.command:
# Connected side, on the export server, once every needed file has downloaded
& "$env:ProgramFiles\Update Services\Tools\wsusutil.exe" export E:\2026-10\wsus-export.xml.gz E:\2026-10\export.log
robocopy D:\WSUS\WsusContent E:\2026-10\WsusContent /E   # the first crossing carries the whole folder
Get-ChildItem E:\2026-10 -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv E:\connected-side-hashes.csv -NoTypeInformation
# Inside, on SBD-WSUS01, with the media as E: (no output from Compare-Object means every hash matches)
$t = 'C:\Evidence\patch-protect\transfer\2026-10'; New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $t | Out-Null
Get-ChildItem E:\2026-10 -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv "$t\lab-side-hashes.csv" -NoTypeInformation
Compare-Object (Import-Csv E:\connected-side-hashes.csv).Hash (Import-Csv "$t\lab-side-hashes.csv").Hash
robocopy E:\2026-10\WsusContent D:\WSUS\WsusContent /E
& "$env:ProgramFiles\Update Services\Tools\wsusutil.exe" import E:\2026-10\wsus-export.xml.gz "$t\import.log"
Copy-Item E:\connected-side-hashes.csv, E:\2026-10\export.log -Destination $t
lessons.check: The export server's scope matches lesson 2's record, every hash matches on both sides, the import log reports success, the month's updates appear on SBD-WSUS01, and the crossing record is complete.
lessons.evidence: Keep the export server's scope settings, both hash lists and their comparison, the custody record, the export and import logs, and the crossing record with the package hash and file count.

model.label: Get updates, step 1
model.text: An authorized operator carries approved update material across the air gap on controlled media — no network session crosses.

quizzes.question: Why must the export server synchronize exactly the recorded scope?
answers: Because everything it holds is exported, and that is what crosses the boundary
Because Microsoft Update charges by product
Because SBD-WSUS01 synchronizes from it over the network
quizzes.explanation: Declining an update doesn't stop it from being exported: the export server's database is the shipment. A tight scope there keeps every crossing small and reviewable.

quizzes.question: The lab-side hash of one file doesn't match the connected-side list. What happens?
answers: Import anyway — clients check signatures
Copy that one file again from the media and carry on
The import stops and the mismatch becomes a finding; the set is carried again
quizzes.explanation: A mismatch means the set isn't what left the connected side. The clients' signature checks are a second line of defence, not a reason to skip the first.

quizzes.question: What does the metadata package carry?
answers: Only the approvals made on the export server
The update metadata — the files travel beside it as the WsusContent folder
The update files and every approval
quizzes.explanation: wsusutil export writes the update metadata from the export server's database, and the files come from its content folder. Both cross, both are hashed, and approvals are made inside, ring by ring.

recap: Two WSUS servers: one outside fills the media, one inside serves the network.
Package and files cross hashed, under custody.
Compare first, copy the files, then import — or stop.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 points every Windows system at its ring.

lessons.title: Target the rings with computer groups and Group Policy
lessons.summary: Rings become mechanics: a computer group per ring on SBD-WSUS01, plus one for SBD-AUDIT01, client-side targeting so each computer files itself into its ring, and one Group Policy object per ring that names the server, the ring and its install behaviour. The domain controllers get a ring of their own: they download on their own but install only when Tier 0 starts it, and SBD-AUDIT01 waits for its audit custodian the same way.
objectives: Create the ring groups and switch WSUS to client-side targeting.
Build and link one Group Policy object per ring, with the pilot set by security filtering.
Set install behaviour and deadlines, and prove every computer reports to its ring.
steps: On SBD-WSUS01, create the four ring groups — Ring 1 - Pilot, Ring 2 - Workstations, Ring 3 - Member servers and Ring 4 - Tier 0 — and Ring 3 - Audit archive for SBD-AUDIT01 alone, and set the Computers option to Use Group Policy or registry settings on computers. The groups must exist first: a computer whose policy names a group WSUS doesn't have waits in Unassigned Computers until the group is created.

From AdminJumpBox01, create one GPO per ring, and one for Ring 3 - Audit archive, around the same core: Specify intranet Microsoft update service location, with https://SBD-WSUS01.sbd.test:8531 for both detection and statistics; Enable client-side targeting, with the ring's group name; and Do not connect to any Windows Update Internet locations, so no system keeps trying the public service. Leave Allow signed updates from an intranet Microsoft update service location disabled, so only Microsoft-signed updates install.

Set each ring's install behaviour in Configure Automatic Updates: option 4, download and schedule the install, at a time that suits the ring's work for Rings 1 to 3, and option 7 — download, then notify to install and to restart, a Windows Server option — for Ring 4, so a domain controller installs only when a Tier 0 operator starts it; Ring 3 - Audit archive uses option 7 too, so SBD-AUDIT01 installs only when its audit custodian starts it in a custodian session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01. Deadlines go on the approvals (two days for Ring 1 and five for Rings 2 and 3 in this sample): at a deadline the update installs whatever the client's own schedule says. Ring 4's approvals carry none, and neither do Ring 3 - Audit archive's.

Link the GPOs where the rings live: Ring 2 at the Workstations OU; Ring 3 at the Servers and Admin Workstations OUs and at Admin Servers, filtered to SBD-ADMIN-SRV01; Ring 3 - Audit archive at the Audit Servers OU; Ring 4 at the Domain Controllers and Tier 0 Servers OUs and at Admin Servers, filtered to AdminJumpBox01. Link Ring 1 above the ring GPO on the Workstations and Servers OUs (link order 1), security-filtered to a new SBD WSUS Pilot group holding SBD-PC01–SBD-PC03 and SBD-WSUS01, and restart those four so the membership reaches their Kerberos tickets.

Prove the targeting on one member of each ring: run gpupdate, read the policy values, and start a detection with the Windows Update Agent's DetectNow call; then confirm on SBD-WSUS01 that each computer sits in its ring's group and that Unassigned Computers is empty. Check Ring 4 from AdminJumpBox01, and record every ring's member list against lesson 1's table.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-WSUS01: the four ring groups and client-side targeting
$wsus = Get-WsusServer
'Ring 1 - Pilot', 'Ring 2 - Workstations', 'Ring 3 - Member servers', 'Ring 3 - Audit archive', 'Ring 4 - Tier 0' | ForEach-Object { [void]$wsus.CreateComputerTargetGroup($_) }
$config = $wsus.GetConfiguration(); $config.TargetingMode = 'Client'; $config.Save()
# On AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): the links in order, and the pilot GPO's security filter
(Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test').GpoLinks | Select-Object Order, DisplayName
Get-GPPermission -Name 'SBD WSUS Ring 1 - Pilot' -All | Select-Object @{ n = 'Trustee'; e = { $_.Trustee.Name } }, Permission
# On one member of each ring, after gpupdate /force: its server, its ring, and a detection now
Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate | Select-Object WUServer, TargetGroup, DoNotConnectToWindowsUpdateInternetLocations
(New-Object -ComObject Microsoft.Update.AutoUpdate).DetectNow()
# Back on SBD-WSUS01: each ring's members, and nobody unassigned
Get-WsusComputer -ComputerTargetGroups 'Ring 1 - Pilot' | Select-Object FullDomainName, LastSyncTime
Get-WsusComputer -ComputerTargetGroups 'Unassigned Computers'   # expected: no computers
lessons.check: The four ring groups and Ring 3 - Audit archive exist and WSUS uses client-side targeting; each ring's GPO is linked where its computers live, with the pilot filter and link order in place; one member of each ring shows SBD-WSUS01 and its ring in its policy values; every Windows computer sits in its ring's group; and Unassigned Computers is empty.
lessons.evidence: Keep the GPO reports with their links and security filtering, the pilot group's members, each ring's member list from SBD-WSUS01, the policy values from one member per ring, and the install-time and deadline table, with SBD-AUDIT01's custodian-started installs.

model.label: Get updates, step 2
model.text: Members ask SBD-WSUS01 for update metadata over HTTPS 8531, at the address and in the ring their Group Policy names.

quizzes.question: A pilot PC receives both the Ring 1 and the Ring 2 GPO. Why does it still report to Ring 1?
answers: The Ring 1 link has the higher precedence on that OU (link order 1), so its target group wins the conflict
WSUS always picks the lowest ring number
A computer can receive only one GPO
quizzes.explanation: Both GPOs apply; where they set the same value, the link with the higher precedence wins. Security filtering keeps the Ring 1 GPO off every PC that isn't in the pilot group.

quizzes.question: Why do the domain controllers use option 7 instead of a scheduled install?
answers: Option 7 makes downloads faster
A Tier 0 operator decides when each controller installs and restarts, so they never go down together and each is checked before the next
Domain controllers can't run scheduled installs
quizzes.explanation: Downloads still happen on their own; only the install and the restart wait for a person — one controller at a time, with replication checked in between.

quizzes.question: A new server's policy names Ring 3, but the group was mistyped on SBD-WSUS01. Where does the server land?
answers: In Ring 4, as the safest ring
Nowhere — it stops checking for updates
In Unassigned Computers, until a group with that exact name exists
quizzes.explanation: Client-side targeting only files a computer into a group WSUS already has. An empty Unassigned Computers list is part of the proof.

recap: A group per ring, plus SBD-AUDIT01's own, and computers file themselves in by Group Policy.
Rings 1–3 install on schedule and by deadline; Ring 4 waits for Tier 0, and SBD-AUDIT01 for its custodian.
An empty Unassigned Computers list: every machine has a ring.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 runs the first monthly cycle through the rings and proves it.

lessons.title: Run the first cycle and prove it
lessons.summary: The design meets a real month: approve the imported updates for the pilot, promote them ring by ring on the written soak times, and install the domain controllers by hand. Then prove the result with WSUS's own reports, spot checks on the systems themselves, and the first SCAP baseline of SBD-WSUS01.
objectives: Promote one monthly cycle through all four rings on the written timing.
Report compliance per ring and spot-check it on the systems themselves.
