Baseline SBD-WSUS01 and hand the course's records to course 1.15.
steps: Approve the month's updates for Ring 1 only, with its deadline, and watch the pilots install and report. Before anything moves, check that the pilot PCs still sign in and apply policy and that SBD-WSUS01 still serves its clients; then approve Ring 2 and Ring 3 on the written soak times — Ring 3 - Audit archive with Ring 3, without a deadline — recording for each promotion the numbers that justified it. SBD-AUDIT01's audit custodian then starts its install in a custodian session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 and records it; ordinary Tier 1 operators don't install there.

If an update fails or does harm, stop: leave it unapproved for the later rings and, where the update supports removal, approve it for removal in the rings that installed it. Windows client quality updates delivered through the Unified Update Platform can't be removed through WSUS, so the pilot is where they have to prove themselves.

Ring 4 is Tier 0 work from AdminJumpBox01. First read the approval history and confirm that every Ring 4 approval was made by a Tier 0 account — WSUS records who approved what, for which group. Then install on SBD-DC02, restart it, and check it with dcdiag and repadmin /replsummary before touching SBD-DC01; the two Tier 0 servers follow, and AdminJumpBox01 goes last.

Report compliance per ring with the UpdateServices cmdlets (the console's built-in reports need Microsoft's Report Viewer runtime, one more package to carry across): computers that still need or failed an approved update, and computers silent for a week. Spot-check one system per ring on the machine itself against WSUS's view of it. WSUS reports what clients tell it, so the spot checks are the independent view.

Close the cycle once every ring has installed: Invoke-WsusServerCleanup declines superseded updates that nothing still needs and expired ones, and removes unneeded files and computers silent for 30 days. Then take SBD-WSUS01's first SCAP baseline with course 1.4's SCC and benchmark versions, run locally in a Tier 1 session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, answer the IIS server and site STIG items for the WSUS web site in a STIG Viewer checklist (staged across the air gap as in course 1.4), and classify every open item as course 1.4 taught — update files on HTTP 8530 are a deviation candidate, justified by signed files whose hashes travel in TLS-protected metadata.

Hand off to course 1.15: the ring table, WSUS's computer list and this cycle's compliance report become inventory sources, the crossing calendar sets when its reconciliation runs, and SBD-MGMT01 joins Ring 3 simply by landing in the Servers OU. Collect the course's records into C:\Evidence\patch-protect on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 and hash them into a manifest.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-WSUS01 (Tier 1): approve for the pilot; deadlines are set in the console's Approve Updates dialog
Get-WsusUpdate -Classification All -Approval Unapproved -Status FailedOrNeeded | Approve-WsusUpdate -Action Install -TargetGroupName 'Ring 1 - Pilot'
Get-WsusComputer -ComputerTargetGroups 'Ring 1 - Pilot' -ComputerUpdateStatus FailedOrNeeded   # expected: none once the ring is clean
Get-WsusComputer -ToLastReportedStatusTime (Get-Date).AddDays(-7)   # computers silent for a week
# On AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): who approved each Ring 4 update, then each controller in turn
$wsus = Get-WsusServer -Name SBD-WSUS01.sbd.test -PortNumber 8531 -UseSsl
$wsus.GetUpdateApprovals((New-Object Microsoft.UpdateServices.Administration.UpdateScope)) | Where-Object { $_.GetComputerTargetGroup().Name -eq 'Ring 4 - Tier 0' } | Select-Object CreationDate, AdministratorName, Action
dcdiag /s:SBD-DC02 /q; repadmin /replsummary   # after SBD-DC02 restarts, before SBD-DC01
# Spot check from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: what a system itself says it installed
Invoke-Command SBD-DHCP01 { Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending | Select-Object -First 3 HotFixID, InstalledOn }
# Back on SBD-WSUS01, once every ring has installed
Invoke-WsusServerCleanup -DeclineSupersededUpdates -DeclineExpiredUpdates -CleanupObsoleteUpdates -CleanupUnneededContentFiles -CleanupObsoleteComputers
lessons.check: Each ring installed the month's updates in the written order with its promotion recorded, SBD-AUDIT01's custodian installed its updates, every Ring 4 approval names a Tier 0 account, both controllers were healthy between installs, no computer is failing or silent without an explanation, the spot checks agree with WSUS, SBD-WSUS01 has its first baseline with every open item classified, and the course's records are hashed.
lessons.evidence: Keep the per-ring approval and install timeline with the custodian's install record for SBD-AUDIT01, the Ring 4 approval history and install record, the compliance and silent-computer reports, the spot checks, the cleanup output, the SCC results and STIG Viewer checklist with classified findings, the manifest, and the handoff note to course 1.15.

quizzes.question: The pilot installs cleanly, but one pilot PC can no longer apply Group Policy. What happens to the promotion?
answers: It stops until the cause is understood: the update stays unapproved for later rings, and is removed where it supports removal
It continues — the install itself succeeded
Approve it for every ring to see whether the problem spreads
quizzes.explanation: An install that succeeds but breaks work is a failed update. The pilot exists to catch exactly this before the systems that matter feel it.

quizzes.question: Why check Ring 4's approval history before a controller installs?
answers: Approvals expire after a day
WSUS can't stop a non-Tier 0 administrator from approving for Ring 4, so the record shows whether the written rule held
Domain controllers can't read approvals
quizzes.explanation: Where a tool can't enforce a boundary, the evidence has to show it held. WSUS records the administrator behind every approval, so the check takes a minute.

quizzes.question: WSUS reports every computer compliant. What does that prove?
answers: That the network has no vulnerabilities
Nothing at all
That every computer reported its approved updates installed — the clients' own report, which the spot checks test
quizzes.explanation: WSUS's view is the clients' own report: useful and automatic, but not independent. Spot checks on the machines themselves are what keep it honest.

recap: The month moves pilot → workstations → servers → Tier 0, on record.
Ring 4: approvals checked by name, controllers one at a time.
Reports, spot checks and a first baseline prove it.
lessons.next: That completes course 1.14. Course 1.15 builds SBD-MGMT01 and the living inventory, with this course's WSUS records among its sources.

prerequisites: Complete courses 1.1–1.14: every system those courses built is running, course 1.13's fleet inventory is filed, and SBD-WSUS01 serves all four update rings.
Provision SBD-MGMT01 (10.0.70.10, VLAN 70) as a Windows Server virtual machine with a separate data volume (D: in this sample) for the record.

Keep the records earlier courses produced within reach: the service-path register, course 1.14's ring table and WSUS computer list, course 1.9's snapshot catalog, each course's baseline sessions, and the exception record.
labNote: Course 1.13 handed over a snapshot of the fleet; this course makes the whole network's component inventory a living record on SBD-MGMT01 — NIST SP 800-53 CM-8 in practice. The server keeps the record and reaches into nothing: the directory, the DHCP leases, the WSUS computer list, SBD-REPO01's records and the baseline sessions it is checked against arrive through the administrators' existing sessions. Column names and the monthly cadence are sample values; the system owner decides.

sources.title: NIST · SP 800-53 Rev. 5 security controls (CM-8 System Component Inventory)
Microsoft · DirectorySearcher class (LDAP searches of Active Directory)
Microsoft · The lastLogonTimestamp attribute may not be accurate
Microsoft · The WSUS Server Cleanup Wizard
Microsoft · Copy-Item (copying to and from a remote session)
Microsoft · Configure Windows Firewall rules with Group Policy
DISA · SCAP content and the SCAP Compliance Checker (SCC)
DISA · SRG/STIG tools (SCC and STIG Viewer)

lessons.title: Design the inventory and its keeper
lessons.summary: Decide what the component inventory must hold before SBD-MGMT01 exists: every component inside the boundary counted once, and the columns that make each one accountable. Then name the records that can contradict it, and give it a keeper that holds the record without reaching into anything else.
objectives: Draw the inventory's boundary and list every component in it.
Choose the columns that make each component accountable.
Name the discovery sources and place SBD-MGMT01 under the tier model.
steps: Draw the boundary as CM-8 asks: every component of this network, each counted once, and nothing from outside it. That is every server and controller (SBD-ROOTCA01 included, offline in the vault), the three administration seats, each of the 50 PCs, the core and the VLAN 80 access switch, and the seven hypervisor hosts (SBD-HV01–SBD-HV07) on which Inside the Network places the virtual machines. The connected-side systems that fill the media stay out; the crossing records name them.

Choose the columns, one per attribute: name, type, role, operating system and version, domain membership, address and VLAN, OU, tier, location (host and rack), update source (a WSUS ring, an SBD-REPO01 snapshot, or by hand at a ceremony), latest baseline, the course that built it, an accountable owner by role (CM-8(4)), and status — planned, active or retired. Record the systems the design names but no course has built yet, SBD-EPO01, SBD-NESSUS01 and the four VLAN 40 servers, as planned, so a reconciliation never mistakes them for missing.

Name the records that can contradict it and what each one proves: the directory shows what joined the domain, the DHCP leases what is on VLAN 80 now, WSUS's computer list what reports for updates and in which ring, SBD-REPO01's catalog and access log which Linux servers take packages, and the baseline sessions which hosts have a measured state. Any disagreement is a finding, and lesson 5 makes the comparison a monthly check.

Place the keeper as Inside the Network does: SBD-MGMT01, Windows Server at 10.0.70.10 on VLAN 70 beside SBD-REPO01, a Tier 1 member server administered only from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (rule A02). The model leaves its listeners to define: define them as management only, and give it no collection path of its own — source data arrives through the administrators' existing sessions, so the server that holds the record can't reach, or be used to reach, anything else. Its domain rows (F01–F03, F06 in Ring 3, F09, F17 and F18) already list it.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: start the course record with the inventory's columns
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force C:\Evidence\management-server | Out-Null
'Name,Type,Role,OS,Domain,Address,VLAN,OU,Tier,Location,UpdateSource,Baseline,BuiltIn,Owner,Status' | Set-Content C:\Evidence\management-server\inventory-columns.csv
# SBD-MGMT01 isn't registered yet; its neighbour on VLAN 70 is
Resolve-DnsName SBD-MGMT01.sbd.test -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue   # expected: no answer
Resolve-DnsName SBD-REPO01.sbd.test | Select-Object Name, IPAddress   # 10.0.70.20
lessons.check: The boundary lists every component once, with the planned systems marked; the columns cover identity, place, tier, update source, baseline and an accountable owner; each discovery source is named with what it proves; and SBD-MGMT01's placement, administration and lack of any collection path are written down.
lessons.evidence: Keep the boundary list, the column definitions, the source table with what each source proves, and SBD-MGMT01's placement and administration decision.

model.label: SBD-MGMT01
model.text: The management tools server on VLAN 70 beside SBD-REPO01, with its listeners left to define.

quizzes.question: Why record the hypervisor hosts when every server is a virtual machine?
answers: They are optional decoration
They run every virtual machine, so whatever controls them controls the servers — they belong inside the boundary
The core requires it
quizzes.explanation: An inventory that lists the guests but not their hosts misses the components with the most reach. Inside the Network gives every server's host and rack for that reason.

quizzes.question: SBD-EPO01 is designed but not built. How does the inventory show it?
answers: It leaves it out until it exists
It lists it as active so the record looks complete
As planned, so the record matches the design and a reconciliation doesn't flag it as missing
quizzes.explanation: Status carries the difference between designed and installed. When the system is built, its row turns active as part of that build.

quizzes.question: Why does SBD-MGMT01 get no collection path of its own?
answers: A server that can reach every source becomes a path to all of them; letting data arrive through existing administration sessions keeps it a keeper, not a hub
Collection paths are slower
Windows Server can't read other servers
quizzes.explanation: Least privilege applies to servers too. Every path the register doesn't need is one an attacker can't use.

recap: Every component inside the boundary, counted once — hosts and network devices included.
Columns that make each component accountable, owner included.
Sources that can contradict the record, and a keeper that reaches into nothing.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 builds SBD-MGMT01 and locks it down.

lessons.title: Build and harden SBD-MGMT01
lessons.summary: Build the inventory's keeper as a small, quiet member server, joined into the Servers OU so the hardening, tier and update policies apply from its first boot. It answers only the Tier 1 seat, and the record sits on its own volume behind permissions that admit administrators alone.
objectives: Build SBD-MGMT01 in its place with the network's policies applied from first boot.
Limit its administration to SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 and prove the limit.
Prepare the record's folders, permissions and version history.
steps: Build SBD-MGMT01 as a Windows Server virtual machine — on SBD-HV07 beside SBD-REPO01, where Inside the Network places it — with the hypervisor's time synchronization turned off, so the domain is its only clock, a separate data volume for the record (D: in this sample), the static address 10.0.70.10/24 with the core's VLAN 70 interface as gateway (10.0.70.1 in this sample), and both domain controllers for DNS. Join it straight into the Servers OU, so course 1.5's STIG policies, course 1.8's tier logon policies, course 1.10's event-forwarding GPO (linked to the Servers OU in course 1.10) and course 1.14's Ring 3 update policy apply from its first boot.

Check that it took its place: time from a domain controller, as course 1.3 set up, and an update policy that names SBD-WSUS01 and Ring 3, with SBD-WSUS01 listing it there. Add it to SBD Event Sources from AdminJumpBox01, widen the collector's WinRM scope to 10.0.70.10 (F17) from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, and restart it so its security events reach SBD-SYSLOG01.

Close it to everything but its administration: Windows Defender Firewall on in every profile, and the existing Remote Desktop and Windows Remote Management rules scoped to SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (10.0.60.20), because allow rules add up and a new, narrower rule would not restrict the broad ones. Install no other role and no agent; course 1.8's Servers OU policy already denies Tier 0 accounts here.

Prepare the record on D:: an Inventory folder with inheritance removed and full control for SYSTEM and Administrators only — the volume's inherited defaults let ordinary users read and create files — holding current, history, sources and findings folders. Every published version is copied into history with its SHA-256 in a hash list, and every change gets a line in a change log: who, what, why, and the change record it answers.

Prove the closure: a remote session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 opens, the same attempt from SBD-ADMIN-PC01 fails at the core because rule A02 names only the Tier 1 seat, and the firewall's remote-address lists show only 10.0.60.20 for management.
lessons.command:
# In a session on SBD-MGMT01 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01
([adsisearcher]"(&(objectCategory=computer)(name=$env:COMPUTERNAME))").FindOne().Path   # ...OU=Servers,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test
w32tm /query /source   # a domain controller, never the local clock
Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate | Select-Object WUServer, TargetGroup   # Ring 3 - Member servers
Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayGroup 'Remote Desktop', 'Windows Remote Management' -Enabled True | Get-NetFirewallAddressFilter | Select-Object InstanceID, RemoteAddress   # 10.0.60.20 only
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force D:\Inventory | Out-Null
icacls D:\Inventory /inheritance:r /grant:r 'SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F' 'Administrators:(OI)(CI)F'
'current', 'history', 'sources', 'findings' | ForEach-Object { New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "D:\Inventory\$_" | Out-Null }
icacls D:\Inventory
# From SBD-ADMIN-PC01: the same management path must fail
Test-NetConnection SBD-MGMT01.sbd.test -Port 5985   # expected: TcpTestSucceeded False
lessons.check: SBD-MGMT01 sits in the Servers OU with the hypervisor's time synchronization off and time from a domain controller, reports to Ring 3 on SBD-WSUS01, forwards its security events, accepts management only from 10.0.60.20 and refuses SBD-ADMIN-PC01, runs no extra role or agent, and holds an Inventory folder that only SYSTEM and Administrators can open.
lessons.evidence: Keep the OU placement, the time source, the update policy values and WSUS listing, the firewall scope, the refused connection from SBD-ADMIN-PC01, and the Inventory folder's permissions.

quizzes.question: Why scope the existing Remote Desktop and remote management rules instead of adding a narrow new rule?
answers: New rules are slower
Allow rules add up: a narrow new rule leaves the broad existing one letting everyone in
Windows allows only one rule per port
quizzes.explanation: Windows Defender Firewall admits a connection if any enabled allow rule matches. Narrow the rules that exist, then prove it from a seat that must be refused.

quizzes.question: SBD-ADMIN-PC01 shares VLAN 60 with SBD-ADMIN-SRV01. Why is its attempt on SBD-MGMT01 refused?
answers: Rule A02 names only SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 as the source for member-server management, so the core denies the Tier 2 seat — and the host firewall would too
Virtual machines can't use the network
SBD-MGMT01 is offline
quizzes.explanation: Sharing a VLAN grants nothing. The register names the seat, the core enforces it between VLANs, and the host firewall enforces it again.

quizzes.question: Why remove inheritance on the Inventory folder?
answers: To make backups faster
Inheritance can't be used on data volumes
A new volume's inherited permissions let ordinary users read and create files; the record should open to administrators alone
quizzes.explanation: Defaults are someone else's decision. The record's permissions are part of its integrity, alongside its version history and hashes.

recap: In the Servers OU: hardened, tiered and patched from first boot.
Management from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 only — proven by a refused attempt.
A record folder for administrators alone, with history and hashes.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 fills it with the first complete inventory.

lessons.title: Build the living inventory
lessons.summary: Course 1.13's fleet inventory was a snapshot of fifty PCs; SBD-MGMT01 makes the whole network's inventory a living record. Every component gets its place, ring, update source, baseline and owner, kept current by the procedures that change it.
objectives: Load every component into the inventory from the records the path already keeps.
Define how the inventory stays current and who owns it.
Publish the first version with its hash.
steps: Start from the records the path already keeps rather than from memory: course 1.13's fleet inventory for the 50 PCs (names, image ancestry, certificate thumbprints, sample status), the service-path register and Inside the Network for names, addresses and locations, course 1.14's ring table for the update rings, course 1.9's snapshot catalog for SBD-REPO01, and each course's baseline set for the latest baseline date.

Load the inventory with every component the boundary lists — the fleet, the servers (SBD-REPO01 included, with its current snapshot as its update source), the admin plane, the core, the access switch and the hypervisor hosts — each with every column filled: the CM-8 component inventory, in one place. Add the planned systems as planned.

Define currency: every build, move and retirement updates the inventory as part of its own procedure (CM-8(1)), so each later course's build lesson adds its rows, and a monthly reconciliation compares the inventory against the directory, the DHCP leases and the WSUS computer list — drift between them is a finding.

Name the owner — a role, with a named deputy — who approves each change, and publish the first version: copy it into history with its hash and log the change. Course 2.2 shows how a record like this one joins the Body of Evidence for the configuration-management controls.
lessons.command:
# In a session on SBD-MGMT01 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, once the record is filled in
$inv = Import-Csv D:\Inventory\current\inventory.csv
$inv | Group-Object Status | Select-Object Name, Count
$inv | Group-Object Name | Where-Object Count -gt 1 | Select-Object Name   # expected: nothing counted twice
$inv | Where-Object { $_.Status -eq 'active' -and (-not $_.Owner -or -not $_.UpdateSource -or -not $_.Location) } | Select-Object Name   # expected: nothing
$stamp = Get-Date -Format yyyy-MM-dd
Copy-Item D:\Inventory\current\inventory.csv "D:\Inventory\history\inventory-$stamp.csv"
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 "D:\Inventory\history\inventory-$stamp.csv" | Export-Csv D:\Inventory\history\hashes.csv -Append -NoTypeInformation
lessons.check: The inventory lists every component in the boundary exactly once with every column filled, planned systems are marked planned, the update-on-change rule and the monthly reconciliation are written with an owner and deputy, and the first version is in history with its hash.
lessons.evidence: Keep the populated inventory export, the status counts and completeness checks, the currency rule with its owner and cadence, and the first version's hash.

quizzes.question: What makes an inventory 'living' rather than a stale spreadsheet?
answers: Pretty formatting
Update-on-change plus a scheduled reconciliation against sources the record doesn't control — the directory and the leases
Monthly printing
quizzes.explanation: Processes keep it current; reconciliation proves it stayed current. Both are written down, so both are checkable.

quizzes.question: A machine appears in DHCP leases but not the inventory. What is that?
answers: Normal churn to ignore
A reason to restart DHCP
A finding — either an undocumented system or a broken process, and both matter
quizzes.explanation: The reconciliation exists to surface exactly this. Unknown hardware on the network is the classic first question of any assessment.

quizzes.question: Which control family consumes this record most directly?
answers: Configuration management — CM-8's component inventory is literally this artifact
Physical security
Awareness training
quizzes.explanation: The authorization path's CM controls ask 'what do you have and how do you know' — this lesson is the answer being built.

recap: One record of everything, with place, ring, update source, baseline and owner.
Every change updates it; a monthly reconciliation keeps it honest.
Owned, versioned, and ready to join the Body of Evidence.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 gathers what the network already knows, to check the record against.

lessons.title: Feed it from what the network already knows
lessons.summary: The inventory says what should exist; the network's own records say what does. Export the directory's computer objects, the DHCP leases, the WSUS computer list, SBD-REPO01's records and the baseline sessions through the sessions administrators already use, and file them on SBD-MGMT01 with hashes, in one shape lesson 5 can compare.
objectives: Export each discovery source through an existing administration path.
Know what each source can and can't prove.
File the exports on SBD-MGMT01 with hashes, in one comparable shape.
steps: Read the directory over LDAP from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: every computer object's name, operating system, distinguished name (which gives its OU) and lastLogonTimestamp. Use an LDAP search rather than the Active Directory module, whose Web Services port the controllers open only to AdminJumpBox01, and read lastLogonTimestamp as a sign of staleness, not of last use: it is updated only when the stored value is 9 to 14 days old.

Export the leases on SBD-DHCP01 in a session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: every lease in the VLAN 80 scope with its address, client ID (the MAC address), host name, state and expiry. A lease shows what is plugged in now, joined or not; course 1.7's DHCP audit log shows what came and went between exports.

Export SBD-WSUS01's computer list the same way: each computer's name, address, last contact, last status report and requested ring. WSUS's cleanup removes computers silent for 30 days (course 1.14), so a machine missing there has been quiet for a month or more.

Copy SBD-REPO01's records over SSH as course 1.9 does, and count its web server's access log by client address to see which Linux servers actually take packages. List the baseline sessions in the evidence folders you hold, by host and date; Tier 0 reports its hosts' dates through the change record, because its evidence stays on AdminJumpBox01.

File the set: hash every export into a dated list, copy both into D:\Inventory\sources on SBD-MGMT01 through a remoting session, and reduce every name to one key — the short host name, so a lease's SBD-PC07.sbd.test and the directory's SBD-PC07 meet. Take all the sources on the same day; sources taken weeks apart disagree about machines that simply moved.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (Tier 1): one dated folder for this month's sources
$d = "C:\Evidence\management-server\sources\$(Get-Date -Format yyyy-MM-dd)"; New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "$d\repo01" | Out-Null
$s = [adsisearcher]'(objectCategory=computer)'; $s.PageSize = 500
$s.FindAll() | ForEach-Object { $p = $_.Properties; [pscustomobject]@{ Name = "$($p.name)"; OS = "$($p.operatingsystem)"; DN = "$($p.distinguishedname)"; LastLogon = if ("$($p.lastlogontimestamp)") { [datetime]::FromFileTime([long]"$($p.lastlogontimestamp)") } } } | Export-Csv "$d\directory.csv" -NoTypeInformation
Invoke-Command SBD-DHCP01 { Get-DhcpServerv4Lease -ScopeId 10.0.80.0 -AllLeases | Select-Object IPAddress, ClientId, HostName, AddressState, LeaseExpiryTime } | Export-Csv "$d\dhcp-leases.csv" -NoTypeInformation
Invoke-Command SBD-WSUS01 { Get-WsusComputer -All | Select-Object FullDomainName, IPAddress, LastSyncTime, LastReportedStatusTime, RequestedTargetGroupName } | Export-Csv "$d\wsus-computers.csv" -NoTypeInformation
scp -r <your-account>@SBD-REPO01.sbd.test:/srv/repo-records/* "$d\repo01\"
# On SBD-REPO01: who fetched packages
sudo awk '{print $1}' /var/log/httpd/access_log | sort | uniq -c
# Back on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: hash the set and file it on SBD-MGMT01
Get-ChildItem $d -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv "$d-hashes.csv" -NoTypeInformation
$m = New-PSSession SBD-MGMT01; Copy-Item $d, "$d-hashes.csv" -Destination D:\Inventory\sources\ -ToSession $m -Recurse
lessons.check: Each source export exists for the same date with the columns lesson 5 needs, the hash list matches the files copied to SBD-MGMT01, every name reduces to one key, and a note says what each source can and can't prove.
lessons.evidence: Keep the dated source exports, their hash list, the REPO01 access-log summary, the baseline-session list, and the note on what each source proves.

quizzes.question: Why read the directory over LDAP instead of with Get-ADComputer from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01?
answers: LDAP is faster for large domains
The Active Directory module needs the controllers' Web Services port, which only AdminJumpBox01 may reach; LDAP is a path every member already has (F03)
Get-ADComputer can't read computer objects
quizzes.explanation: The register decides which tools work from which seat. Reading what every member may read keeps the inventory owner in Tier 1.

quizzes.question: A PC has no lease today. What does that prove?
answers: That it was stolen
That it was retired
Little on its own — it may simply be switched off; check the audit log and the other sources before calling it missing
quizzes.explanation: Each source proves something narrow. Absence from one is a question for the others, not a verdict.

quizzes.question: Why reduce every name to one key before comparing?
answers: So SBD-PC07.sbd.test in the leases and SBD-PC07 in the directory count as one machine, not two findings
To save disk space
Because WSUS requires capital letters
quizzes.explanation: Most false findings come from formatting, not drift. Normalize once, in one place, and the comparison means something.

recap: Five sources, gathered through paths administrators already use.
Each proves something narrow; together they test the record.
Same day, one name key, hashed and filed on SBD-MGMT01.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 reconciles the record with the sources and proves the checks work.

lessons.title: Reconcile the inventory and prove it
lessons.summary: Compare the record with what the network reports, classify every difference, and prove the comparison catches drift before trusting a clean result. Then take SBD-MGMT01's first SCAP baseline and hand a reconciled inventory — and the monthly habit — to the courses that follow.
objectives: Reconcile recorded and discovered components and classify every difference.
Prove the reconciliation catches drift with a deliberate test.
Baseline SBD-MGMT01 and hand off the reconciled record.
steps: On SBD-MGMT01, compare the inventory's active rows with each source by the name key: the domain-joined rows against the directory, the VLAN 80 rows against the leases, and the Windows rows against WSUS's computer list and its rings. In a source but not the record is an unrecorded component; recorded but absent where it should appear is a gap; present in both with a different value — a ring, an OU, an address — is drift.

Prove the comparison works before trusting a clean result: run it against a test copy of the inventory with one PC's row removed — the PC must appear as found in the directory but not in the record — and against another copy with one ring changed, which the ring comparison must report. Test copies are never published.

Classify every real difference and close it: correct the record through the change log, bring the component under management or remove it, or record the explanation — a PC switched off for a week has no lease and isn't missing. An unrecorded device is reported to the system owner the day it is found (CM-8(3)), and drift that keeps coming from one procedure is fixed in that procedure.

Take SBD-MGMT01's first SCAP baseline with course 1.4's SCC and benchmark versions, run locally in a Tier 1 session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, classify its open items as course 1.4 taught, and enter the date in its own inventory row.

Hand off: publish the reconciled version with its hash, set the monthly reconciliation in the week after course 1.14's cycle closes so the WSUS list is fresh, and note what later courses add — course 1.18 turns the VLAN 40 servers' planned rows active as it builds them, and course 1.19 carries D:\Inventory into the recovery set.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-MGMT01 (session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01): the newest sources against the active record
$src = (Get-ChildItem D:\Inventory\sources -Directory | Sort-Object Name | Select-Object -Last 1).FullName
$short = { $args[0] -replace '\..*$' }
$active = Import-Csv D:\Inventory\current\inventory.csv | Where-Object Status -eq 'active'
$directory = (Import-Csv "$src\directory.csv").Name
$leases = Import-Csv "$src\dhcp-leases.csv" | Where-Object HostName | ForEach-Object { & $short $_.HostName }
$rings = Import-Csv "$src\wsus-computers.csv" | ForEach-Object { '{0}|{1}' -f (& $short $_.FullDomainName), $_.RequestedTargetGroupName }
Compare-Object ($active | Where-Object Domain -eq 'sbd.test').Name $directory   # <= recorded only, => directory only
Compare-Object ($active | Where-Object VLAN -eq '80').Name $leases
Compare-Object ($active | Where-Object UpdateSource -like 'Ring*' | ForEach-Object { '{0}|{1}' -f $_.Name, $_.UpdateSource }) $rings
# Prove it: with SBD-PC07's row left out of a test copy, SBD-PC07 must show as directory only
Compare-Object ($active | Where-Object { $_.Domain -eq 'sbd.test' -and $_.Name -ne 'SBD-PC07' }).Name $directory
lessons.check: Every difference between the record and the sources is listed and classified, the deliberate tests were caught, unrecorded components were reported to the system owner, SBD-MGMT01 has its first baseline, and the reconciled version is published with its hash and the next reconciliation date.
lessons.evidence: Keep the comparison output, the classified findings with their resolutions, the tests that proved detection, the SCC results with classified findings, the reconciled version's hash, and the handoff note.

quizzes.question: Why run the comparison against a deliberately broken copy first?
answers: A clean result proves nothing until you have seen the same check catch a known difference
To make the report longer
Because the real record might be deleted
quizzes.explanation: A check that can't fail isn't a check. One planted difference, caught, turns 'no findings' into evidence.

quizzes.question: The directory holds SBD-PC51, which no record mentions, and it has a lease. What happens?
answers: Delete it from the directory and move on
It is reported to the system owner the day it is found and investigated as an unrecorded component, and the procedure that let it in is fixed
Add it to the inventory so the counts match
quizzes.explanation: Unknown hardware is the classic first question of an assessment. Making the record agree without asking why would hide the very thing CM-8 exists to catch.

quizzes.question: Why schedule the reconciliation after course 1.14's monthly cycle closes?
answers: Because WSUS is offline the rest of the month
Because the directory changes only once a month
Because the WSUS computer list and rings are freshest then, so a difference is drift, not timing
quizzes.explanation: Sources taken at the right moment produce findings worth acting on. Timing is part of the method.

recap: Recorded against discovered: unrecorded, gap or drift — each classified.
A planted difference, caught, makes a clean result mean something.
Reconciled, baselined and handed on — every month from now on.
lessons.next: That completes course 1.15. Courses 1.16 and 1.17, endpoint protection and credentialed scanning, are coming soon; course 1.18 stands up the business services and turns their planned rows in this inventory active.

prerequisites: Complete courses 1.1–1.15: the domain with its DNS, time and hardened OUs, the course 1.6 PKI and its autoenrollment GPO, DHCP and the admin seats, SBD-REPO01 and its Linux client package, the logging pipeline with course 1.11's KDS root key, SBD-SPLUNK01 as the Linux server pattern, the fleet, the update rings, and the SBD-MGMT01 inventory.

Provision the VLAN 40 hosts as virtual machines on SBD-HV05: SBD-FS01 (10.0.40.10), SBD-SQL01 (10.0.40.20) and SBD-APPS01 (10.0.40.30) on Windows Server, and SBD-WEB01 (10.0.40.40) on the Red Hat Enterprise Linux–family release course 1.9 chose, with Apache, to be joined to sbd.test with SSSD as SBD-SPLUNK01 was in course 1.12.

Have the service-path register, the course 1.6 SBD Server Authentication template, course 1.9's client package and Linux assessment set, and course 1.4's SCC media within reach — every service here gets a documented path, a real certificate and a first baseline.
labNote: The users finally get what the network exists for: files, licensing, and an internal web application with its application tier and database. The model's rule governs the whole course — permit only documented business service paths — so every service arrives with its register rows, its service identity, and its certificate, and nothing reaches it any other way.

sources.title: Microsoft · What's new in Windows Server (newest release)
Microsoft · Delegated Managed Service Accounts overview
Microsoft · Create a Key Distribution Service (KDS) root key
Microsoft · Encrypt connections to SQL Server by importing a certificate
Microsoft · Advanced audit policy configuration (File System, Detailed File Share)
Microsoft · Configure Windows Firewall rules with Group Policy
Red Hat · Integrating RHEL systems directly with Windows Active Directory
Red Hat · Using shared system certificates
DISA · Security Content Automation Protocol (SCC and SCAP benchmarks)
DISA · SRG/STIG tools (SCC and STIG Viewer)

lessons.title: Design the service paths and identities
lessons.summary: Four services, and before any of them exist: who talks to what over which port, which identity each service runs as, and which groups own access — the register and the directory answer all three before a role installs.
objectives: Write the register rows for every business service path.
Choose managed service identities instead of password accounts.
Define the access groups that will own each service's data.
steps: Write the service-path rows into the register, with the IDs Inside the Network gives them and an owner each: the fleet to SBD-FS01 on SMB 445 (F05), to SBD-APPS01 on its licensing port, recorded per application (F12), and to SBD-WEB01 on HTTPS 443 (F13); SBD-WEB01 to SBD-APPS01 for the application API on HTTPS 443 (F21); and SBD-APPS01 — and only SBD-APPS01 — to SBD-SQL01 on TCP 1433 with TLS (F22). Add the explicit deny from SBD-WEB01 to SBD-SQL01 (F14): the web tier has no database dependency. All four servers share VLAN 40, so the router never sees their traffic to each other — each server's host firewall enforces those rows. Everything else toward VLAN 40 stays denied, including endpoint-to-SQL directly.

Add the rows every new server needs: administration from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (A02), and for the three Windows servers the domain rows (F01–F03, F09), Ring 3 updates (F06), event forwarding (F17), certificate publication (F18) and enrollment to SBD-SUBCA01 on the row course 1.6 confirmed. SBD-WEB01's Linux rows already name it: packages from SBD-REPO01 only (F19, HTTP with GPG-signed packages, course 1.9), syslog over TLS to the collector, SBD-SYSLOG01 (F07, TCP 6514), and time from both domain controllers (F09) — the same paths SBD-SPLUNK01 has used since course 1.12.

Choose the service identities: group managed service accounts (gMSAs) for the SQL and application services, so passwords rotate themselves. They rely on the forest's one KDS root key, which course 1.11 created: confirm it with Get-KdsRootKey and never create another. Each account is created from AdminJumpBox01 once its host has joined, allowed to that one computer, as course 1.11 did (lesson 3). Note delegated managed service accounts, introduced in the newest Windows Server release, as the migration path for any legacy service account this lab later inherits.
Create the access groups under the course 1.5 Groups OU from AdminJumpBox01 — per-share and per-application role groups — because permissions will be granted to roles, never to named humans.

Plan the server certificates: one SBD Server Authentication certificate (course 1.6) each for SQL01, APPS01 (for its application API), and WEB01, with the host's DNS name in the subject alternative name. Each host requests its own in its build lesson through the course 1.6 process, so the private key never leaves it — the template allows exportable keys only where course 1.19's recovery plan says so. Course 1.6's autoenrollment GPO, linked at the domain root, already reaches every new member, so no other enrollment policy is created.
lessons.command:
# From AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): the course 1.11 KDS root key, the existing gMSAs, and the role groups
Invoke-Command SBD-DC01 { Get-KdsRootKey | Select-Object KeyId, EffectiveTime }   # one key, from course 1.11
Get-ADServiceAccount -Filter * | Select-Object Name, Enabled   # course 1.11's three; this course's arrive with their hosts
Get-ADGroup -SearchBase 'OU=Groups,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Filter * | Select-Object Name
lessons.check: The register carries every VLAN 40 service row with its ID and owner — the SQL path restricted to APPS01 alone (F22), the WEB01-to-SQL01 deny (F14), and WEB01's repository, syslog and time rows — the course 1.11 KDS root key is the forest's only one, the role groups exist, and each server certificate is planned for the host that will request it.
lessons.evidence: Keep the service-path rows, the identity and group design, the KDS root key check, and the certificate plan.

quizzes.question: Who may reach SQL01 on 1433?
answers: Any domain member
WEB01 and APPS01
Only APPS01 — the application tier is the database's whole audience
quizzes.explanation: Browsers talk to the web tier, the web tier calls the application API, and only the application tier queries the database. The register encodes that chain — including an explicit deny from WEB01 to SQL01 — and denies shortcuts around it.

quizzes.question: Why gMSAs instead of a user account named svc-sql?
answers: The directory manages and rotates the password itself — no human knows it, nothing expires unnoticed
gMSAs run queries faster
Password accounts cannot start services
quizzes.explanation: Service account passwords are a classic standing weakness. Managed accounts remove the password from human hands entirely.

quizzes.question: Why grant access to role groups rather than people?
answers: Groups are alphabetical
Access follows the job: membership changes are one record, and permissions never accumulate on individuals
Permissions cannot hold user names
quizzes.explanation: Role-based access is what makes 'who can touch this data' answerable from group membership instead of archaeology.

recap: Every path is a row; the database hears only SBD-APPS01.
Service identities are managed accounts, not passwords.
Access belongs to roles; each certificate is planned for its own host.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 builds the file service the fleet will actually use.

lessons.title: Build SBD-FS01 with least-privilege shares
lessons.summary: The file server is where access control meets daily life. Build the shares against the role groups, require SMB signing on the server instead of trusting client defaults, and make 'who can read this' a one-lookup question.
objectives: Build SBD-FS01 in its place and create the shares with role-group permissions and no individual grants.
Confirm the SMB signing and encryption posture end to end.
Verify access and denial per role from the fleet.
steps: Build SBD-FS01 as a Windows Server virtual machine at 10.0.40.10/24, with the core's VLAN 40 interface as gateway (10.0.40.1 in this sample), both domain controllers for DNS, a separate data volume for the shares, and the hypervisor's time synchronization turned off. Join it straight into the Servers OU, so course 1.5's STIG policies, course 1.8's tier policies, course 1.10's event-forwarding GPO and course 1.14's Ring 3 update policy apply from its first boot, and check that it takes its time from a domain controller. Lessons 3 and 4 build SBD-SQL01 and SBD-APPS01 the same way.

Create the planned shares, granting NTFS permissions to the lesson-1 role groups only — share permissions stay simple, the filesystem carries the detail, and no named human appears in an access control list (ACL).
Enable access-based enumeration so users see only what their roles permit — the quiet UX of least privilege.

Confirm the SMB posture. The newest Windows client release (Pro, Enterprise, and Education) requires SMB signing for both inbound and outbound connections, but the newest Windows Server release requires it only for its own outbound connections — so require signing on SBD-FS01 as well (RequireSecuritySignature in its SMB server configuration), and opt the sensitive share into SMB encryption. Verify both on a live connection from a fleet machine rather than assuming the defaults.

Test as members of two different roles from fleet machines: each sees and opens exactly its shares, and the other's are invisible and, opened by path, denied. Turn on Audit Detailed File Share (failure) for SBD-FS01 in a GPO security-filtered to it, recorded as a documented addition as course 1.11 did for SBD-AUDIT01, so each refusal is event 5145 in its Security log; lesson 5 sends that event to the collector.
lessons.command:
# In a Tier 1 session on SBD-FS01 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01
([adsisearcher]"(&(objectCategory=computer)(name=$env:COMPUTERNAME))").FindOne().Path   # ...OU=Servers,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test
w32tm /query /source   # a domain controller, never the local clock
Get-SmbShare | Select-Object Name, Path, FolderEnumerationMode, EncryptData
Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select-Object RequireSecuritySignature   # expected True
icacls D:\Shares\Projects | Select-String 'SBD'
auditpol /get /subcategory:"Detailed File Share"   # Failure
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=5145} -MaxEvents 5 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Message
# On the fleet machine, during the test session
Get-SmbConnection | Where-Object ServerName -like 'SBD-FS01*' | Select-Object ShareName, Dialect, Signed, Encrypted
lessons.check: SBD-FS01 sits in the Servers OU with time from a domain controller, shares grant to role groups only, FS01 requires signing, a live connection from the fleet shows Signed True — or, on the encrypted share, Encrypted True, where Signed reads False because encryption, which also protects integrity, takes the place of signing — and the two-role test proves both the access and the invisible-denied behavior, with each refusal recorded as event 5145.
lessons.evidence: Keep the OU placement and time source, the share and NTFS permission reports, FS01's signing setting and the live connection's signing/encryption output, and the two-role test record with its 5145 events.

model.label: Open a file, step 3
model.text: A workstation presents its service ticket and opens the approved share on SBD-FS01.

quizzes.question: Where does the fine-grained permission detail live?
answers: In the share permissions
On the NTFS filesystem, granted to role groups — shares stay simple on top
In a spreadsheet
quizzes.explanation: The classic split: simple share grants, precise filesystem ACLs, and roles everywhere — auditable at a glance.

quizzes.question: What does the live Get-SmbConnection check prove that settings review doesn't?
answers: That the actual connection negotiated signing or encryption — posture in effect, not posture on paper
That the share has files
Nothing extra
quizzes.explanation: Defaults differ by edition and direction — the newest Windows Server release requires signing only for its own outbound connections — so the evidence standard of this whole path is observed behavior: inspect the connection itself.

quizzes.question: A user can't see a share their colleague uses. What is that?
answers: A replication failure
A help desk ticket to grant access immediately
Access-based enumeration doing its job — visibility follows role membership
quizzes.explanation: Invisible-unless-permitted is the designed behavior; the role group, not an exception, is the path to access.

recap: Roles own the ACLs; humans own role memberships.
Signing and encryption are verified on a live connection.
Both the access and the denial are on record.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 builds the database the applications will depend on.

lessons.title: Build SBD-SQL01 behind its applications
lessons.summary: The database runs as a managed identity, encrypts its connections with a real certificate, and answers exactly one caller, SBD-APPS01 — the narrowest audience on the network, by design.
objectives: Build SBD-SQL01 and run the database service under its gMSA.
Bind the SBD Server Authentication certificate and force encrypted connections.
Prove the one-caller rule: SBD-APPS01 connects; a VLAN 40 neighbour and the fleet are refused.
steps: Build SBD-SQL01 (10.0.40.20) and the host of its one caller, SBD-APPS01 (10.0.40.30), as SBD-FS01 was built in lesson 2. Then, from AdminJumpBox01, create one gMSA per service, each allowed to one computer as course 1.11 did: SBD-SQL$ for SBD-SQL01$ and SBD-Apps$ for SBD-APPS01$ (sample names). Install the database engine with SBD\SBD-SQL$ as its service account and no password — the install itself demonstrates the managed account working where a password account used to live.

Add SBD-SQL01 to the SBD TLS Servers group, then on SBD-SQL01 request its SBD Server Authentication certificate through the course 1.6 process, with SBD-SQL01.sbd.test in the subject alternative name. Give the gMSA read on the certificate's private key — without it the service won't start with the certificate — select the certificate in SQL Server Configuration Manager, set Force Encryption to Yes, and restart the service; the chain validates against pki.sbd.test like every other certificate on this network.

Create the application databases with role-based database access for one login only, SBD\SBD-Apps$, the identity SBD-APPS01's services run as in lesson 4 — least privilege continues inside the engine, not just at its port. Record the databases and the logins they depend on: course 1.19 backs them up, so this course sets up no backup job.

Prove the audience: allow TCP 1433 in SBD-SQL01's host firewall from 10.0.40.30 alone (F22), and turn on its dropped-packet logging if it is off. A connection from APPS01 succeeds. The same attempt from SBD-FS01 is refused by SBD-SQL01's host firewall — the two share VLAN 40, so the router never sees it, which is exactly how SBD-WEB01 will be refused in lesson 4 — and one from a fleet machine dies at the router with a deny-log entry.
lessons.command:
# From AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): one gMSA per service, each allowed to one computer
New-ADServiceAccount SBD-SQL -DNSHostName SBD-SQL.sbd.test -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword 'SBD-SQL01$'
New-ADServiceAccount SBD-Apps -DNSHostName SBD-Apps.sbd.test -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword 'SBD-APPS01$'
# In a Tier 1 session on SBD-SQL01 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: identity, encryption, certificate, firewall scope
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='MSSQLSERVER'" | Select-Object Name, StartName, State   # StartName SBD\SBD-SQL$
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Microsoft SQL Server\*\MSSQLServer\SuperSocketNetLib' | Select-Object ForceEncryption, Certificate   # 1 and the thumbprint
$cer = Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My | Where-Object Subject -like '*SBD-SQL01*' | Export-Certificate -FilePath "$env:TEMP\sql01.cer"
certutil -verify -urlfetch $cer.FullName   # chain and revocation from pki.sbd.test
Get-NetFirewallPortFilter | Where-Object LocalPort -eq 1433 | Get-NetFirewallRule | Where-Object { $_.Enabled -eq 'True' -and $_.Direction -eq 'Inbound' } | Get-NetFirewallAddressFilter | Select-Object RemoteAddress   # 10.0.40.30 only
# From SBD-APPS01: expected TcpTestSucceeded True. From SBD-FS01 and from a fleet machine: expected False.
Test-NetConnection SBD-SQL01.sbd.test -Port 1433
lessons.check: The service runs as the gMSA, Force Encryption is on with the issued certificate bound and its chain validating, the database role admits SBD\SBD-Apps$ alone, TCP 1433 is open to 10.0.40.30 only, APPS01 reaches it, and both other attempts fail with a record: SBD-FS01's at SQL01's host firewall, the fleet's at the router.
lessons.evidence: Keep the service identity proof, the encryption setting, certificate binding and urlfetch output, the database role grants, the firewall scope, and APPS01's successful connection paired with both refusals and their log entries.

model.label: Attack drill, step 5
model.text: A compromised SBD-WEB01 reaches for SBD-SQL01 and is refused at SQL01's host firewall: rule F14 denies it, because SBD-APPS01 is the only registered SQL consumer.

quizzes.question: What demonstrates the gMSA actually working?

A password in the evidence folder
The account's description field

A diagram of VLAN 40
APPS01's successful connection plus the refused attempts from a VLAN 40 neighbour and a fleet machine, each with its log entry

lessons.title: Build SBD-APPS01 and SBD-WEB01
lessons.summary: The application server and the internal web server complete the dependency chain: fleet to web, web to application, application to database — each hop a register row, the web tier hardened against its Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) guidance, and HTTPS served from the lab's own trust.
objectives: Stand up SBD-APPS01's licensing service and application API on their registered paths.

Build the domain-joined Linux Apache server the way courses 1.9 and 1.12 built theirs, hardened per its DISA Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) and serving HTTPS with the internal certificate.
Prove the full chain: fleet → web → application → database, with the web-to-database shortcut refused.
steps: On SBD-APPS01, built in lesson 3, and added to the SBD TLS Servers group, request its SBD Server Authentication certificate through the course 1.6 process and run both of its services as SBD\SBD-Apps$, or record an exception where the product can't use a gMSA: the licensing service, verified from the fleet on its registered vendor port (F12), and the application API on HTTPS 443 (F21), with its host firewall admitting the API from SBD-WEB01 (10.0.40.40) alone. APPS01 is the network's one SQL consumer — and the template for any future service: identity, row, evidence.

Build SBD-WEB01 at 10.0.40.40/24 from hashed install media of the Red Hat Enterprise Linux–family release course 1.9 chose, with both domain controllers for DNS and the hypervisor's time synchronization turned off. Before anything else, install course 1.3's chrony file (both domain controllers, maxdistance 16) and confirm a controller is selected with a small, steady offset; then apply course 1.9's client package, checked against its hashes, so SBD-REPO01 is its only package source (F19), and update from the current snapshot. Place the course 1.6 root in its system trust store by hand (/etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors, then update-ca-trust), its SHA-256 checked against course 1.6's record, as course 1.9 did for SBD-REPO01.

Join sbd.test with realm join into the Servers OU, as SBD-SPLUNK01 was joined in course 1.12, permit sign-in only to SBD Tier 1 Admins with realm permit -g, and give that group sudo through a drop-in file. Make the host firewall the register's copy: HTTPS 443 from the fleet (F13) and SSH from 10.0.60.20 alone. Then send its syslog over TLS to SBD-SYSLOG01 (F07) as course 1.10 enrolled SBD-REPO01: rsyslog-gnutls from the snapshot, the collector's certificate name checked, and SBD-WEB01 added to the collector's TCP 6514 sender list.

Request SBD-WEB01's SBD Server Authentication certificate through the course 1.6 process, with the key and request made on the host with openssl and SBD-WEB01.sbd.test in both subject and subject alternative name, and the key readable by root alone. Serve the internal application over HTTPS with its chain, and harden Apache against the DISA Apache Server 2.4 UNIX STIGs that course 1.9 staged — the 2,048-bit key floor from course 1.6's templates applies here as everywhere. Export the hardened configuration and hash it as the change record (course 1.19 backs up SBD-APPS01's and SBD-WEB01's configuration and certificates); lesson 5 measures the host.

Prove the chain from a fleet machine: the HTTPS page loads with a validating certificate, and its data travels fleet → WEB01 → APPS01 → SQL01, every hop a register row — on SBD-SQL01, sys.dm_exec_connections shows APPS01's session (10.0.40.30) with encrypt_option TRUE. Then prove the shortcuts stay shut: a direct attempt from SBD-WEB01 to SQL01 on 1433 is refused by SQL01's host firewall, and the fleet still cannot touch 1433 at all — three courses of design visible in one browser request.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-WEB01 (Tier 1 SSH session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01): time, packages, domain, firewall, logging, web
chronyc sources -v; chronyc tracking   # ^* one controller, ^+ or ^- the other
dnf repolist --all   # expected: only the sbd-repo01 repositories enabled
realm list   # sbd.test, kerberos-member, permitted group SBD Tier 1 Admins
sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
openssl s_client -connect SBD-SYSLOG01.sbd.test:6514 -verify_hostname SBD-SYSLOG01.sbd.test </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep 'Verify return code'   # 0 (ok): the SBD root is trusted
logger -t sbd-web-proof 'SBD-WEB01 syslog over TLS test'
sudo apachectl -S   # one HTTPS site on 10.0.40.40:443
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://SBD-APPS01.sbd.test/   # use your application's health path
timeout 5 bash -c '</dev/tcp/SBD-SQL01.sbd.test/1433' && echo open || echo 'refused or timed out'   # expected: refused or timed out
# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: the issued certificate's chain and revocation
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\business-services\web01.cer
# From a fleet machine: the page answers, the database does not
Test-NetConnection SBD-WEB01.sbd.test -Port 443
Test-NetConnection SBD-SQL01.sbd.test -Port 1433   # expected: False
# On SBD-SQL01, in a query: APPS01's live session is encrypted
# SELECT client_net_address, encrypt_option, auth_scheme FROM sys.dm_exec_connections WHERE client_net_address = '10.0.40.30'
lessons.check: The licensing path and the application API work as registered under the managed identity; SBD-WEB01 takes its time from the controllers and its packages only from SBD-REPO01, trusts the SBD root, is domain-joined with SSSD in the Servers OU, and sends its syslog to the collector over TLS; the Apache host serves HTTPS with a validating internal chain from a hardened, hashed configuration; and the end-to-end request proves fleet → web → application → database, encrypted to the database, with both shortcuts denied.
lessons.evidence: Keep APPS01's identity and path proof, WEB01's time, repository, trust, domain-join and syslog checks, its hardened config export with hashes, the certificate validation output, the end-to-end chain test with SQL01's connection record, and the refused WEB01-to-SQL01 attempt.

A USB stick from home
SBD-REPO01 — the one approved source course 1.9 built for Linux software (F19)

Its uptime counter

What a scanner can't read, such as most of the Apache STIG, a person answers with evidence, and the configuration's hash shows later whether it changed.

quizzes.question: What does one successful page load from the fleet actually demonstrate?
answers: The whole designed chain — the registered fleet-to-web path, validating internal HTTPS, the web tier's call to the application API, and the application tier's registered path into the database
Only that Apache started
That the fleet can reach the database directly

The router drops it at the core

recap: APPS01 serves licensing and the application API; WEB01 joins the domain like the other Linux servers.
The web tier is built the Linux way — chrony, SBD-REPO01, the SBD root by hand — hardened to its guidance and serving the lab's own trust.

lessons.title: Reconcile, scan, and hand off
lessons.summary: The business services close the way every build course has: the register reconciled against live behavior, the new systems baselined, the inventory updated — and for the first time, the network is functionally complete.
objectives: Enrol the new servers and reconcile the full register against observed permits and denies.
Baseline the four service hosts with the tool each platform takes.
Update the living records and write the course's handoff.
steps: Enrol the three Windows servers in the record: from AdminJumpBox01, add SBD-FS01, SBD-SQL01 and SBD-APPS01 to SBD Event Sources (course 1.10). On the collector, in a Tier 1 session, widen the WinRM 5985 scope to 10.0.40.10, 10.0.40.20 and 10.0.40.30 (F17) and add a query to SBD-ForwardedSecurity for SBD-FS01's event 5145, filtered to that computer as course 1.11 did for SBD-AUDIT01. Restart the three servers and confirm their events reach ForwardedEvents; SBD-WEB01 already sends its syslog over TLS (lesson 4).

Run the full-register reconciliation one more time: every business-service row proven from its real source, every adjacent deny probed and logged, including WEB01 to SQL01 — the VLAN 40 rows join the register's evidence beside the earlier courses' proofs.

Take the first baselines. SBD-FS01, SBD-SQL01 and SBD-APPS01 get course 1.4's SCC and Windows Server benchmark versions, run locally in Tier 1 sessions from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 as course 1.14 did for SBD-WSUS01, plus DISA's SQL Server STIGs for the instance, staged across the air gap as course 1.4 taught and answered in a STIG Viewer checklist. SBD-WEB01 gets SCC for Linux and the distribution benchmark from course 1.9's set in C:\Staging\DISA\linux, scanned the course 1.9 way, with the Apache STIG items in its checklist. Classify every open item as course 1.4 taught — fix by GPO, deviation candidate or POA&M candidate, with fix now (no GPO applies to Linux) for SBD-WEB01. Credentialed vulnerability scanning arrives with course 1.17, coming soon.

Update the living records: the four hosts' planned rows in the SBD-MGMT01 inventory turn active through its change log (course 1.15), with their identities, certificates, rings and baselines; the new rows' owners go into the register; and any service-hardening deviations go to the owner of the exception record, C:\Evidence\exception-record.csv on AdminJumpBox01.

Write the handoff: every modeled system that isn't marked coming soon is now built, watched, patched, and evidenced. This course sets up no backups: course 1.19 defines and schedules them for the VLAN 40 servers — SBD-FS01's share data with its NTFS permissions, SBD-SQL01's databases and the logins they depend on, and SBD-APPS01's and SBD-WEB01's configuration and certificates — and proves the network can come back from the dead; then path 2 takes the whole record to authorization.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-SYSLOG01 (Tier 1 session): the new sources report
wecutil gr SBD-ForwardedSecurity   # SBD-FS01, SBD-SQL01 and SBD-APPS01: Active
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='ForwardedEvents'; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} | Group-Object MachineName | Select-Object Name, Count
Select-String -Path D:\Logs\Syslog\*\*.log -Pattern 'sbd-web-proof' | Select-Object -First 1
# On SBD-ADMIN-SRV01: collect the course's records and hash them
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\business-services -Recurse -File | Select-Object FullName, LastWriteTime
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\business-services -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\business-services-hashes.csv -NoTypeInformation

lessons.evidence: Finish the checklist: the enrolment proof, the reconciliation record, the baselines and checklists with classified findings, the updated living records, and the handoff note to course 1.19.

Reconciliations are decorative

quizzes.question: What distinguishes WEB01's closing evidence from FS01's?
answers: WEB01 has none
FS01 is exempt from scans
Only the instrument: FS01 is scanned with SCC and the Windows Server benchmark, WEB01 with SCC for Linux and its distribution's benchmark plus the Apache checklist — same standard

quizzes.question: What remains before the authorization path begins?
answers: Backing up and proving recovery — course 1.19, which backs up the VLAN 40 servers with everything else — so the Body of Evidence includes the network coming back, not just running
Nothing at all
Rebuilding the domain controllers

recap: Register and reality reconcile across the finished network.
Every service host carries its platform-appropriate evidence.
One course remains: proving the network can be brought back.
lessons.next: That completes course 1.18. Course 1.19 closes the Build path by backing up and proving recovery — directory, CA, policy, logs, and the VLAN 40 services built here — before authorization begins.

prerequisites: Complete courses 1.1–1.18 (courses 1.16 and 1.17 are coming soon and aren't needed): the full network, the VLAN 40 business services, their records, the protected log archive, and the living inventory all exist.

Provision the backup storage this course schedules into: a protected backup volume (E: in this sample) on every Windows server in the recovery set — both domain controllers, SBD-SUBCA01, SBD-DHCP01, SBD-MGMT01, SBD-FS01, SBD-SQL01 and SBD-APPS01 — never one of the volumes being backed up and written only by the backup jobs, and a separate volume mounted at /srv/backup, readable by root alone, on SBD-REPO01, SBD-SPLUNK01 and SBD-WEB01. Earlier courses set up no backup jobs; this course defines and schedules every one. Also provide an offline backup cabinet with removable media and a custody register, and an isolated recovery network segment (or host) for the restore rehearsal.

Have the custody records handy: the sealed Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) passwords set in course 1.1 and the course 1.6 ceremony record for SBD-ROOTCA01's protected backup — recovery is where those promises come due.
labNote: The model's final chapter: a network that cannot come back was never really built. This course is the one place every backup in the network is defined and scheduled — the directory, both CAs, Group Policy, DHCP, the repository and analysis configuration, the VLAN 40 business services with their permissions, logins and certificates, the log record, and the living records — then proves one real restore in isolation and files the tested-recovery evidence the authorization path expects.
