lessons.title: Decide what recovery must prove
lessons.summary: Recovery starts as a list of promises: which systems and records must be restorable, how old a restored copy may be, how long restoration may take, and the one schedule that says how each is backed up — written as commitments the rest of the course exists to keep.
objectives: Name the recovery set: what must come back, in what order.
Set the recovery point and time objectives per item.
Write the backup schedule: every backup in the network, defined in one place.
Decide where backups live and who can touch them.
steps: Write the recovery set in dependency order — the order the path built it: the directory on both controllers first, because everything trusts it; then the certificate authorities (SBD-SUBCA01's database and key, and SBD-ROOTCA01's course 1.6 ceremony backup); Group Policy; SBD-DHCP01 (course 1.7); the boundary's records (the service-path register and the core router's configuration); SBD-REPO01's snapshot catalog and snapshots (course 1.9); SBD-SPLUNK01's configuration (course 1.12); the log archive and its catalog on SBD-AUDIT01 (course 1.11); the inventory on SBD-MGMT01 (course 1.15); the VLAN 40 business services (course 1.18) — SBD-FS01's share data with its NTFS permissions, SBD-SQL01's databases and the logins they depend on, SBD-APPS01's and SBD-WEB01's configuration and certificates; and the exception record.

Set the two numbers per item: how much history may be lost (recovery point) and how long restoration may take (recovery time) — lab-honest values you will actually measure against in lesson 5, not aspirations. A directory backup older than the forest's tombstone lifetime (180 days by default) can't be restored at all, so the directory's recovery point stays well inside it.

Write the backup schedule, the one place every backup in this network is defined: for each item, what is captured, the tool, when it runs, where it lands, and who restores it. No earlier course scheduled a backup; the one build-time copy is SBD-ROOTCA01's, taken inside the course 1.6 ceremony, and the schedule accounts for it rather than repeating it. Lessons 2 and 3 put each row into effect.

Decide backup placement: each protected backup volume is written only by its backup jobs and readable by the recovery role, and custodians of the matching tier carry copies to the offline backup cabinet on media — the air-gapped network's version of an off-site copy. There is no backup server and no network path to the cabinet.

Confirm the standing custody items: the DSRM passwords set in course 1.1 are sealed and findable, and SBD-ROOTCA01's protected backup from the course 1.6 ceremony is accounted for — recovery depends on secrets that must exist before the bad day.
lessons.command:
# On each Windows server in the recovery set: capture the current protection state before this course changes it.
wbadmin get versions
Get-Volume -DriveLetter E | Select-Object DriveLetter, FileSystemLabel, SizeRemaining   # the protected backup volume
# The tombstone lifetime bounds the directory's recovery point (empty means the 180-day default).
(Get-ADObject "CN=Directory Service,CN=Windows NT,CN=Services,$((Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext)" -Properties tombstoneLifetime).tombstoneLifetime
lessons.check: The recovery set is ordered by dependency with point and time objectives per item, the backup schedule defines every backup in one place, the placement and access rules are written, and the DSRM and root-key custody records check out.
lessons.evidence: Keep the recovery requirements sheet, the objectives table, the backup schedule, the placement and access decisions, and the custody verification notes.

quizzes.question: Why does the directory lead the recovery order?
answers: It has the most data
Everything else authenticates against it — services restored before identity have nothing to trust
Alphabetical order
quizzes.explanation: Recovery order mirrors build order for the same reason: the dependency chain starts at identity.

quizzes.question: What makes a recovery time objective honest?
answers: Making it very small
Leaving it unstated
Setting a value you will actually measure a rehearsal against
quizzes.explanation: Lesson 5 times a real restore. An objective nobody measures is marketing, not a commitment.

quizzes.question: What is the offline media copy for?
answers: Surviving a failure that takes the online backup with it — the air-gapped answer to off-site
Faster restores
Decoration for the evidence binder
quizzes.explanation: Replication and online backups share failure modes with what they protect. One custody-tracked copy stands apart.

quizzes.question: What does this course do about the offline root's backup?
answers: Copies it onto the network for convenience
Ignores it
Accounts for the ceremony backup in the schedule and verifies its custody — it already exists, offline, and stays that way
quizzes.explanation: The root's backup is the one build-time copy, taken inside the course 1.6 ceremony. Its protection is its isolation, so this course checks the promise rather than breaking it with a networked copy.

recap: The recovery set is ordered by dependency, directory first, VLAN 40 included.
Point and time objectives exist to be measured, not admired.
One schedule defines every backup in the network.
Backups get a protected home plus one offline, custody-tracked copy.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 puts the Tier 0 rows of the schedule into effect.

lessons.title: Back up Tier 0: directory, CA, and policy
lessons.summary: The Tier 0 rows of the schedule: system state from both controllers, the issuing CA under ceremony-grade protection, and the whole Group Policy estate with its links — plus the quiet feature that handles the most common 'disaster' of all: the Recycle Bin for deleted directory objects.
objectives: Schedule system state and critical-volume backups on both domain controllers, and verify and catalog them.
Back up the issuing CA's database, key, and configuration under ceremony-grade protection.
Schedule the Group Policy backup with its link export.
Enable the Active Directory Recycle Bin for object-level recovery.
steps: In a Tier 0 session from AdminJumpBox01, schedule Windows Server Backup on SBD-DC01 and SBD-DC02, each to its own protected backup volume, with the system state and all critical volumes (wbadmin's -systemState and -allCritical): the system state is what a directory restore in DSRM needs, and the critical volumes let the same backup rebuild a controller whose hardware is gone. Two controllers, two independent backups — replication is availability and was never recovery, as course 1.1 put it.

After the first run, verify each backup's completion, record its version identifier in the backup catalog (C:\Evidence\recovery on AdminJumpBox01), and hash the catalog — an unverified backup is a hope with a timestamp.

Back up the issuing CA. Schedule SBD-SUBCA01's own system state and critical-volume backup to its protected volume, so the server can be rebuilt; then take the CA's own backup — database and private key — with certutil to E:\Backups\CA, with its registry configuration exported beside it, on the cadence the schedule sets and after every CA key renewal. It prompts for the password that protects the key, so it is a Tier 0 task, never an unattended one. Never write it to C:\Evidence: the private key is a secret, and secrets never go into evidence. Record custody and put only the hashes in evidence; SBD-ROOTCA01's ceremony backup is verified against its record, never duplicated or brought onto the network.

Schedule the Group Policy backup: a daily task on SBD-DC01, running as SYSTEM from a script folder only Tier 0 administrators can write, that runs Backup-GPO -All into a dated folder on E:\Backups\GPO and exports every link beside it — a restored GPO brings back its settings and permissions, not its links. That covers the whole estate, course 1.6's SBD Certificate Autoenrollment and course 1.8's tier logon GPOs included; the GPO reports and link exports courses 1.5 and 1.6 filed stay as their change records.

Enable the Active Directory Recycle Bin from the Tier 0 seat — a one-way, forest-level change run against the domain naming master (SBD-DC01) and recorded as the change it is — so a deleted user or OU comes back intact without touching system state. Objects deleted before it was enabled can come back only from a backup.

Write the restore decision tree: deleted object → Recycle Bin; corrupted DC on its own hardware → system state restore in DSRM (lesson 5's rehearsal); DC whose hardware is gone → full server (bare-metal) recovery from the critical-volumes backup; a damaged GPO → Restore-GPO from the dated set, then its links from the export; whole-forest loss → the Microsoft forest recovery guide, referenced and staged with the evidence rather than improvised on the day.
lessons.command:
# Tier 0 session from AdminJumpBox01: daily schedules on each controller and the issuing CA (E: is never a volume being backed up)
Invoke-Command SBD-DC01.sbd.test, SBD-DC02.sbd.test, SBD-SUBCA01.sbd.test { wbadmin enable backup -addtarget:E: -schedule:21:00 -systemState -allCritical -quiet }
Invoke-Command SBD-DC01.sbd.test, SBD-DC02.sbd.test { wbadmin get versions }   # after the first run
# On SBD-SUBCA01 (Tier 0 session): the CA's own backup, to its protected volume, never to the evidence folder
certutil -backup E:\Backups\CA   # prompts for the password that protects the exported key
reg export HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CertSvc\Configuration E:\Backups\CA\certsvc-config.reg
Get-ChildItem E:\Backups\CA -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv E:\Backups\ca-backup-hashes.csv -NoTypeInformation   # only this list goes to C:\Evidence\recovery
# On SBD-DC01: C:\Scripts\Backup-SbdGpo.ps1 (writable by Tier 0 administrators only) runs these lines, then the task runs it daily
#   $d = 'E:\Backups\GPO\{0:yyyy-MM-dd}' -f (Get-Date); New-Item -ItemType Directory $d -Force | Out-Null; Backup-GPO -All -Path $d
#   @('DC=sbd,DC=test') + (Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter *).DistinguishedName | ForEach-Object { (Get-GPInheritance -Target $_).GpoLinks } | Select-Object Target, Order, DisplayName, Enabled, Enforced | Export-Csv "$d\gpo-links.csv" -NoTypeInformation
Register-ScheduledTask 'SBD GPO backup' -Action (New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute powershell.exe -Argument '-NoProfile -File C:\Scripts\Backup-SbdGpo.ps1') -Trigger (New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Daily -At 22:00) -User 'NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM' -RunLevel Highest
# Back on AdminJumpBox01: the Recycle Bin, then the catalog
Enable-ADOptionalFeature 'Recycle Bin Feature' -Scope ForestOrConfigurationSet -Target sbd.test -Server SBD-DC01.sbd.test
Get-ADOptionalFeature -Filter {Name -like 'Recycle Bin*'} | Select-Object Name, EnabledScopes
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\recovery\backup-catalog.txt
lessons.check: Both DCs and SBD-SUBCA01 show scheduled, completed system state and critical-volume versions on their protected volumes; the CA backup and its configuration sit on SBD-SUBCA01's protected volume with key custody recorded and only hashes in evidence; the GPO task has written a dated set with its link export; the Recycle Bin reports an enabled scope; and the decision tree names the tool for each failure class.
lessons.evidence: Keep the backup schedules and version listings, the CA backup's hash list and custody record (never the backup itself), the GPO task definition and its first set's hashes, the hashed catalog, the Recycle Bin enablement record, and the restore decision tree.

quizzes.question: Both DCs replicate — why back up both?
answers: Replication copies mistakes as faithfully as data; independent backups are the history replication doesn't keep
Backups run faster in pairs
Only one actually holds the directory
quizzes.explanation: The course 1.1 teaching point, finally implemented: availability and recoverability are different capabilities with different tools.

quizzes.question: An administrator deletes an OU by mistake. First tool?
answers: Rebuild the forest
The Recycle Bin — object-level restore with attributes intact, no system state needed
Ask users to recreate their accounts
quizzes.explanation: The decision tree's first branch: match the restore to the loss. Most disasters are small, and the small tool is already enabled.

quizzes.question: Why does the CA key backup get ceremony-grade handling?
answers: A copied issuing key is the power to mint trusted certificates — the backup is as sensitive as the CA itself
Keys are large files
certutil requires it
quizzes.explanation: Backups inherit the sensitivity of what they contain. The course 1.6 custody discipline applies to every copy of key material, forever.

quizzes.question: Where does the issuing CA's backup go?
answers: Into C:\Evidence, so assessors can inspect it
Onto SBD-SUBCA01's protected backup volume, with only its hashes and the custody record in evidence
Onto pki.sbd.test, beside the CRLs
quizzes.explanation: The backup holds the CA's private key, and secrets never go into evidence. Evidence records that the backup exists and is intact: its hashes and its custody, not its contents.

quizzes.question: What makes a backup more than a hope?
answers: A long retention setting
Its file size
Verified completion, a recorded version, and a hashed catalog entry — and eventually a rehearsed restore
quizzes.explanation: The evidence standard applies to safety nets too: recorded, verifiable, and — in lesson 5 — actually exercised.

recap: Two independent system state schedules, verified and cataloged.
CA database, key, and configuration: backed up to the protected volume, custody recorded, only hashes in evidence.
Every GPO is backed up daily with its links beside it.
The Recycle Bin handles the everyday disaster in seconds; a decision tree matches each failure class to its tool.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 puts the member servers' rows into effect, VLAN 40 included.

lessons.title: Back up the member servers and records
lessons.summary: The rest of the schedule: SBD-DHCP01 and the inventory, SBD-REPO01 and SBD-SPLUNK01, and the business services — SBD-FS01's shares with their permissions, SBD-SQL01's databases with the logins they depend on, SBD-APPS01's and SBD-WEB01's configuration and certificates — then the log archive and the boundary's records, all in one hashed catalog.
objectives: Schedule the Tier 1 infrastructure backups — SBD-DHCP01, SBD-MGMT01, SBD-REPO01, SBD-SPLUNK01 — with the restore notes each needs.
Schedule the VLAN 40 backups so permissions, logins and certificates come back with the data.
Fold the log archive, the boundary records and the living records into the same catalog.
steps: In Tier 1 sessions from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, schedule SBD-DHCP01: a daily task, running as SYSTEM from a script folder only SBD Tier 1 Admins can write, takes Backup-DhcpServer into the default backup folder, copies it to a dated folder on E:\Backups\DHCP with an Export-DhcpServer of the configuration and leases, and hashes both. File course 1.7's restore note with it: after Restore-DhcpServer, set the DNS update credential again with Set-DhcpServerDnsCredential from the sealed record, because the backup doesn't carry it. On SBD-MGMT01, schedule Windows Server Backup of D:\Inventory (course 1.15) to its E:.

Schedule SBD-FS01: Windows Server Backup of D:\Shares to its E: every night. It keeps each file's NTFS permissions, and a file recovery restores them by default — never run it with -notRestoreAcl. Beside it, after every access change, save the readable record: icacls /save of the share tree's ACLs and an export of the share definitions (the LanmanServer Shares registry key, which also holds the share permissions), so permissions can be checked or reapplied without restoring data.

Schedule SBD-SQL01 inside the engine: a nightly SQL Server Agent job backs up each application database and the master, model and msdb system databases WITH CHECKSUM to E:\Backups\SQL, then checks each file with RESTORE VERIFYONLY. The engine writes the files as its gMSA, so grant SBD\SBD-SQL$ modify on that folder alone. master is where the logins live, msdb holds the Agent jobs, and the application databases' users map to the SBD\SBD-Apps$ login by its directory SID — so record the logins and each database's user mappings, and write the restore order: the instance and master (or the logins, recreated from the record) before the application databases. Use the simple recovery model unless your lesson 1 recovery point needs log backups, and a rebuilt SBD-SQL01 requests a new certificate through the course 1.6 process.

Schedule SBD-APPS01's Windows Server Backup with system state and critical volumes to its E:, so its services' configuration and its certificate, private key included, come back with the server — which is why the course 1.6 template never needs exportable keys. On SBD-WEB01, a root cron job in /etc/cron.d writes a dated tar archive of /etc/httpd, /etc/pki/tls (the certificate and its root-only key) and /etc/sssd, with SELinux contexts and ACLs, to /srv/backup with its SHA-256; SBD-REPO01 does the same for /srv/repo-records and the current snapshot each time it changes, so the previous one is already on media (course 1.9), and SBD-SPLUNK01 for /opt/splunk/etc (course 1.12 — the indexes are a working copy, and the record itself lives on SBD-AUDIT01). The WEB01 and Splunk archives hold keys, so they stay on protected media.

Account for the log archive: SBD-AUDIT01's hashed archives in D:\LogArchive and their catalog (D:\LogArchive\Catalog\catalog.csv) are themselves the record, so their backup is the audit custodian's offline copy on the schedule's cadence (lesson 4), and no job runs on that server.

Export the boundary and living records into the set: the service-path register, the exception record (C:\Evidence\exception-record.csv), this course's own sheets, and a read-only export of the core router's configuration taken with the router's own export function from AdminJumpBox01 — this course reads the router's configuration and changes nothing on it. Record every first run's hashes in C:\Evidence\recovery on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01. A recovered network without its records would pass no assessment.
lessons.command:
# Tier 1 sessions from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01. On SBD-DHCP01, the task script (C:\Scripts, writable by SBD Tier 1 Admins only):
$b = 'E:\Backups\DHCP\{0:yyyy-MM-dd}' -f (Get-Date); New-Item -ItemType Directory $b -Force | Out-Null; $dir = Join-Path $env:windir 'System32\dhcp\backup'
Backup-DhcpServer -Path $dir; Copy-Item $dir (Join-Path $b 'database') -Recurse; Export-DhcpServer -File (Join-Path $b 'SBD-DHCP01.xml') -Leases
# On SBD-MGMT01, SBD-FS01 and SBD-APPS01: one daily schedule each, to the local E:
wbadmin enable backup -addtarget:E: -include:D:\Inventory -schedule:22:00 -quiet   # SBD-MGMT01
wbadmin enable backup -addtarget:E: -include:D:\Shares -schedule:22:00 -quiet   # SBD-FS01; then, after each access change:
icacls D:\Shares\* /save E:\Backups\FS01\shares-acl.txt /t /c; reg export HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Shares E:\Backups\FS01\shares.reg /y
wbadmin enable backup -addtarget:E: -schedule:22:30 -systemState -allCritical -quiet   # SBD-APPS01
# On SBD-SQL01: the engine's identity may write the backup folder; the Agent job's step runs this T-SQL for each database
icacls E:\Backups\SQL /grant 'SBD\SBD-SQL$:(OI)(CI)M'
#   BACKUP DATABASE [master] TO DISK = N'E:\Backups\SQL\master.bak' WITH CHECKSUM, INIT;   -- then model, msdb, each application database
#   RESTORE VERIFYONLY FROM DISK = N'E:\Backups\SQL\master.bak' WITH CHECKSUM;
sqlcmd -S SBD-SQL01.sbd.test -E -Q "SELECT name, type_desc, sid FROM sys.server_principals WHERE type IN ('U','G','S')"   # the login record
# On SBD-WEB01 (and the same pattern on SBD-REPO01 and SBD-SPLUNK01): the cron job's work, run once by hand
sudo tar --selinux --acls --xattrs -czf /srv/backup/web01-$(date +%F).tar.gz /etc/httpd /etc/pki/tls /etc/sssd
sudo sha256sum /srv/backup/web01-*.tar.gz
lessons.check: Every member-server row in the schedule has run once and verified: SBD-DHCP01's set with its restore note, D:\Inventory, SBD-FS01's shares with the ACL record and share definitions, SBD-SQL01's application and system databases verified with RESTORE VERIFYONLY and the login record filed, SBD-APPS01's full-server backup, and the dated archives on SBD-WEB01, SBD-REPO01 and SBD-SPLUNK01 — and the catalog covers them with the log archive, router export, and living records.
lessons.evidence: Keep the task, job and cron definitions, each first run's hashes, the DHCP and SQL restore notes, the ACL record and share export hashes, the login record, and the complete recovery catalog — never the WEB01 or Splunk archives themselves, which hold keys.

quizzes.question: SBD-SQL01's application database is backed up nightly, but master isn't. What breaks on a rebuilt instance?
answers: Nothing: everything lives in the application database
The logins live in master, so the restored database's users have no login to map to until master is restored or the logins are recreated from the record
The database restores read-only
quizzes.explanation: Microsoft lists master, model and msdb as system databases you must always back up. master records the logins; without it or a login record, the application data comes back unreachable.

quizzes.question: SBD-FS01's Projects folder is restored from Windows Server Backup. What happens to its permissions?
answers: They come back with the files, because file recovery restores ACLs unless -notRestoreAcl is used
They are always reset to the parent folder's
They have to be granted again by hand
quizzes.explanation: Windows Server Backup restores each file's security ACLs by default. The icacls record and share export let you check or reapply them without restoring data.

quizzes.question: Why do the register, inventory, and exception record join the backup set?
answers: They are the largest files
A restored network without its records has lost its assessable story — the evidence must survive what it evidences
Backups require ten items minimum
quizzes.explanation: This path's real product is a defensible record. Recovery that saves the machines and loses the story saves the wrong half.

quizzes.question: Why does SBD-WEB01's nightly archive stay on protected media, out of the evidence?
answers: Archives are too large for evidence
It holds the web server's private key in /etc/pki/tls, and secrets never go into evidence
Linux files can't be hashed
quizzes.explanation: Backups inherit the sensitivity of what they contain. Evidence records the archive's hash and custody; the archive itself is handled like the key it carries.

recap: SBD-DHCP01, the inventory, the repository and Splunk's configuration each run on schedule, with their restore notes.
The business services come back whole: shares with their permissions, databases with their logins, applications with their certificates.
The log archive, the boundary's records and the living records join one hashed catalog.
Every backup in the network is now defined and scheduled in this course.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 moves the copies to the offline cabinet, by hand and on record.

lessons.title: Carry the copies to the offline cabinet
lessons.summary: A backup that sits on the server it protects fails with it. Move a copy of each backup to the offline cabinet by hand, under the same custody rules as any media crossing a boundary, and keep the custody record that proves it.
objectives: Define which custodian carries which backup, by tier.
Transfer the copies to offline media with hashes and custody records.
Prove a copy can be found, verified, and returned for a restore.
steps: Assign custodians by tier: a Tier 0 custodian handles the controllers' system state, the issuing CA's database and key backup, the Group Policy set, and the router configuration export; the audit custodian (SBD Audit Custodians, course 1.8) handles the log archive and its catalog from SBD-AUDIT01; a Tier 1 server custodian handles the member-server sets — SBD-DHCP01, SBD-REPO01, SBD-SPLUNK01, SBD-MGMT01, and the VLAN 40 servers SBD-FS01, SBD-SQL01, SBD-APPS01 and SBD-WEB01. No one carries a tier they do not hold.

On the cadence the backup schedule sets, for each copy, write the media ID, hash the backup on its protected volume, copy it to encrypted removable media, and verify the hash on the media before it leaves the room. Keep Windows Server Backup's WindowsImageBackup folder layout on the media so wbadmin can read it there.

Carry the media to the offline backup cabinet and record the handoff in the custody register: who, what, when, the hashes, and the storage slot. This is the course 1.4 media procedure used for backups.
Pull one copy back as a test: find it from the register, verify its hash, and confirm it is readable. Lesson 5's rehearsal restores from a copy that has made this round trip.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-DC02 (Tier 0), with encrypted media MEDIA-0012 attached as F:: hash on the volume, copy, hash on the media
Get-ChildItem E:\WindowsImageBackup\SBD-DC02 -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv F:\MEDIA-0012-volume.csv -NoTypeInformation
Copy-Item E:\WindowsImageBackup -Destination F:\ -Recurse
Get-ChildItem F:\WindowsImageBackup\SBD-DC02 -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv F:\MEDIA-0012-media.csv -NoTypeInformation
Compare-Object (Import-Csv F:\MEDIA-0012-volume.csv).Hash (Import-Csv F:\MEDIA-0012-media.csv).Hash   # no output means the copy matches
wbadmin get versions -backupTarget:F: -machine:SBD-DC02   # the media is readable as a backup
lessons.check: Every item in the recovery set has an offline copy with matching hashes on the volume and the media, a custody entry with a named custodian of the right tier, and one copy has been retrieved and verified.
lessons.evidence: Keep the custodian assignments, the hash pairs (copied into C:\Evidence\recovery on the tier's seat), the custody register entries, and the retrieval test record.

model.label: Offline backup & recovery
model.text: The offline cabinet has no network path. Copies arrive only by custodian under the media procedure.

quizzes.question: Who carries the domain controllers' system-state backup to the cabinet?
answers: Any server operator who is free
A Tier 0 custodian
The help desk
quizzes.explanation: A DC backup holds the directory's secrets. Whoever can handle it can rebuild or read the domain, so it stays with Tier 0.

quizzes.question: Why is there no network path to the offline backup cabinet?
answers: So ransomware or an intruder on the network cannot reach or encrypt the copies
Because backups are too large to send
Because NIST forbids network backups
quizzes.explanation: An offline copy survives an attack that takes the whole network. The custody record replaces the network path as the proof of what happened.

quizzes.question: The hash on the media does not match the hash on the volume. What do you do?
answers: Store it anyway and note it
Delete the original
Do not store it; recopy and investigate, because the copy is not trustworthy
quizzes.explanation: A mismatch means the copy is not the backup you verified. Storing it would put an untrusted copy where you will look on the worst day.

recap: Custodians carry only the backups their tier allows.
Every copy has matching hashes and a custody entry.
A copy has been retrieved and verified before anyone needs it.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 stops trusting the backups and tests one.

lessons.title: Rehearse a real restore, in isolation
lessons.summary: One restore, actually performed: a domain controller's system state brought back on the isolated segment, timed against the objective, verified against the directory — plus the small restore everyone will someday need, from the Recycle Bin.
objectives: Restore a DC's system state in Directory Services Restore Mode on the isolated recovery segment.
Measure the restore against the time objective and verify directory health.
Perform and record an object-level Recycle Bin restore.
steps: Stage the rehearsal: the isolated recovery segment has no path to the production VLANs — a restored controller believing it is authoritative must never meet the live directory; that isolation rule is written before the restore starts. Turn the hypervisor's time synchronization off on the rehearsal copy, as for every virtual machine in the path.

Restore SBD-DC02 from the offline copy retrieved in lesson 4, timing the work from decision to directory services running against the lesson 1 objective. A system state restore needs the same server instance, so use a copy of SBD-DC02's virtual machine attached only to the isolated segment, start it in DSRM (bcdedit /set safeboot dsrepair, restart, sign in with the DSRM password), and run wbadmin start systemstaterecovery with -authsysvol: the copy is the only controller in its isolated world, so its SYSVOL must be authoritative or SYSVOL and NETLOGON never come up. Restoring to different hardware needs a full server (bare-metal) recovery from the critical-volumes backup instead.

Remove the DSRM boot setting (bcdedit /deletevalue safeboot), restart normally, and verify the restored directory the course 1.1 way — services, the SYSVOL and NETLOGON shares, a directory query. Then check the clock: the copy comes back with the time it was saved with, and with no SBD-DC01 to follow nothing corrects it, so compare it with the reference and record the offset; a restored SBD-DC01 in production is checked against the reference before any member follows it (course 1.3). Record what the rehearsal taught — surprises, the measured time, decision-tree updates — then tear the rehearsal down completely.

Back in production, from AdminJumpBox01, run the everyday restore: delete a disposable test object, bring it back from the Recycle Bin with attributes intact, and file both rehearsals — the big one and the small one — as the tested-recovery evidence.
lessons.command:
# On the isolated copy of SBD-DC02: start in DSRM, then sign in with the DSRM password.
bcdedit /set safeboot dsrepair
shutdown /r /t 0
wbadmin get versions -backupTarget:F: -machine:SBD-DC02   # F: = the retrieved media
wbadmin start systemstaterecovery -version:<version-id> -backupTarget:F: -machine:SBD-DC02 -authsysvol
bcdedit /deletevalue safeboot   # then restart normally
# After the restart, on the restored copy
Get-Service NTDS, DNS, Netlogon, DFSR | Select-Object Name, Status
Get-SmbShare -Name SYSVOL, NETLOGON
Get-ADDomain -Server localhost | Select-Object DNSRoot, PDCEmulator
w32tm /query /status   # then compare Get-Date with the reference clock and record the offset
# Back in production, from AdminJumpBox01: the Recycle Bin rehearsal
Get-ADObject -Filter "Name -eq '<test object name>'" -IncludeDeletedObjects | Restore-ADObject
lessons.check: The isolated restore ran in DSRM and reached a healthy directory within (or honestly against) the time objective, its clock offset is recorded, the DSRM boot setting is removed, the teardown is confirmed, and the production object restore returned the test object intact.
lessons.evidence: Keep the timed rehearsal log with its verification output and clock reading, the lessons-learned and decision-tree updates, the teardown confirmation, and the object-restore record.

quizzes.question: Why must the rehearsal segment be isolated from production?
answers: To make the restore faster
A restored controller carries old directory state — meeting the live forest would inject the past into the present
Isolation is optional for labs
quizzes.explanation: The rehearsal's first rule protects production from the rehearsal. Old authoritative state on a live network is its own disaster.

quizzes.question: The restore took longer than the objective. What now?
answers: Hide the timing
Declare the objective met anyway
Record the honest number and either fix the process or revise the objective — both are legitimate; silence is not
quizzes.explanation: The rehearsal exists to replace belief with measurement. Either outcome — better process or truer objective — improves the real bad day.

quizzes.question: Why rehearse the Recycle Bin restore too?
answers: The most likely recovery event deserves the same tested-and-recorded treatment as the rare one
It is required before system state restores
Deleted objects expire daily
quizzes.explanation: Recovery evidence should match recovery reality: object-level loss is the common case, so its tool gets proven, not presumed.

quizzes.question: Your recovery host is new hardware. Which restore applies?
answers: A system state restore, exactly as on the original server
A full server (bare-metal) recovery from the critical-volumes backup — system state restores are for the same server instance
Copying NTDS.dit across by hand
quizzes.explanation: Microsoft's forest recovery guidance calls for a full server recovery when you restore to different hardware or a different operating system instance. A system state restore runs on the original instance, in DSRM.

recap: One real restore, isolated, timed, verified, and torn down.
The measured number replaced the hoped-for one.
The everyday restore is proven alongside the dramatic one.
lessons.next: The final lesson files the recovery record and closes the Build path.

lessons.title: File the recovery record and close the path
lessons.summary: The Build path ends the way it worked: owners, schedules, and evidence. The recovery record joins the living documents, the closing SCAP results snapshot the finished network, and the Body of Evidence is ready for the authorization courses to assemble.
objectives: Assemble the tested-recovery record with owners and review dates.
Take the closing SCAP snapshot across the finished network.
Hand the complete evidence set to the authorization path.
steps: Assemble the recovery record: the requirements and objectives, the backup schedule and catalog, both rehearsal results with the measured times, the decision tree, the DHCP and SQL restore notes, and a named owner with a scheduled next rehearsal that rotates through the set — an SBD-FS01 folder restored with its permissions, an SBD-SQL01 database with its logins, SBD-DHCP01 with its credential step — recovery is a practice with a calendar, not a binder. Keep its Tier 0 half in C:\Evidence\recovery on AdminJumpBox01 and its Tier 1 half on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, each sealed with a manifest.

Take the closing snapshot: current Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) results for every system on the course 1.5 cadence, each tier from its own seat — Tier 0 from AdminJumpBox01, the Windows and Linux member servers from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, the fleet from SBD-ADMIN-PC01 — with the recorded benchmark versions, triaged as always: the dated 'as-authorized' picture path 2 will reference. Credentialed vulnerability scanning joins it when course 1.17 (coming soon) arrives.

Reconcile the three living records one final time — the inventory on SBD-MGMT01 against the directory, DHCP leases, and WSUS rings (the course 1.15 method), the register against observed behavior, and the exception record against open findings — so the authorization path inherits agreement, not archaeology.

Write the Build path's closing note: what exists, where every record lives, and what is intentionally open — then start course 2.1, where this network stops being a project and becomes a system seeking authorization.
lessons.command:
# On AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0), then the same on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (Tier 1): seal each half of the recovery record
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence -Directory | Select-Object Name
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\recovery -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\recovery-manifest.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\recovery-manifest.csv
lessons.check: The recovery record is complete with an owner and next-rehearsal date and sealed on both seats, the closing SCAP snapshot is filed with triage, and all three living records reconcile cleanly into the handoff note.
lessons.evidence: Finish the checklist: the recovery record and its two manifests, the closing SCAP snapshot, the three reconciliations, and the Build path's closing note.

quizzes.question: What makes recovery 'a practice with a calendar'?
answers: A named owner and a scheduled next rehearsal — the test repeats as the network changes
Laminating the decision tree
Buying more storage
quizzes.explanation: One rehearsal proves today's backups. The schedule is what keeps tomorrow's honest.

quizzes.question: Why take a closing SCAP snapshot at path's end?
answers: Scanners need exercise
It is the dated security picture the authorization decision will actually be about
To fill the evidence folder
quizzes.explanation: Path 2's assessors and the authorizing official evaluate a system at a moment. The snapshot is that moment, captured.

quizzes.question: What does path 2 inherit from the Build path?
answers: Just the virtual machines
A to-do list
A reconciled, evidenced system: inventory, register, exceptions, scans, scheduled backups, and tested recovery — the Body of Evidence, already real
quizzes.explanation: The authorization path was never going to invent evidence; it organizes what the Build path produced on purpose, course by course.

recap: Recovery has an owner, a date, and a measured track record.
The closing snapshot freezes the as-authorized picture.
The Body of Evidence exists — path 2 assembles, it doesn't excavate.
lessons.next: That completes the Build the Network path. Continue with course 2.1 to carry this network — and its evidence — through the Risk Management Framework to an authorization decision.
